events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description:
The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.
Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.
The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.
Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.
Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.
Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | De y para el pueblo / By and for the People: Revolutionary Mexican Prints
events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description:
At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.
The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.description:
Worth Ryder Art Gallery and the VIDRINE present four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light's BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels.
Featured Artworks: Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner — AnointedMichael Light — BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023Michael Pinsky — MammothDavid Buckland Bikini TextsAbout Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley (http://ourlifeishere.org)
In 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with Marshallese youth and elders. This expedition—organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, with support from Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell—was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. Throughout 2026–27, the project runs across campus in exhibitions at Doe Library, Giannini Hall, Memorial Glade, Worth Ryder, and BAMPFA, along with courses and public programs. It culminates in an exhibition of original works at the David Brower Center, September 2027 – February 2028. ourlifeishere.org (https://art.berkeley.edu/ourlifeishere.org)
About Worth Ryder Art Gallery / VIDRINE (https://art.berkeley.edu/gallery)
The Worth Ryder Art Gallery (WRAG) is an educational art space that has served as a cultural and artistic resource and community center for undergraduate and graduate students, faculty, alumni, and the Bay Area community since 1960, and is a central social and artistic hub of the UC Berkeley Department of Art Practice. The gallery supports students in exhibiting their artwork in a professional gallery context, serves as an exhibition platform for emerging contemporary artistic strategies, and brings challenging and thought-provoking artwork to the UC Berkeley campus. It is named after painter and founding chair of the department, Worth Ryder. VIDRINE is Worth Ryder Art Gallery's ancillary space showcasing video, digital art, and installation. It is located around the corner from the Worth Ryder Art Gallery in the lobby of the Anthropology and Art Building.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: A computable wandering and tracelike vector for modular orbits in the Bergman space
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote online talk
events.description: Speaker: Luis Daniel Abreu, University of ViennaWe construct a function Φ such that the orbit under the representation of $\Gamma = PSL(2,Z)$ is an orthonormal basis for the Bergman space with weight $q=12$. Moreover, we show that Φ is effectively computable as a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane (in the precise sense of computable analysis), by providing an effective procedure. This constructs a wandering and tracelike vector for $PSL(2,Z)$, whose abstract existence was proved by Sir Vaughan Jones in his last paper, where the corresponding construction was left as a problem. The construction of the function, which can also be represented as an orthonormal wavelet in the half-line, reproduces the method used in the signal approximation practice: the off-diagonal decay of the Gramian operator allows to control its restriction to nested finite subsets of $PSL(2,Z)$, where it becomes a finite matrix and can be inverted, leading to a convergent sum where all objects and bounds are computable in the cyclotomic field generated by the 12th-root of unity over the rationals. Since modular actions on the Bergman kernel enter the construction, Φ displays Bergman and modular reminescences, despite appearing to be modular itself. As suggested by Jones, it provides a computable implementing vector for th abstract anti-isomorphism between the von Neumann algebra $M_{12} (\Gamma )$and its commutant. With minor adaptations, the construction works for any cocompact Fuchsian group, but the more involved proof of computability is only executed for $PSL(2,Z)$.

events.title: IES Rapid Response | Student Protests in France
events.description:
Hundreds of thousands of people have engaged in protest across France since mid September. The movement started with high school students dissatisfied with overcrowded, decrepit classrooms, missing teachers, and an opaque university placement system that seemed to work against the disadvantaged. Parents, teachers, labor unions, and members of local government have joined the high school students. The backdrop for these protests is a program of economic liberalization pursued by French president Emmanuel Macron since 2017 that combined tax cuts with reduced spending on public services including education. Join us for a rapid response lecture by expert in French politics and economic liberalization, Professor Jonah Levy, for a deep dive into the issues animating the student protests in France and the implications of these protests for the French economy and society as well as for far-right and far-left parties in the upcoming 2027 elections. Professor Jonah D. Levy teaches courses in the areas of comparative political economy, welfare policy, French and West European politics, and the politics of dystopian novels. In 2023, Levy published Contested Liberalization: Historical Legacies and Contemporary Conflict in France (Cambridge University Press, 2023), which describes and analyzes the contentious politics surrounding economic liberalization in France. In 2025, Levy published Rethinking Economic Liberalization (Edward Elgar), which traces progressive opportunities within liberalizing reforms. Levy has received a Phi Beta Kappa award for excellence in teaching and been selected as the UC Berkeley, Undergraduate Political Science Association Professor of the Year.
Photo Credit: The Wallstreet Journal, https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/france-offers-concessions-to-quell-student-protests-2e164758 (https://www.wsj.com/world/europe/france-offers-concessions-to-quell-student-protests-2e164758)

events.title: Life Course and Developmental Ecosystem Lenses For Human Thriving and Health: Why Now, More than Ever?
events.description:
The Institute of Human Development (IHD) is the birthplace of life course theory. This session will explore how life course frameworks for human development have evolved and how they are applied to a range of health and educational challenges. We will consider how a developmental ecosystem perspective can help us understand troubling trends in child health, morbidity, and mortality while broadening our understanding of the relationships and conditions that generate early relational health and healthy development. We invite participants to consider how life course and developmental ecosystem frameworks might inform and enliven their own research, practice, and interests.
Speakers:Neal Halfon, MD, Founding Director of the UCLA Center for Healthier Children, Families and Communities Emily Ozer, PhD, Director of the Institute of Human Development (IHD) and Professor of Public Health Moderator: Dean Michael Lu, MD, UC Berkeley School of Public HealthRSVP (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSePT0lScr3JhzGE-pKVWhsFLW2oAjrBD6sKCiREYO5e59lvWQ/viewform) For more information, please see: https://ihd.berkeley.edu/fall-2026-colloquium-series (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://ihd.berkeley.edu/fall-2026-colloquium-series&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1787080597707872&usg=AOvVaw04YjoBvi1rdt5nQNY9hmyI)

events.title: TAC Seminar - Leon Chan (Colorado)
events.description:
Title: Understanding (some) Black-hole Driven Transients with Numerical ModellingAbstract: The coming decade will be a golden era for timedomain astronomy, and transients will become a central focus of interest. Modelling transients is challenging because they span orders of magnitude in spatiotemporal scales and involve complex physics interactions. I will discuss my efforts to understand some blackhole (BH)driven transients through numerical modelling. I will first show an unexpected result of relativistic tidal disruption events (TDEs), in which the stellar pericenter approaches the BH's event horizon. I find that newly returning debris experience weaker relativistic effects than they should, slowing down the diskformation process, which takes 10-20 fallback times . The returning debris remains eccentric and mechanically supported at , with only about 1% of the fallback mass being accreted by the BH. Shocks, rather than accretion stress, power the event. This might suggest that TDE disk formation is slow regardless of the strength of apsidal precession. I will then present highresolution simulations of collapsars as a model for long gammaray bursts (LGRBs). I find that an accretiondisk dynamo operates and can convert toroidal magnetic fields into largescale, strong, coherent poloidal loops to power relativistic jets, with the jet power being comparable to that inferred for LGRBs. The jet morphology is highly variable and misaligned with the BH spin, and the stochastic dynamo can generate poloidal loops of alternating polarity, resulting in striped jets that might lead to magnetic dissipation. This might explain the origin of the largescale magnetic field required to power jets in collapsars.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Harold Hwang: Superconductivity in layered nickelates
events.description:
Superconductivity in layered nickelates Unconventional superconductivity in proximity to various strongly correlated phases has been a recurring theme in materials as diverse as heavy fermion compounds, cuprates, pnictides, and twisted bilayer graphene. Here we will discuss a growing family of layered nickelate superconductors. The initial discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates was motivated by looking for an electronic analog of the cuprates. Notable aspects are a doping-dependent superconducting dome, strong magnetic fluctuations, and a landscape of unusual normal state properties from which superconductivity emerges. The subsequent discovery of superconductivity in bulk La3Ni2O7 under high pressure is quite intriguing, in that the d-electron configuration is a priori quite different. Recently, we have used epitaxial strain in (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films to stabilize superconductivity at ambient pressure, which has enabled their extend experimental study and development.
Speaker Bio: Harold Y. Hwang is the Shadi and Omid Farokhzad Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, of Applied Physics (Stanford University), of Photon Science (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), Senior Fellow of the Precourt Institute for Energy, and Director of the Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. He received a BS in Physics, BS and MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT (1993), and a PhD in Physics from Princeton University (1997). He was formerly a Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories (1996-2003) and on the faculty at the University of Tokyo (2003-2010). His research is in condensed matter and materials physics, with a focus on correlated electrons and emergent phenomena in quantum materials, and heterostructures for energy applications and devices. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and member of the National Academy of Sciences. Recognitions include the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award (2005), the IBM Japan Science Prize (Physics, 2008), the Ho-Am Prize (Science, 2013), the Europhysics Prize (2014, with Jochen Mannhart and Jean-Marc Triscone), and the McGroddy Prize (2024).

events.title: Path-Dependent Ergodic Optimal Control and Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (Nizar Touzi, NYU)
events.description: Title: Path-Dependent Ergodic Optimal Control and Backward Stochastic Differential Equations Abstract: We investigate a new class of infinite-horizon backward stochastic differential equations for ergodic optimal control where the cost and state dynamics are time and path-dependent. The state process is defined on an unbounded underlying domain and satisfies an extended dissipativity condition. In contrast with the time-homogeneous Markovian setting, the optimal ergodic cost in our framework is characterized by the asymptotic behavior of a deterministic function, rather than by a single real constant. We obtain well-posedness, verification and stability properties, which extend the previous results in the literature on the Markov case. Bio: Nizar Touzi is a Professor at New York University, Chair of the Department of Finance and Risk Engineering at the Tandon School of Engineering. He has been an invited session speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians (Hyderabad 2010). He received the Louis Bachelier Natixis prize of the French Academy of Sciences in 2012, the Paris Europlace prize of Best Young Researcher in Finance in 2007, and he was awarded an Advanced ERC grant 2012-2017. He is co-editor and associate editor in various international journals in the fields of financial mathematics, applied probability, and control theory.

events.title: Seminar 271, Development: Samuel Bazzi - "Authority Figures and the Polarization of Gender Norms"
events.description: Abstract: This paper examines how authority figures in higher education shape gender norms over the long run. We exploit the random assignment of first-year students to faculty advisors at an elite university in the Middle East and combine administrative records with an alumni survey measuring gender attitudes up to 24 years later. Women assigned to female advisors adopt more egalitarian views about politics and work, while men move in a more conservative direction. Polarization is strongest in male-dominated STEM fields, where female authority is especially counter-stereotypical, and among more religious students. A simple framework combining belief updating and identity-based status threat helps explain these patterns of female empowerment and male backlash. We identify a distinct role for authority in transmitting gender norms: randomized exposure to high-achieving female peers has little effect, while the largest impacts come from high-value-added and more senior female advisors. Overall, our findings reveal a progress paradox whereby increased female representation in positions of authority can empower women while provoking backlash among men, thereby deepening gender polarization.

events.title: Robert Saxton (Chemistry/MCB Seminar): "Decoding the Molecular Logic of Tissue-Intrinsic Inflammatory Signaling"
events.description: Inflammation is regulated not only by immune cells, but also by receptor signaling circuits within tissues themselves. Epithelial and stromal cells produce cytokines that act locally on neighboring cells or feed back on the producing cells to regulate tissue responses to injury and inflammation. However, the molecular mechanisms governing these tissue-intrinsic signaling pathways, and their role in chronic inflammatory disease, remain poorly understood. In this talk, I will discuss our work on two epithelial cytokines, IL-24 and IL-17C. Combining structural biology, protein engineering, and mouse models, we are investigating how these cytokines engage their receptors to regulate tissue inflammation, as well as how this knowledge can guide the development of new therapeutics for chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics (Joint with Theory): David Dillenberger "Pure Risk"
events.description: Abstract: We introduce a behavioral notion of domain-specific risk aversion that separates attitudes toward risk from deterministic utility: an agent is more pure risk averse in one domain than in another if, for prizes that are indifferent under certainty, he is more averse to risk in the former domain than in the latter. We develop a model that goes beyond expected utility by allowing risk attitudes to vary across domains, while preserving expected utility within each domain. The domains are subjective and need not be specified in advance; they are identified from choice behavior. We establish uniqueness of the model's parameters and provide an axiomatic characterization. Paper Link: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7342358 (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id%3D7342358&source=gmail-imap&ust=1791993757000000&usg=AOvVaw2PzujPEXNQFPUv9FYn_2Be)

events.title: Analysis and PDE Seminar: Many Body Asymptotics for the Toda Lattice
events.description: Speaker: Amol Aggarwal, StanfordThe Toda lattice prescribes the evolution of many particles interacting under certain Hamiltonian dynamics; it is an archetypal example of a completely integrable system. In this talk we describe several results providing the long-time asymptotics of this system, under random, dense initial data. The proofs proceed by finding a way to interpret the Toda lattice as a collection of "quasi-particles" that behave similarly to solitons, and providing a framework to study how these quasi-particles asymptotically evolve in time. The arguments use ideas from random matrix theory, particularly the analysis localization phenomena for eigenvectors of random tridiagonal matrices.

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Wallace Marshall: Learning without a brain — how a single cell processes information
events.description:
Learning without a brain –– how a single cell processes information Cells show a range of complex behaviors which might normally associated with cognition, including basic forms of learning such as habituation. The giant single-celled ciliate Stentor coeruleus is a pond-dwelling organism that attaches to substrates like pond plants and filter feeds by means of a ring of cilia at one end of the cell. Stentor cells can contract in response to mechanical stimulation, an effective escape mechanism but energetically costly. To avoid contracting due to random collision with non-threatening things like algae or pond plants, but still allow contraction when a large predator attacks, Stentor cells use a simple form of learning: when a cell is mechanically stimulated over and over again, it will gradually stop responding, representing a case of habituation. Our goal is to understand how a single cell learns, without a nervous system. We have developed automated devices for applying series of mechanical stimuli under computer control, which we are now using to test predictions of computational models for learning based on known or plausible biochemical mechanisms. Using this approach we have formulated a simplified biochemical model invoking known or suspected processes, which can account for all prior observations as well as new experiments designed to test the model. Based on this framework, we have investigated the molecular pathways involved in learning in Stentor, which suggests a role for CamKII kinase signaling in the learning process. Currently we are using a frequency domain analysis to probe the learning process, and find that the cell acts like a low pass filter with a fractional order transfer function, which provides us with a new way to discriminate among potential learning mechanisms.
Speaker Bio: Wallace Marshall is Professor of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California San Francisco. A native Long‐Islander, he received his bachelor's degrees in Electrical Engineering and Biochemistry from the State University of New York at Stony Brook, and his Ph.D. in Biochemistry from UC San Francisco, where he studied organization of chromosomes within the nucleus with John Sedat. He then moved to Yale University for postdoctoral studies with Joel Rosenbaum, where he became interested in questions of organelle size control and cell organization, using cilia, flagella, and centrioles as model systems. In 2003, he joined the faculty at UCSF where he continues to study questions of cellular organization in a variety of model organisms including green algae, yeast, ciliates, and mammalian cells. In recent years, his research program has expanded to include cellular engineering and the study of learning and computation in single cells. Dr. Marshall is an elected Fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology, former co‐director of the Physiology summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and he currently is Director of the Center for Cellular Construction, an NSF Science and Technology Center (STC) devoted to engineering cells and tissues.

events.title: Sunrise Lecture by Leif Weatherby: "Has Reason Finally Actually Lost Its Mind?"
events.description: As the Cold War ended, a prominent group of scholars told the story of how reason had "almost lost its mind" in the excesses of Game Theory and optimization. According to that story, the episode was bizarre and dangerous, but had more or less dissipated along with the Soviet Republics. The idea of a quantitative rationality, an automatic basis for executing social judgments, had splintered into various disciplines and quieted down. We know today that this is not what happened. Out-of-control Bayesians and other so-called "rationalists" are in control of technology, markets, and even policymaking, writing what amounts to science fiction about a reason far more literally automated - superceding the human mind - than any rational choice or decision theorist could have dreamed. The ideology of perfectly automated reasoning now also has "evidence" in the form of AI models that scour the written record for solutions to mathematical conjectures and clever ways to commit random cybercrimes. This talk argues that reason was never in possession of the type of mind implied by the earlier, triumphalist stories of the historians of science, and turns to the philosophy of culture that traces from German Idealism to the present to recast the problem of reason in the age of AI. Leif Weatherby is the director of the Digital Theory Lab and Professor of German at New York University. He writes about systems of representation, especially computation and language, especially in their cultural aspects. His book, Language Machines, about AI and literary theory, appeared in 2025. He is currently a fellow of the Ideas Workshop of the Open Society Foundations working on a new book titled The Mismeasure of Mind: Against the Prediction of Everything. There is a workshop that goes with this lecture on November 10th, 10 am. Sign up here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScrZwzVwX9zV5RIxmih3fINUcClvefUOyZdND9gvs3vjz07oQ/viewform).

events.title: The Bomb in/and/out of the Archive. feat. Zoé Samudzi
events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture with Zoé Samudzi Postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at Ohio State University - Monday, November 9, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeykJAzTsXRPcjwOetCQvBjTYgUR_hNZbyFZzKTNKnwucsB-Q/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MHRhNmwwNmJwZGxrMGFvZjlkZ3M5MG1xc2IgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Begun during her 2026 residency at La Becque in Switzerland, Zoé Samudzi presents the inaugural project of the research constellation "Can the African Steal?" Through archival photographs of the Belgian Congo (c. 1929-30) at Photo Elysée in Lausanne, Samudzi stitches together a variegated visual forensic through image absence through the deployment of the black planetary (after Canham and Seedat) as an onto-epistemic and transnational geographic frame. The negative spaces in the Swiss archive enable a positively articulated materiality of the atomic bomb. Her tracing of uranium extraction and/as warcraft conjoins King Leopold's free state and the Katangese mines in the Belgian Congo, the Trinity test in Los Alamos and Operation Crossroads in the Marshall Islands, and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and nuclear afterlives in Japan. About Zoé Samudzi Zoé Samudzi is a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at The Ohio State University. She holds a PhD in Medical Sociology from the University of California, San Francisco. Her research contends with genocide memory and the multiplicity of denialisms, political mythologies of the postcolonial African state, visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing and witnessing, and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. An art critic and writer, Samudzi is an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine, a popular magazine dedicated to psychoanalytic thinking. She is a 2026 Public Parking editorial resident, a 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom," a 2026 resident at La Becque's Principal Residency Program, and an awardee of the 2026 Fire Station Studios' International Curator Residency.

events.title: POSTPONED, New Date TBD: One In A Million: film screening and Q&A
events.description: Join us for a screening of Frontline's new award-winning documentary One in a Million. Filmed over 10 years, it follows Israa's epic journey from Syria to Germany and back again. She and her family navigate war, exile, and heartbreak in a foreign land, revealing the complexities of the refugee experience. After the film, producer and Frontline Editor-In-Chief Raney Aronson-Rath will discuss the film and take questions. Snacks will be available before the screening in the lobby. RSVP HERE (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeWjaO2EXvnExACSuCMOGInO8-TQ4f1rSaYPWarYbBSZu61cg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). In September 2015, filmmakers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes met Israa, an 11-year-old Syrian girl selling cigarettes on a street corner in Turkey, alongside her father, Tarek. The family had fled Aleppo to join the largest movement of people since the Second World War. Together they trekked through Eastern Europe before finding refuge in Germany, where more than one million asylum seekers were registered by the end of that year. For ten years, the filmmakers continued to document Israa's life as the challenges of integration and cultural adjustment led to family breakdown as Western culture clashed with Syrian traditions. Following the fall of the Assad regime in 2025, the film culminates when the filmmakers follow Israa, now a mother herself, back to the ruins of Aleppo as she confronts her own questions of identity and belonging. The film is a Sundance Winner for both the 'Audience Award: World Cinema Documentary' and the 'World Cinema Documentary Directing Award'.

events.title: Yes Duffy: Who Gave You Permission? | Arcus Social Justice Corps Lecture
events.description:
An Activist Architect on Designing Good TroubleWho Gave You Permission? traces a journey from graffiti artist to architect and civic changemaker. From designing treehouses to transit-oriented housing to farmworker land trusts, it explores how designing for social impact can challenge exclusion and shift power through creative collaboration, unexpected common ground, and a willingness to redesign the rules, not just the buildings. The talk also reflects on the uncertainty, setbacks, and compromises involved in sustaining a social-justice practice. It invites emerging designers to trust their lived experience and see how their unique passion, perseverance, and creativity can design more inclusive cities, and the systems that shape them.
Yes Duffy is an architect, activist, graffiti writer, skateboarder, and founder of YES Community Architects (YCA) (https://www.yescommunityarchitects.com/), a Bay Area–based architectural practice dedicated to designing systems of inclusion that focus on housing, community, and social justice. Moving fluidly between street culture, architecture, community organizing, and public policy, Yes challenges the systems that determine who gets to belong, build wealth, and shape the places they call home. Grounded in the belief that great design belongs to everyone, YCA seeks to redistribute creative power, opportunity, and agency toward systematically marginalized communities. Yes holds a Master of Architecture and a Master of City Planning from UC Berkeley and previously served as chair of Berkeley's Zoning Adjustments Board. YCA's work and Yes's academic contributions have received numerous honors from the AIA, APA, ASLA, and UC Berkeley.

events.description: Speaker: Audrey Rosevear, UC BerkeleyI'll discuss 2-dimensional foliations on 3-manifolds with the property that every transverse flow has a closed orbit. Say that such a foliation forces closed orbits. I'll classify $C^2$ finite depth foliations on atoroidal 3-manifolds which force closed orbits, and show that the forcing property is unstable for many foliations. Varoquaux will give a 30-minute talk, introduced by Fernando Pérez (https://bids.berkeley.edu/people/fernando-perez) (BIDS Faculty Director), followed by a panel discussion on AI in open source and open science (https://blog.probabl.ai/maintaining-open-source-age-of-gen-ai) with Varoquaux, Pérez, and moderator Jarrod Millman (https://bids.berkeley.edu/people/jarrod-millman). → To attend in person: Register on this page. → To attend online: Sign up here to receive a Zoom link (https://forms.gle/fKjzxbKFScfAMxks5).Abstract Scikit-learn is the industry standard for machine-learning. events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Exhibition Team:Lauren Graves, Guest CuratorAlissa Schapiro and Hannah Weisman, Coordinating CuratorsAndrea Calderon, RegistrarDavid Sullivan, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Special thanks to Michael S. events.title: Rachel Rutishauser: Targeting virus-specific CD8+ T cells to cure HIV
events.description:
Antigen-specific CD8+ T cells are a key component of antiviral defense. Due to chronic antigen exposure, HIV-specific CD8+ T cells in the majority of people living with HIV are dysfunctional (poor effector function and proliferative capacity). However, they are highly functional and may mediate viral control in the rare individuals who control the infection spontaneously and are therefore an attractive target for immunotherapies seeking to achieve durable HIV remission in the absence of antiretroviral therapy. We will discuss T cell-intrinsic regulatory programs that promote HIV-specific CD8+ T cell function and dysfunction and new approaches being tested in pre-clinical and clinical settings to enhance HIV-specific CD8+ T cell function.
This seminar is partially sponsored by NIHDivision(s): Division of Immunology and Molecular Medicine

events.title: Cognition Colloquium: Cognitive tools for uncovering useful abstractions
events.description: In the 17th century, the Cartesian coordinate system was groundbreaking. It exposed the unity between algebra and geometry, accelerating the development of the math that took humans to the moon. It was not just another concept, but a cognitive tool that people could wield to express abstract ideas in visual form, thereby expanding their capacity to think and generate new insights about a variety of other problems. Research in my lab investigates how the mind uses such tools, guided by the hypothesis that even the most rarefied cognitive tools are forged by the need to coordinate perception, cognition, and action in the service of concrete goals. I will begin with an overview of our work investigating drawing—one of humanity's most enduring and versatile cognitive tools. A recurring theme is that what a drawing looks like underdetermines what it means: people produce and interpret drawings at varying levels of abstraction depending on what they can see, what they know, and what they wish to communicate. Next, I will describe an emerging line of work investigating data visualization, a modern cognitive tool used to make sense of phenomena that would otherwise be too difficult to observe directly. I will then share our work using physical assembly tasks as a way to track the emergence of useful abstractions: as people build a structure, they discover procedural abstractions that support planning, and use speech, drawing, and gesture to converge on shared ways of thinking and communicating about problems. I will close by noting how evaluating AI systems on the same tasks can help to locate human cognition within the broader space of possible solutions to them, and how such studies might inform the development of new tools for expanding people's capacity to learn, share knowledge, and create new things.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Kaitlyn Lee (CTML GSR)
events.description: Connect with the CTML community! This week's seminar on Tuesday, November 10th, will feature CTML GSR Kaitlyn Lee (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/kaitlyn-lee) presenting her talk, "Off-the-Shelf Bregman-Riesz Regression via Data Augmentation." The seminar will take place at 12:00 PM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401. Abstract: Doubly robust estimators of many causal effects require estimating a Riesz representer (e.g., inverse propensity weights for the ATE). Riesz regression estimates it directly, but its loss involves counterfactual evaluations, which makes it hard to fit with standard learners. In this talk, we first discuss the Riesz representer and the role it plays in semiparametric estimation. We then show that for a broad class of estimands, including the ATE, ATT, and shift interventions, a simple data-augmentation step turns Riesz regression into an ordinary row-wise loss. Off-the-shelf learners like XGBoost can then be used to directly fit the Riesz representer. We implement this in an open-source Python package that extends scikit-learn. Bio: Kaitlyn Lee is a PhD candidate in Biostatistics at the University of California, Berkeley, mentored by Dr. Alejandro Schuler. She previously earned her MA in Biostatistics at UC Berkeley and her BA in Physics from Harvard University. Her research focuses on developing causal inference methods that combine machine learning and semiparametric statistics to produce statistically rigorous solutions for problems in health and social policy. Her current work centers on developing new machine learning algorithms that are flexible and computationally efficient for estimating causal effects. She has also interned at Genentech, where she worked on methods for incorporating covariates into the analysis of clinical trials.

events.title: Recovery from Democratic Backsliding: Lessons From—and For—Europe, with Prof. Tom Ginsburg (Chicago; Berkeley Law JD + JSP PhD)
events.description:
Institute for European Studies Director's Theme Lecture Series for 2026-2027: Democracy in Peril This year's election in Hungary ending 16 years of Viktor Orban's rule raises important questions about the tactics of recovery from backsliding in Europe and around the world. Questions of sequencing, institutional redesign, and the balance between looking backward and forward have come to the fore, echoing the democratic transitions of 35 years ago. Are the answers different? Drawing on the experience of several countries, this lecture argues that today's transitions raise distinct challenges and require different tools those of the prior generation. Shoring up the core institutions and practices of constitutional democracy is the immediate challenge. Tom Ginsburg is the Leo Spitz Distinguished Service Professor of International Law at the University of Chicago, where he serves as Faculty Director for the Forum on Free Inquiry and Expression, as well as the Malyi Center for the Study of Institutional and Legal Integrity. He holds B.A., J.D. and Ph.D. degrees from the University of California at Berkeley, and currently co-directs the Comparative Constitutions Project, an NSF-funded data set cataloging the world's constitutions since 1789, that runs the award-winning Constitute website. The second edition of his book with Aziz Huq, How to Save a Constitutional Democracy has just been published, and he is the author of numerous other volumes on comparative constitutional studies and international law. He currently serves a senior advisor on Constitution Building to International IDEA and is also on the faculty of the American Bar Foundation. events.title: Seminar 221 Industrial Organization: Allan Hsiao – Critical Minerals, Geopolitics, and the Green Transition
events.description: Abstract: The green energy transition will be powered by the mining and processing of lithium, nickel, and cobalt, which are critical for the production of advanced batteries. These minerals are concentrated geographically but traded globally, allowing key mining countries to exercise market power through policy intervention. Advanced batteries use multiple minerals in combination, and this joint use creates interdependence across mineral markets. We study the geopolitical implications of these forces and their consequences for green technology adoption worldwide. We quantify supply chain vulnerability, international policy spillovers, and the potential for mineral cartels.

events.description:
Title: LLMs and Operations Research: A Two-Way TransformationSpeaker: David Simchi-Levi, Distinguished Professor of Management, Purdue University& William Barton Rogers Professor of Engineering Systems, MIT (Retired)
Abstract:Large Language Models (LLMs) and Operations Research (OR) are transforming eachother in powerful and complementary ways. On one hand, LLMs are makingoptimization more accessible, interpretable, and actionable, enabling business users tointeract with complex models, automate decision-making, and improve optimizationworkflows. On the other hand, OR provides the mathematical foundations andalgorithms needed to make LLM systems more efficient, scalable, and cost-effective.
In this talk, I will explore this two-way transformation through recent research and real-world applications, including AI-driven supply chain planning, automated optimizationmodel debugging, real-time inventory management, and optimization of LLM servinginfrastructure. Together, these advances illustrate how the convergence of LLMs andOR is opening new frontiers in intelligent decision-making and autonomous systems.
Bio: David Simchi-Levi (https://cee.mit.edu/people_individual/david-simchi-levi/) David Simchi-Levi is the William Barton Rogers Professor in Energy, and Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Engineering Systems at MIT. He also serves as the head of the MIT Data Science Lab. (https://dsl.mit.edu/) He is considered one of the premier thought leaders in supply chain management and business analytics. His Ph.D. students have accepted faculty positions in leading academic institutes including U. of California Berkeley, Carnegie Mellon U., Columbia U., Cornell U., Duke U., Georgia Tech, Harvard U., U. of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, U. of Michigan, Purdue U. and Virginia Tech. Professor Simchi-Levi is the current Editor-in-Chief of Management Science, one of the two flagship journals of INFORMS. He served as the Editor-in-Chief for Operations Research (2006-2012), the other flagship journal of INFORMS and for Naval Research Logistics (2003-2005). In 2023, he was elected a member of the National Academy of Engineering. In 2020, he was awarded the prestigious INFORMS Impact Prize for playing a leading role in developing and disseminating a new highly impactful paradigm for the identification and mitigation of risks in global supply chains. He is an INFORMS Fellow and MSOM Distinguished Fellow and the recipient of the 2020 INFORMS Koopman Award given to an outstanding publication in military operations research; Ford Motor Company 2015 Engineering Excellence Award; 2014 INFORMS Daniel H. Wagner Prize for Excellence in Operations Research Practice; 2014 INFORMS Revenue Management and Pricing Section Practice Award; and 2009 INFORMS Revenue Management and Pricing Section Prize. He was the founder of LogicTools which provided software solutions and professional services for supply chain optimization. LogicTools became part of IBM in 2009. In 2012 he co-founded OPS Rules, an operations analytics consulting company. The company became part of Accenture in 2016. In 2014, he co-founded Opalytics, a cloud analytics platform company focusing on operations and supply chain decisions. The company became part of the Accenture Applied Intelligence in 2018.

events.title: Operator Algebras Seminar: Irreducibility and weak spectral gap for centralizers of free product states
events.description: Speaker: Brent Nelson, Michigan State UniversityLet $(M,\varphi )=(M_1,\varphi _1)*(M_2,\varphi _2)$ be a free product of non-trivial von Neumann algebras equipped with faithful normal states. In 2011, Ueda showed that the diffuse summand of $M$ is a factor if and only $dim(M_1)+\dim (M_2)\geq 5$, and in this case one further has that the diffuse summand has no asymptotically central sequences. That same year, Ueda established a related result in the case that the states $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _2$ are almost periodic in the sense of Connes—this is a condition that allows the states to be non-tracial but in a tame enough way that tracial techniques can often still be employed. In this case, Ueda proved that $\dim (M_1)+\dim (M_2)\geq 5$ implies the centralizer of the free product state $M^\varphi =\{x\in M : \varphi (xy) = \varphi (yx) \forall y\in M\}$ has diffuse summand whose inclusion into the diffuse summand of $M$ is irreducible with weak spectral gap. In joint work with Aldo Garcia Guinto, Fehmi Ekin Giritlioglu, Yoonkyeong Lee, and Rahul Kumar R., we show that the only obstruction for non-almost periodic states is if either $\varphi _1$ or $\varphi _2$ is ergodic in the sense that the corresponding centralizer is trivial. Provided that both $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _2$ are non-ergodic, we give a dimension characterization of when the inclusion of the diffuse summand of $M^\varphi $ into the corresponding corner of $M$ is irreducible with weak spectral gap.

events.title: Chocolate Rebellion: Reclaiming Power in the Chocolate Industry
events.description: Chocolate is enjoyed across the world, but the labor of growing cacao is often undervalued. That imbalance has deep roots: under colonial systems, growers were deliberately kept from the knowledge of transforming their own harvests into chocolate, so the value and wealth flowed abroad. In this talk, Goddard will share how she is returning that knowledge to growers, building a cooperative network of community-owned chocolate enterprises across the Caribbean and sub-Saharan Africa aiming to own every step from bean to bar to the ship that carries it. For Goddard, chocolate is a vehicle: the network has grown to include a local marketplace, conservation work, and community tourism, creating a resilient economy rooted in the land. Gillian Goddard, a community organizer and chocolate-maker, co-founded the Alliance of Rural Communities, a nonprofit dedicated to regenerating the environment and creating thriving communities across the Caribbean and sub-Saharan Africa. Goddard's work seeks not only to enhance the well-being of rural populations but also to explore complex issues of power, decolonization, and emancipation across grassroots, commercial, and academic spaces.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
John Eiler, Robert P. Sharp Professor of Geology and Geochemistry, CaltechExploring the organic chemistry of the early solar system using molecular isotopic structureOrganic chemistry is ubiquitous across extraterrestrial environments and dominates the processing and delivery of carbon and nitrogen to rocky planetary bodies. Extraterrestrial settings and materials also present the most clearly revealed and diverse collection of constraints on the ways in which 'prebiotic' chemistry takes its first steps towards life. Some of the most detailed and nuanced constraints on this subject come from the laboratory study of the thousands of organic compounds sampled by carbonaceous meteorites and returned samples of asteroids. However, detailed understanding of these materials has been challenging because they may be intimate mixtures of the products of chemistry operating across many settings and processes. I will explore the origin and evolution of early solar system organic materials through application of molecular isotopic structure — the study of the distributions of naturally occurring rare isotopes (D, 13C, 15N, etc.) at scales of individual atomic positions and considering the very rare versions of molecules that contain two or more rare isotopes. These studies were enabled by more than two decades of inventions in mass spectrometry, studies of the chemical physics of previously unexamined isotopic forms of molecules, and applications to meteorites, returned samples, ancient earth materials and their laboratory analogues. The results reveal the long, complex journey of carbon and other volatile materials from synthesis in the interstellar medium, through the early history of the protoplanetary disk and into the 'prebiotic cauldron' of solar system bodies.
The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "How Does Monetary and Fiscal Policy Affect the Economy in the Face of Large Shocks?"
events.description: Abstract: We build a model that combines (i) heterogeneous households with incomplete markets, and (ii) state-dependent pricing with strategic complementarities by firms, to analyze the effects of large macroeconomic shocks and policy interventions. Both features significantly influence the transmission of fiscal stimulus and monetary policy—heterogeneous households because of failures of Ricardian equivalence, and state-dependent pricing because of its nonlinear effects on inflation. We use our model to quantify how monetary and fiscal policy shaped macroeconomic dynamics in response to the large shocks of 2020, and how alternative policy choices could have led to different aggregate and distributional outcomes. We find large departures from Ricardian equivalence and strong stepping-on-a-rake effects of interest rate changes. The large unfunded fiscal transfer program helped prevent deflation in 2020 and significantly raised output throughout 2021 and 2022, but led to permanently higher prices. The monetary easing through 2020 and 2021 also contributed to preventing deflation, but had a minimal impact on GDP. The monetary tightening from 2022 lowered the maximum inflation rate, but contributed to persistently above-trend inflation. These policies led to net welfare gains for low-wealth households and net welfare losses for high-wealth households, but those welfare effects are due to incomplete markets for idiosyncratic risk not aggregate stabilization. Alternative commitments to funding fiscal stimulus could have achieved similar short-term effects on inflation and output with a much smaller long-term increase in the price level.

events.title: The Land Returns: Film Screening & Discussion
events.location: Native Community Center in Anthony Hall
events.description:
Across the United States, a growing grassroots movement is bringing Indigenous nations, local communities, and unexpected allies together to return ancestral lands to their original stewards. The Land Returns explores three remarkable stories: the Pawnee Nation's return to its Nebraska homelands through a private land donation; the return of a sacred island in northern California to the Wiyot people; and ongoing efforts by the Arapaho and Cheyenne to regain land in Colorado's Boulder Valley. The documentary extends the exhibition's exploration of land ownership, competing claims, and the changing relationships between people and place in the American West. These hopeful stories highlight how partnerships and local action are creating new opportunities for Indigenous nations to reclaim land and strengthen their connections to ancestral homelands. The screening is followed by a reception and discussion with the filmmakers and the mak'warep Land Trust (https://www.ohloneland.org/)
Producer/Writer/Director Margaret D. Jacobsis a settler scholarwho isthe Charles Mach Professor of History and the former Director of the Center for Great Plains Studies at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. She has written four books and three dozen articles, mostly about Indigenous child removal and family separation. Since 2015, she has focused her work on collaboration and engagement with Native communities to promotetruth and reconciliation. In 2017, Margaret co-founded the Genoa Indian School Digital Reconciliation Project to digitally repatriate government records related to the boarding school to Native families and tribes. In2018, she co-founded Reconciliation Rising with Lakota journalist Kevin Abourezk to showcase Indigenous and non-Indigenous people who are working together to honestly confront traumatic histories, promote meaningful dialogue, and create pathways to reconciliation. In 2021, Margaret and Kevin co-produced the documentary short "Return of the Pawnees," which won a Heartland Emmy Award and a Telly Award. That same yearMargaret publishedAfter One Hundred Winters: In Search of Reconciliation on America's Stolen Lands. Since 2022, Margaret has co-led a partnership between the Center for Great Plains Studies and the Otoe-Missouria Tribe of Oklahoma to reconnect the tribe with their ancestral homelands in southeast Nebraska and to engage non-Natives with their history, culture, resurgence, and return.
Editor Candice Dalsing(Mescalero Apache descendant) is an award-winning Director/Producer based in Portland, Oregon. She co-founded Deer Woman Productions, a non-profit Native/women run production company. Candice's portfolio includes a variety of projects, including feature films, documentaries, short films and music videos. She served as Impact Producer for Bring Them Home, which was nominated for two Emmys in 2026. Beyond her work behind the camera, Candice is an active advocate for Indigenous and LGBTQ+ rights and their representation in the media. She frequently collaborates with nonprofit organizations, conducts workshops, and participates in panel discussions.

events.title: Joshua Jelly-Schapiro, "Daylight Come: Harry Belafonte and the World He Made"
events.description: Join Joshua Jelly-Schapiro for a talk and conversation on his acclaimed new book, Daylight Come: Harry Belafonte and the World He Made. Jelly-Schapiro will discuss Belafonte's vexed but vital relation to folk cultures of the Caribbean, and the ways the "folk revival" in New York's Greenwich Village helped this Harlem-born son of Jamaican immigrants recorded the first LP in history to sell a million copies; how he used his resulting royalties to bankroll the Civil Rights Movement; and how this angry and joyous human, wrestling with his demons and those of America, transformed our politics by evolving our culture. * "Joshua Jelly-Schapiro's Daylight Come takes us places no biography in recent memory has…This book fills the heart and the mind, and is essential reading for our times." -Hilton Als * Joshua Jelly-Schapiro earned his PhD in Geography at Berkeley, and is the author of books including Island People, and, with Rebecca Solnit, Nonstop Metropolis: A New York City Atlas. His work appears regularly in The New Yorker, The New York Review of Books, and the New York Times, among many other publications. He teaches journalism at NYU and is Director of Publishing at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn, where he hosts the Author Talks series and is co-editor-in-chief of Pioneer Works Broadcast.

events.title: Commutative Algebra and Algebraic Geometry Seminar: The Golod property of curves in P^3
events.description: Speaker: David Eisenbud, UC BerkeleyLet S = \(k[x_0,\dots ,x_3]\) be the homogeneous coordinate ring of P^3. For a curve X in \(P^3\) with homogeneous coordinate ring \(A = S/I\), the Golod property is equivalent to the statement that the multiplicative structure on \(Tor^S_*(A,k)\) is trivial. It has the surprising consequence that there are, up to isomorphism, only finitely many indecomposable summands of A-syzygies of k.I'll describe some of the history of this notion, and sketch the proof of a new theorem:If \(X\subset P^3\) is not a complete intersection, then A is Golod.

events.title: Ilyas Chattha | Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974
events.description:
A talk by Ilyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934), Associate Professor of History at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), on his new book, Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/history/south-asian-history/citizens-traitors-bengali-internment-pakistan-19711974?format=HB&isbn=9781009568241) (Cambridge University Press, 2025). Drawing on previously untapped sources, the book examines Pakistan's internment of thousands of Bengalis after the 1971 war and explains why this history has largely been overlooked.
Sadia Saeed (https://www.usfca.edu/faculty/sadia-saeed), Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of San Francisco will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, November 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKThe breakup of Pakistan in 1971—following a brutal civil war and military defeat by India—remains shrouded in layers of silence, myth, and contested memory. When the war ended, more than 90,000 Pakistani prisoners of war captured in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, were transferred to Indian custody. In response, Pakistan interned a comparable number of Bengalis living in West Pakistan, treating them as leverage in negotiations for the prisoners' return. Neither group was allowed to go home immediately, creating what became one of the largest episodes of reciprocal mass internment since 1945. Drawing on a wide range of previously untapped sources, this book reconstructs the resulting crisis of captivity. It traces how Bengalis in West Pakistan were stripped of meaningful citizenship and recast as "traitors" and "enemies" in the aftermath of the Bangladesh War. More than half a century later, their internment remains largely absent from accounts of the most consequential political crisis in Pakistan's history. By recovering this neglected history, the book not only reveals the human and political consequences of mass detention but also explains how—and why—the experience of interned Bengalis was erased from the historical record. SPEAKER BIOIlyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934) is Associate Professor of History at Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a historian of modern South Asia. Educated at the universities of Warwick and Southampton in the United Kingdom, he has previously been affiliated with the Centre for Imperial and Post-Colonial Studies at the University of Southampton, the University of Warwick, and SOAS University of London. Dr Chattha's research focuses on late colonial Punjab, Partition, migration, borders and borderlands, collective violence, and the formation of the early postcolonial Pakistani state. He has written extensively on the long-term consequences of the partitions of 1947 and 1971, with particular attention to displacement, citizenship, internment, property, and state-building. He is the author of Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (Cambridge University Press, 2025), which examines the wartime and postwar experiences of Bengalis interned in West Pakistan; The Punjab Borderland: Mobility, Materiality and Militancy, 1947–1987 (Cambridge University Press, 2022); and Partition and Locality: Violence, Migration and Development in Gujranwala and Sialkot, 1947–1961 (Oxford University Press, 2012). His current book project explores the history of evacuee and enemy property in Pakistan.

events.title: Andrew Hogan // The New Rules of Design
events.description:
The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Andrew Hogan, Head of Insights at Figma. Drawing on years of research at Figma and his time as an analyst at Forrester, Andrew studies how design is changing in an era where AI, new tools, and new roles are reshaping how digital products get made. His work focuses on the real behavior inside teams: who is actually doing design, how decisions get made, and what separates the organizations that ship consistently great experiences from everyone else. ​In his talk, The New Rules of Design, Andrew will present empirical findings on the changing role of designers and the increasing participation of "designers by another name" across product, engineering, marketing, and other functions. He will examine how AI-generated interfaces and accelerated prototyping are reshaping design practice, and identify domains where distinctly human judgment, interpretation, and taste remain central. Moving from popular discourse to research-backed insights, he will articulate emerging principles for contemporary design work, including cross-disciplinary collaboration, pathways for junior practitioners in a senior-leaning labor market, and strategies for sustaining a distinctive design language in a world where interface creation is widely accessible. This event is free and open to the public. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.

events.title: [AALJ x SALSA x APALSA x Miller Institute] Diwali Ram ke Naam Film Screening + Discussion
events.description:
Join us for a screening of Anand Patwardhan's (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anand_Patwardhan) Ram ke Naam scheduled for Tues. 11/10, 6-8pm followed by a discussion moderated by AALJ Associate Editor Aman Madan (https://www.linkedin.com/in/madanaman/). We will also be providing dinner. The documentary examines the Hindu nationalist campaign to build a Ram temple at the site of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya. Given the association of Diwali with Rama's return to Ayodhya, we thought the occasion would provide an opportunity to examine how religious narratives shape political movements and legal claims. The discussion would ask what happens when a political movement co-opts a religious tradition, and how that shapes the interpretation and enforcement of constitutional protections for religious freedom and equality. While grounded in India, these questions have global relevance as movements elsewhere — including in the United States — invoke religion to justify state power and define whose rights the law should protect. We will reach out prior to the screening for some optional readings to provide further context for our discussion.
Please RSVP (https://forms.gle/SEzQcGZZtpPsfxty8) by Sun. 11/8 12pm (put reminder on your calendar (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=NWowdWkxOHFtY3Vkc2I5OTBhNGs2MnI3dDUgY19hNjE2N2JjNmUxMjVhYjhjNDJjZWFkZjA3YTZjMDcwOWYzYTAwODVkZDQxMTVhZTAyOTU3OWEwNzEyMDAzZWIwQGc&tmsrc=c_a6167bc6e125ab8c42ceadf07a6c0709f3a0085dd4115ae029579a0712003eb0%40group.calendar.google.com)) so we can make the food order in advance.

events.title: Performance: Breath in this World
events.description: Join us at the Arts Research Center for Breath in this World, a solo performance of spoken word, sung voice, and body by poet, artist, and performer Aine Nakamura. About the work: The moon holds no light of its own. It receives the sun's light while the earth's shadow reshapes it. Two years ago, Nakamura began to consider the moon's shape as a membrane between stories, between inside and out. Since then, its swaying line and rings of light have led her toward questions of soul, wounds, and the human eye. In this work she follows light and darkness, line and shape through voice and breath. Premiered in March 2026 at Indexical in Santa Cruz, Breath in this World has traveled to the UCSD Music Spring Festival, ZK/U Berlin, Baiju Theatre near Beijing, UrBANBUILD in Kyoto, and Chicago. It continues to evolve through each performance and the time shared with audiences, who help shape what it means to see. About the artist:Aine Nakamura, is a performer of voice and body, poet, and artist. She focuses on the potentialities of an injured voice and the listening and sensing bodies. She often writes words and considers shapes as if her throat is a membrane and each body part is a shape, phenomenon among worldly phenomena, in relations. Through her practice, while aiming to be a vessel, she understands about herself and pursues meanings of lines, seeing and connecting. She is a PhD candidate at UC Berkeley and is based in the Bay Area/East Bay, presenting works locally and internationally. Her recent works include solo performance "Breath in this World" premiered at Indexical in SC, which continues to evolve at ZK/U Berlin, Baiju Theater near Beijing, UrBANGUILD in Kyoto, Chicago, and will be presented at Arts Research Center; month-long site-specific exhibition and performance project "hands on tape," presented at The Lab in SF; solo performance "Under an Unnamed Flower" during an invitation to the 50th International Theatre Festival at the Venice Biennale; solo multiple performance project "Circle hasu We plant seeds in the spring of mountains" presented at Theatertreffen at Berliner Festspiele after its premiere at the Gallatin Galleries in NY. She also engages in listening and walking in relation to long-term soul work, which resulted in her performance at The Listening Biennial Singapore. In exploring the presence of wounds and repair, she seeks the concepts of fragile kindness and love to access pathways to vulnerability. She is also a committed collaborator and improviser, through which she develops her approach to attunement, spaces and listening.

events.title: Silicon Valley Alumni: The Founder’s Edge – What Separates Startups in the Age of AI
events.location: Silkroad Innovation Hub, 724 Oak Grove Ave #100, Menlo Park, CA 94025, USA
events.description:
Join the Berkeley Haas Alumni Network and Founder Institute Silicon Valley for an intimate fireside conversation with Mercedes Bankston (Leader, Founder Institute SV; Startup Advisor & Investor), moderated by Zhanara Amans.

AI has lowered the barrier to starting a company—products are built faster and teams stay leaner. But when building gets easier, what actually creates a durable competitive advantage? Mercedes will share pattern-recognition insights on what separates startups that break through from those that stumble.

Key Discussion Topics:

The Founder Edge: Qualities that distinguish exceptional founders in the AI era.

Building Sustainable Advantage: Where moat and defensibility come from when tech is accessible to all.

Idea vs. Traction: Signals that an idea is worth pursuing and what to prove before raising capital.

​The New Startup Playbook: How assumptions around team size, capital, and speed are shifting.

6:45 PM: Audience Q&A

events.title: William Kentridge's The Head & the Load
events.location: Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, Oakland
events.description: Thursday, November 12, 7:30pm Friday, November 13, 7:30pm Saturday, November 14, 7:30pm Sunday, November 15, 3pmTheater William Kentridge'sThe Head & the LoadWith music composed and conceived by Philip Miller with Thuthuka SibisiWilliam Kentridge, concept and director Philip Miller, composerGregory Maqoma, choreography Thuthuka Sibisi, music director and co-composer Visionary South African artist William Kentridge returns to Cal Performances after two previous visits, featuring the US premiere of SIBYL in 2023 and the Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No in 2025. This time, he brings the West Coast premiere of a seminal work that—through dance, projection, speech, song, shadow play, costume, and music—chronicles the untold history of more than two million Africans who labored, fought, and died during the First World War. The Head & the Load takes its name from a Ghanaian proverb, "The head and the load are the troubles of the neck," and continues Kentridge's exploration of history, language, and artistic and political movements through richly layered and inventive performance works. Kentridge's production unfolds on a massive stage, weaving together texts by anticolonial authors and Dada poets in multiple languages, with original music by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi that intermingles traditional African songs with quotes from WWI-era European music by Satie, Hindemith, and Schoenberg. Through Cal Performances' Golden Bear Circle program, UC Berkeley students are eligible to purchase a limited number of $10 tickets for this evening's performances. Information about this and more student events and discounts is available at calperformances.org/ucb-students.
