events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.

events.title: Zoe Samudzi | Autotheorizing German Genocide Denial: A Dresden Museum Case Study
events.description: Following decades worth of efforts to broaden the historiographic and political boundaries of national genocide memory, German institutions have been pushed to contend with the country's history of colonial genocide, namely the attempted annihilation of Ovaherero and Nama people in the former colony of South West Africa (present-day Namibia). This lecture traces the contours of conflict that emerged from an invitation by the Staatlichen Kunstsammlungen Dresden (the Dresden State Art Collections) to produce an exhibition engaging the ethnopolitical threads of genocide denialism undergirding the relationship between East Germany and the South West Africa People's Organization (SWAPO) in relation to the history (and present afterlife) of the genocide. The institution's objection to a central claim that Germany had not fully recognized the Nama and Ovaherero genocide — one that reiterated existent tensions between the state's regime of memory as enforced by cultural institutions — compels consideration of how anti-black disciplining by a state institution might lead one to embrace withdrawal as an ethical imperative. Dr. Zoé Samudzi is a Provost's Fellow to Faculty scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies and an affiliated faculty in the Department of the History of Art. Her work contends with genocide memory and registers of denialism; political mythologies of the postcolonial African nation-state and the relationship between ethnicity and the national question; visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing; human remains and the state and community politics around repatriation and restitution; and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. She is a writer and critic, as well as an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine; and she is 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom."If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: A collections-based approach to bryophyte diversity and disjunct distributions between the Neotropics and Africa
events.description:
How do we explain patterns of biodiversity when our knowledge of species and their distributions is incomplete? Despite their diversity and ecological importance, bryophytes remain poorly documented across much of the tropics, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of where species occur and why. Historical herbarium collections offer opportunities to reveal overlooked diversity, refine our knowledge of species distributions, and investigate the ecological and evolutionary processes shaping regional floras. Realizing this potential requires attention to both the specimens themselves and the histories of collecting and access that shape our knowledge.
In this seminar, I will talk about three connected themes in my ongoing collections-based research on bryophytes in Madagascar, sub-Saharan Africa, and the Neotropics. The first focuses on how revisiting historical collections can reveal previously unreported species occurrences and inform our understanding of species richness and endemism. The second focuses on the "silent herbaria" of sub-Saharan Africa: how the history of botanical exploration, the visibility of local collections, and their representation in digital resources such as GBIF influence our understanding of bryophyte diversity. This raises a fundamental challenge for ecological inference: distinguishing biological patterns from gaps in collecting and access to knowledge. The third addresses bryophyte species with disjunct distributions between the Neotropics and Africa. Integrating herbarium specimens, genomic data, and spatial modelling provides a framework for testing hypotheses about long-distance dispersal, historical isolation, and intercontinental gene flow, and for examining how niche evolution shapes colonization and diversification across continents.

events.title: Portraits of Unbelonging: Returning and Belonging
events.description:
Lecture Abstract: In 1896 Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II issued a decree that allowed Ottoman Armenians - and only Ottoman Armenians - to emigrate on the condition that they expatriate and never return. A key step in this process was sitting for a photograph. While these photographs look like family portraits and were often produced by professional Armenian studio photographers, they are binding legal documents of exclusion. These photographic subjects were no longer Ottoman subjects. As emigrants left on steamships from ports on the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, their likenesses entered police files in the empire's capital, Constantinople where Gürsel encountered them more than a century later in the Ottoman state archives. Portraits of Unbelonging is a history of mass migration told on an intimate scale that interrogates nationality and subjecthood and the rise of the document-based global security regimes that govern citizenship and mobility today. In this talk Prof. Gürsel will trace the story of two women to highlight the gap between the law as it is pronounced by a sovereign and as it is experienced by individuals, families and communities.
Bio: Zeynep Devrim Gürsel is a media anthropologist and Associate Professor in the department of Anthropology at Rutgers University. She is the author of Image Brokers: Visualizing World News in the Age of Digital Circulation (2016) and Portraits of Unbelonging: Photographic Journeys Across Borders (https://www.sup.org/books/middle-east-studies/portraits-unbelonging) (Stanford University Press, 2026). She is also the director of Coffee Futures (2009), an award-winning ethnographic film that explores contemporary Turkish politics through the prism of the everyday practice of coffee fortune telling. Her current projects investigate the emergence of the global surveillance regimes policing mobility and nationality and the critical role of photography in this history. Her article, "Classifying the Cartozians: Rethinking the Politics of Visibility Alongside Ottoman Subjecthood and American Citizenship," was awarded a 2023 Ottoman and Turkish Studies Association Article Prize. She was a NOMIS Fellow at eikones Center for the Theory and History of the Image in Basel, Switzerlandand a Mid-Career Fellow at the Leonard A. Lauder Center for Research in Modern Art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

events.title: The Revolutionary Center: The Lost Genius of Liberalism
events.description: Wooldridge will speak on November 12, 12:30 - 2 pm in 223 Philosophy Hall as he reflects on the cultural history of liberalism - one of our most widely used yet misunderstood terms. He reveals why the world urgently needs a more liberal mindset. Liberalism was once a revolutionary social idea built on individualism, tolerance, and skepticism of power, rather than big or small government. It has lost its way due to technocratic complacency, elite self-indulgence, and internal splintering. Now it must reclaim its bold, critical roots to survive global authoritarianism and populismSpeaker Bio Adrian Wooldridge is an author and political columnist, currently working for Bloomberg Opinion. Wooldridge received a Doctorate of Philosophy from Oxford University as a Fellow of All Souls College. Wooldridge was also a Harkness Fellow at our very own UC Berkeley! Prior to taking on his role as a writer for Bloomberg, he spent 32 years working for The Economist, where he fulfilled numerous columnist roles. Wooldridge served as its Washington Bureau Chief, covering Washington D.C and the American government, and later as its Lexington Columnist, which covered American politics and culture. Wooldridge eventually became The Economist's Schumpeter Columnist where he offered commentary and analysis on entrepreneurial and business trends. Wooldridge was awarded the Gerald Loeb Award in 2017 as a result of his work as the Schumpeter Columnist. In 2021 Wooldridge was appointed The Economist's Bagehot Columnist, covering British culture and politics, before going on to work for Bloomberg Opinion in 2022. While working as a columnist, Wooldridge published numerous books! In 2018, Wooldridge co-wrote Capitalism in America: A History with former Federal Reserve Chair Alan Greenspan. Wooldridge wrote The Aristocracy of Talent: How Meritocracy Made the Modern World in 2021, which went on to become The Times Book of the Year. In 2026, he published The Revolutionary Center: The Lost Genius of Liberalism, a book highlighting liberalism's strength as an ideology capable of adaptation, change, and reform, and what it may need to become in order to ensure that it can surpass the challenges posed to it by the world's autocracies and upstart populist movements.

events.title: Critical Conversations: Transforming the Field of Black Studies - Shaun Ossei-Owusu
events.description:
Law on Trial: An Unlikely Insider Reckons with Our Legal System The law promises justice. Too often, it delivers inequality. This contradiction raises a basic question: Why does a legal system that claims to stand for fairness and equality fail to uphold these ideals over and over? In Law on Trial (https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324091264), legal scholar and Bronx native Shaun Ossei-Owusu draws on more than a decade of observation and reflection—first as a scholar of racial inequality, then as a law student, practicing lawyer, and now as an Ivy League law professor—to provide an unvarnished account of the legal system. He reveals that the promise of justice is too often a convenient fiction invoked by lawyers, recited by textbooks, and betrayed in practice.
Shaun Ossei-Owusu is an interdisciplinary legal scholar with expertise in legal history, criminal law and procedure, civil rights, and the legal profession. He has held fellowships and visiting professorships at Harvard, Princeton, Columbia, the University of Chicago, and the University of Southern California. His work sits at the intersection of law, history, and sociology and focuses on how governments meet their legal obligations to provide protections and benefits to poor people and racial minorities. He also works on stratification in legal education and the legal profession. His first book project, Law on Trial (https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324091264): An Unlikely Insider Reckons with Our Legal System, (https://www.amazon.com/Law-Trial-Unlikely-Insider-Reckons/dp/1324091266) was published by W.W. Norton in 2026. His second book project, Steps Toward Equality: A Multiracial History of Legal Organizing, will be published by Princeton University Press in 2027. He received his PhD from the Department of African American Studies at UC Berkeley and his JD from Berkeley Law. He previously practiced litigation and healthcare enforcement law at Sidley Austin LLP in Washington, D.C., and worked as a Loaned Associate focusing on public benefits appeals with the Barbara McDowell Appellate Advocacy Project at the Legal Aid Society of the District of Columbia. He is a proud Bronx-born native.

events.title: Simons Institute Lecture: Bouncing balls and quantum chaos OR my adventures with AI
events.location: Auditorium Calvin Laboratory (Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing)
events.description:
Speaker: Maciej Zworski, UC BerkeleyFor classically ergodic billiards we observe quantum ergodicity: almost all high energy eigenfunctions uniformly distribute in phase space (Shnirelman's Theorem). Can a unique quantum ergodicity fail, that is, can we have sequences of eigenfunctions which are not equidistributed? For almost every Bunimovich stadium (a stadium: rectangle plus two half discs; a beautifully simple ergodic billiard), Hassell showed, in a celebrated 2011 paper, that such sequences do exist but without specifying them. Yet, we all know, from numerics and experiments (most recently reported in Nature in 2024) what they are: they are given by the bouncing ball modes in the rectangle.
With the aid of ChatGPT, Zhenhao Kevin Li and the speaker showed that if we stretch the stadium horizontally (so that the half circles become half ellipses; the billiard does remain ergodic), for almost every stretching parameter, there are bouncing ball modes which concentrate in the rectangle. I will describe the short and (relatively) elementantary proof and the interactive process in which it was arrived at, stressing the crucial idea suggested by AI: complexification of the stretching parameter.

events.title: All Education is Political: Students on Agency, Power and the Myth of the Neutral Classroom
events.location: 554 Social Sciences Building (the Barbara Christian Conference Room)
events.description: What do students today consider to be the "appropriate" time, place, and manner for political engagement in the classroom? Although many educators employ "political neutrality" as a default practice, such approaches feel outdated. Further, scholars, educators, and students alike would argue that a truly politically neutral classroom has never existed. From school segregation to ongoing debates over how race and history are taught, education in the U.S. has always been shaped by political choices about whose stories are told and whose are left out. This session asks, How can students' political education be constituted, supported, and valued? Are students expecting it? Where has political engagement in the classroom been successful and why? When students' political engagement is shut down, how have students successfully organized to reclaim their political agency? To explore these questions, the event will engage participants collaboratively. In addition to a student panel, attendees will work in collaborative discussion circles, thinking alongside students on this topic of political education, praxis, and organizing.

events.title: Astronomy Colloquium - Sarah Millholland (MIT)
events.description:
Title: Tidal Sculpting of Short-Period Exoplanets Abstract: A large fraction of exoplanetary systems contain planets that orbit very close to their host stars. With orbital periods in the range of days to weeks, tidal forces lead to significant orbital and physical effects on the planets. In particular, time-varying tidal deformations lead to planetary orbital decay and tidal heating in the planetary interiors, which manifests physically as radius inflation. I will focus on various observational mysteries of short-period exoplanet demographics and show how tidal dynamics offer a compelling explanation for these puzzles. I will highlight how our tidal theories can be tested with novel JWST observations.
Host: Courtney Dressing

events.title: Ashon Crawley: Open Rehearsal 1
events.description: Open Rehearsals open a door onto work still in the middle of itself. The Arts Research Center's Open Rehearsals invite artist-scholars to bring unfinished work, an animating question, process material, or a place they're stuck—not to present it, but to think with it, out loud. This is a space for contemplation that understands itself as rehearsal. It welcomes thinking undertaken with materials, or as practice. It makes room for work that, in its improvisational open-endedness, knows itself to be incomplete, unfolding over time and across practitioners and institutions. About the Artist:Ashon Crawley is a multidisciplinary artist working in the visual and the sonic, and a Professor of Religious Studies and African American and African Studies at the University of Virginia. Crawley has been an interdisciplinary arts fellow at Yaddo and MacDowell, a New City Arts Initiative Fellow, and a LIT (Learning It Together) Artist Fellow, and his work has been featured on the National Mall in Washington DC, Bridge Projects, and the California African American Museum. He is author of Blackpentecostal Breath: The Aesthetics of Possibility (Fordham University Press), an investigation of aesthetics and performance as modes of collective, social imagination; and The Lonely Letters (Duke University Press), an epistolary exploration of the interrelation of blackness, mysticism, quantum mechanics and love. His third book, From Infinite World:The Sound of the Hammond Organ and the Tragedy of AIDS in the Black Church (WW Norton Dec 2026), addresses the impact of the AIDS crisis for black social life. Entering the conversation by considering musicians, singers and choir directors that labored for black churches, "From Infinite World" explores the ways gender, sex, sexuality remain unthought and untheorized but are no less real practices of the living and the dead. All his writing and his approach to art practices is about what he calls otherwise possibility.

events.title: Lecture | Biography of a Revolution: Rethinking Egypt's 2011 through Feminist Genealogy
events.description: Abstract: Why does a revolution need a biography? In Biography of a Revolution: The Feminist Roots of Human Rights in Egypt (2025), Lucia Sorbera argued against a still-persistent framing of the 2011 Egyptian and Arab revolutions as a sudden rupture. Drawing on a collective biography of the Egyptian women's movement across a century of nationalist, Marxist, labor, student, and democratic movements, she showed that 2011 was the culmination of decades of slow, relational, often unrecorded feminist labor — not its origin. In this talk, Sorbera returns to that argument more than a decade after the 2013 coup foreclosed the political openings the revolution seemed to promise, to ask what is at stake in continuing to recover this genealogy today: not only a historical correction, but a methodological one. She reflects on how testimony, intimacy, and relationality as historical evidence — informed by decolonial and indigenous feminist epistemologies — model a way of writing revolutionary history that resists both event-based narratives and Western-centric periodisations of Middle Eastern political history. Sorbera closes by turning from the book to the field: what new research agendas does this genealogical approach open for scholars of Egypt and the wider region, and how might we study movements that persist, transform, and go underground rather than culminate and end? Bio: Dr. Lucia Sorbera is Associate Professor in Arab, Islamic and Middle East Studies at the University of Sydney, where she serves as Chair of the Discipline of Arabic Language and Cultures. Her research focuses on the colonial and postcolonial history of Southwest Asia and North Africa, with particular attention to women, gender, and sexuality. She is the author of Biography of a Revolution: The Feminist Roots of Human Rights in Egypt (UC Press, 2025), along with numerous other books and essays on women's and gender history in the region. She co-leads the Research Cluster on Cooperation and Conflict at the University of Sydney's Vere Gordon Childe Centre, and co-edits the "Third Space" section of the Journal of Middle East Women's Studies.

events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Tracy Ke: Estimating Weak Spikes with Cycle Counts and Newton-Prony Identities
events.description: Title: Estimating Weak Spikes with Cycle Counts and Newton-Prony Identities Time: Thursday, November 12, 2026, 4:00–5:00 pm Pacific Abstract: How to estimate the population spikes in high-dimensional low-rank signal-plus-noise models is a challenging problem, especially in the weak-spike setting where the spikes are comparable to the spectral norm of the noise matrix in magnitude. A conventional approach is to use the empirical eigenvalues, but the approach is significantly biased, and existing bias-correction methods typically rely on restrictive assumptions on the noise variance profile. We propose two estimators for weak spikes under a generalized spiked model with heterogeneous and unknown noise variances. Our key idea is to use cycle-count statistics to estimate the power sums of the population spikes, and then recover the individual spikes by either a Newton-Prony procedure or a direct optimization procedure. We show that, when the spikes lie above the critical signal level, both approaches are consistent at algebraic rates; the optimization approach further accommodates repeated spikes and achieves spike-dependent convergence rates. At the same time, in the equal-variance setting, we establish a matching lower bound showing that below the critical level, consistent spike estimation may not exist. Together, these yield a sharp phase transition. Using our ideas, we also propose a consistent estimator of the number of spikes. Simulations and a network community-detection application demonstrate substantial improvements over methods that are directly based on empirical eigenvalues.

events.title: The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon
events.description: The Flying Death: Poison, Plunder, and the Quest for a Miracle Medicine in the Amazon Thursday, November 12, 4:00 - 5:30 pm Dwinelle Hall Room 3335REGISTER (https://forms.gle/HUaNJxa4CNMmpXBH8) "In the fall of 1938, a young, frail American explorer set off down a river in the western Amazon in search of curare, a poison he thought might save his life. Richard Gill had learned that local tribes used curare-laced blow darts to kill animals, but it was also potentially a cure for many ailments, including his own. He also thought he could make a fortune by connecting the knowledge of two worlds. Obsessed with curare, he raced to make deals with Indigenous poison masters in the Amazon and pharmaceutical companies back home, even as his Russian-born rival Boris Krukoff sought to do the same. In The Flying Death, the historian Matt O'Hara asks who and what we are willing to sacrifice in the name of discovery and profit. O'Hara brings to life Gill's epic quest, a stranger-than-fiction true story that moves from unexplored territory in the Amazon to rogue medical trials and cutthroat corporate boardrooms in the United States. Navigating treacherous terrain and politics, Gill and Krukoff successfully created a veritable curare–industrial complex, as the plant became a key element in shock therapy, transformed surgery in the United States and across the globe, and eventually led to a Nobel Prize. The Flying Death offers a thrilling ride across Indigenous knowledge, scientific exploration, and exploitation, unearthing a story of discovery that poses searching questions about the price of progress, who pays it, and who gets credit."

events.title: Under Pressure: Attitudes Towards China Among American Foreign Policy Professionals | Lecture by Rory Truex
events.description: How do social norms and professional incentives affect policy discourse within the Washington foreign policy community? We conducted over 50 semi-structured interviews and a survey of nearly five-hundred American foreign policy and national security professionals about their views towards the People's Republic of China. Over one fifth of survey respondents noted instances of professional pressure to voice a more hawkish point of view towards China, and many feared being perceived as naive or compromised by their views on, ties to, and experiences in China. These pressures were particularly acute for foreign policy professionals that are traditionally marginalized from power–those who are younger, non-white, or female. Our interview subjects reported a number of different coping strategies, including trying to communicate their views in the language of the perceived consensus. This "discourse mirroring" is distinct from preference falsification and self-censorship but may still contribute to difficulties in gauging peoples' true attitudes. Speaker BioRory Truex is Associate Professor of Politics and International Affairs at Princeton, where his research and teaching focuses on authoritarianism. He is the host of Civic Forum, a podcast about the big questions facing democracy, in the US and elsewhere.

events.title: Mathematics Department Colloquium: Dynamical approaches to static questions
events.description: Speaker: Bryna Kra, NorthwesternResolving a conjecture of Erdos and Turan from the 1930's, in the 1970's Szemeredi showed that a set of integers with positive upper density contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions. Soon thereafter, Furstenberg used ergodic theory to give a new proof of this result, leading to the development of combinatorial ergodic theory. This talk will trace the developments of the field over the past 50 years. The dynamical tools led to uncovering new patterns that occur in any sufficiently large set of integers, and until recently all such patterns have been finite. In work with Joel Moreira, Florian Richter, and Donald Robertson, we resolved questions and conjectures of Erdos on infinite patterns.

events.title: A World of Marvels: Tommaso Garzoni (1549-1589) between magic, science and literature
events.description:
The talk focuses on the Italian Renaissance poligrafo Tommaso Garzoni and his Serraglio degli stupori del mondo (1613). Tracing the early modern discussion on marvels and superstition, the talk offers new insight on the circulation of scientific knowledge in Italy beyond the intellectual elite, examining the intermingling of learned culture and popular creeds, and considering the scientific and epistemological impact of such debates.
Valentina Serio is Marie Sklodowska-Curie fellow at Ca' Foscari University of Venice. She earned her PhD in Renaissance Civilization from the Scuola Normale of Pisa, with a dissertation examining the correlation between melancholy and political dissent. She has published articles on Leon Battista Alberti, Niccolò Machiavelli, and on theater as a philosophical and literary metaphor. She co-edited Figures of Melancholy: A Fil NoirBetween Philosophy, Art, And Literature (Carocci, 2020), and the forthcoming volume Niccolò Machiavelli and the Anatomy of Passions (Brill).

events.title: Asif Saleh and Tamara Hasan Abed | Bangladesh's Next Chapter: Back to Basics, and What Comes Next
events.description:
Bangladesh is at a turning point. The economy is under strain, hard-won gains for women are being tested, and global aid is shrinking. What should the country's agenda be for the years ahead, what role can institutions like BRAC play, and how can Bangladeshis abroad help shape it? Join Asif Saleh (https://www.bracusa.org/about/people/asif-saleh/), Executive Director of BRAC and a 2026 TIME100 Philanthropy honoree, and Tamara Hasan Abed (https://www.bracinternational.org/about-us/people/tamara-hasan-abed/), Managing Director of BRAC Enterprises and Chair of the BRAC University Board of Trustees, for a candid conversation about Bangladesh's future.
Asif (https://www.bracusa.org/about/people/asif-saleh/) will make the case for getting the basics right: jobs and livelihoods, women's safety and economic participation, and partnering with government and markets to change systems at scale. Tamara (https://www.bracinternational.org/about-us/people/tamara-hasan-abed/) will speak to how social enterprises like Aarong connect tens of thousands of artisans, most of them women, to markets, and how BRAC University is preparing the next generation of policy and technology leaders. Together, they will explore how the Bangladeshi diaspora, with its talent, capital, and networks, can connect with this agenda in ways that go beyond remittances and donations. The conversation will be moderated by Jessica Olney (https://iis.berkeley.edu/people/jessica-olney), Executive Director of the Institute of International Studies. Welcome remarks by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. Please note that this is an in person event and will NOT be live streamed. ————–DATE: Thu, November 12, 2026 TIME: 5-6 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall ———– ABOUT THE SPEAKERSAsif Saleh (https://www.bracusa.org/about/people/asif-saleh/) is the executive director of BRAC. events.title: Building on Discontent: AI and the Arts, Sciences and Humanities at UC Berkeley
events.description: An open colloquium about UC Berkeley's possibilities for local AI including Chelle Gentemann, Alma Halgren, Lance Legel, Joie Li, Greg Niemeyer, Vivien Slagle, Jennifer Chayes, Dean, CDSS, Elena Vindrola, UCOP, Nathan Jandl, Office of Sustainability, UC Berkeley and others. We gather to discuss a central question: How can Berkeley help shape AI's future while preserving its intellectual independence and public mission? We will bring students, staff and faculty together around three practical questions:How can we shape AI's transformative in research, teaching and learning? What campus computing resources could support open-weight AI tools managed by the Berkeley community? Could locally managed computing give us greater accountability for AI's environmental and social impacts? The stakes are institutional as well as technical. If universities do not help shape how AI develops and enters public life, we risk having our roles in education, research, and knowledge creation defined for us, and transformed beyond our purpose. Current grad students are likely to be the most affected by how we we handle this challenge. For Berkeley, meeting this challenge may mean demonstrating what an independent public university can make possible that commercial platforms alone cannot. Can we develop a collective mandate to shape concrete possibilities for UC Berkeley AI futures?

events.title: Unthinking Medieval Poetry: Troubadours, Machaut
events.location: Wu Performance Hall (Morrison Hall 125), UC Berkeley
events.description:
This lecture examines how contemporary poet-translators and artists "unthink" medieval poetry through a creative translation of the conventions and forms of medieval lyric in a mode that is instinctual and sensual, yet formal and critical. By translating the verse of the troubadours and Guillaume Machaut into new media and poetic assemblages, the Brazilian concrete poet Augusto de Campos (b. 1931) and Occitanist musician-poet and Gérard Zuchetto (b. 1951) and sculptor Jean-Luc Séverac (1936–2022) return to the craft of this poetry as word and sound. Their translations allow us to encounter the ritualized performance of absence and circularity in time and space anew and in multiple modes: for instance, verse as prosody and music, and mediated by a manuscript. By engaging with the troubadour craft of entrebescar (the interweaving of word and sound) as a sculptural poetics in material, and Machaut's verbal and musical deployment of the poetic rondeau and musical palindrome through manuscripts and Portuguese translation, Zuchetto-Séverac and Campos demonstrate how creative translation unthinks medieval poetry through an experimental, artisanal process, one that transfers phenomenological aspects of medieval lyric into various situations, matters and beings, so that we can experience this song in a more expansive way as sensory-bound, performed art. I will frame this discussion with how unthinking medieval poetry can help us approach global song—including indigenous and Global South song traditions—by expanding our disciplinary notions of premodern poetry and creating conversant song ecologies.
About the speakerMarisa Galvez is Professor of French and Italian at Stanford University, where she also directs the Stanford Center for Poetics and the Program in Structured Liberal Education. She works on medieval literature in Occitan and Old French, with particular interests in the troubadours, vernacular poetics, the meeting of performance and literary culture, and the history of medieval studies as a discipline. Her first book, Songbook: How Lyrics Became Poetry in Medieval Europe (University of Chicago Press, 2012), won the Medieval Academy of America's John Nicholas Brown Prize. Her second, The Subject of Crusade: Lyric, Romance, and Materials, 1150–1500 (Chicago, 2020), examines how crusade poetry and romance negotiated secular ideals of love and chivalry. Her new book, Before the Global South: Unthinking Medieval Poetry (Chicago, 2026) will be out in a few short weeks. It follows contemporary poets and artists, among them Augusto de Campos and Édouard Glissant, as they remake medieval European lyric forms.

events.description: The Department of Art Practice is excited to welcome Carmen Argote for our Fall '26 Visiting Artist Lecture Series. This lecture will take place from 5-6:30pm in Room 285, Anthropology and Art Practice Building (AAPB). All artist talks are free and open to the public. "Conversings: Playing with materials and improvisational gestures in art and life" In this lecture, Carmen Argote will give voice to centering a practice on constantly changing conditions, and how entering art through the action of play prompts the imagination to carry on without needing reassurance that a work requires closure or resolution. Where you start allows for a surrender to what is not yet known and what is to become. The process of artmaking and its iterative conversations points towards something seemingly finished so it can be shared with others as art, to the point where it both transcends itself and can be sensed. Carmen Argote is a multidisciplinary artist based in Los Angeles whose work examines the relationships between body, class, architecture, and personal history. Argote investigates networks of labor, consumption, and systems that shape everyday spaces through drawing, painting, sculpture, installation, video, and performance. They received their BFA and MFA from the University of California, Los Angeles. Their work has been presented in solo exhibitions at Silverlens Gallery, New York, Commonwealth and Council, Los Angeles, the Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles; Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego; and the New Museum, New York, among others. Argote is the recipient of the City of Los Angeles Cultural Trailblazer Award, the Louis Comfort Tiffany Foundation Award, and the Artadia Los Angeles Award. events.description:
Sponsor(s):The Redwood Center (https://redwood.berkeley.edu/), Simons Institute (https://simons.berkeley.edu/homepage) Today's AI systems are powerful, but they work on principles very different from those of the human brain. They typically learn from large, static datasets, operate as black boxes, and need retraining for each new task. The brain, by contrast, learns continuously through active interaction with the world, builds structured models of what it senses, and generalizes across many kinds of tasks with remarkable efficiency. In this talk, Jeff Hawkins explains how the brain's sensorimotor principles allow it to understand the world, and why reverse-engineering the neocortex may provide a blueprint for a new kind of artificial intelligence. The Thousand Brains Project is an open-source effort to turn these principles into a practical framework for researchers and developers. Reception at 5:30pm, talk at 6pm. Please register (https://redwood.berkeley.edu/intelligence/) in advance if you plan to attend. Speaker:Jeff Hawkins (https://simons.berkeley.edu/people/jeff-hawkins)

events.title: Understanding catalytic reactivity at dynamic solid liquid interfaces
events.description: Catalytic properties have traditionally been linked to the concentration and nature of active sites. At gas-solid interfaces, characterizing these sites has largely sufficed to explain catalytic action, even though reacting molecules may modify them. At solidliquid interfaces, however, the dense and mobile environment changes the elementary steps themselves, as it influences the adsorption of reactants, intermediates, transition states and products, as well as the chemical and electronic state of the catalyst. The lecture will explore how activity and selectivity can be tailored by engineering the local chemical environment of active sites. In highly ionic media, for example, transition states in carbenium-ion chemistry for alkane conversions are strongly stabilized, lowering true activation energies by more than 100 kJ mol⁻¹ and enabling demanding reactions such as carbon–carbon bond cleavage near ambient temperature. Beyond acid–base catalysis, the local concentration of hydronium ions at the catalyst surface alters hydrogenation mechanisms on supported metals by shifting the rate-determining step, and applying an external electric potential can increase hydrogenation rates by nearly an order of magnitude. Together, these examples show that the catalytic microenvironment is a design parameter in its own right, as important as the active site, and one that opens routes to reactions that are otherwise hard to achieve.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Dr. Nalini Singh, UC Berkeley | Gaussian Splatoms: Direct Atomic Structure Identification in Atomic Electron Tomography
events.description: Abstract: Atomic electron tomography (AET) computationally reconstructs the three-dimensional atomic structure of materials from a series of two-dimensional projection measurements. In this talk, I will describe a new atom-centric parameterization for these samples. Instead of a conventional volumetric representation with a grid of voxels, we model the sample as a list of atoms. Each atom is a three-dimensional Gaussian characterized by its location, scale, and amplitude, whose values are learned during the reconstruction process. Our parameterization and associated optimization strategy enforce atomicity by imposing isotropy of atoms, a minimum interatomic distance, and realistic atomic radii; these characteristics are difficult to impose on a volumetric reconstruction. We show that our method improves the robustness of AET to real-world experimental challenges, such as a limited number of tilt measurements and low electron dose. Beyond tomography, our simple, intuitive representation is a promising tool for studying atoms in materials with any atomic resolution imaging modality (e.g., electron ptychography). Bio: Dr. Nalini Singh is a postdoctoral researcher in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at UC Berkeley. Her research focuses on inverse problems in medical and scientific imaging. Previously, she earned a PhD and a Bachelor's degree from MIT and was a student researcher at Google. She has received a Google PhD Fellowship, Best Paper Award at MIDL, and Outstanding Reviewer awards at CVPR and ICLR.

events.title: Laurent Warlouzet | Liberty, Solidarity and Community: Capitalism and European Integration, 1945 to the Present
events.description: How have European countries coped with the challenge of industrial capitalism and the rise of superpowers? Through an analysis of European integration from 1945 to the present day, Laurent Warlouzet argues that the European response was to create both new institutions, in particular the European Union, and an original framework of governance for capitalism. Beyond the European case, he demonstrates that capitalism is not just a contest between free marketeers and their opponents, those in favour of welfare and environmental policies, because there is a third camp that defends protectionism and assertive defence policies. Hence, the governance of capitalism has three foundational principles– liberty, solidarity, and community. The book explores debates among Europeans about how to address global interdependence in political, economic, and environmental terms. It is based on fresh archival evidence collected in eight countries. Laurent Warlouzet is professor of history at Paris Sorbonne Université. A former postdoctoral fellow at the London School of Economics (LSE) and at the European University Institute (EUI), he works on the international economic history of the post-1919 period, particularly European integration and comparative European history. His previous monograph in English (Governing Europe in a Globalizing World, 2018) was reviewed in Foreign Affairs. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Capitalism. European integration and capitalism is an updated version of Europe contre Europe, originally published in French and reviewed in the mainstream media, including Le Monde, Le Grand Continent and Mediapart. The book will be published in German by Hamburger and in Italian by Luiss UP. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Community is available in open-access on the Cambridge UP here (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/liberty-solidarity-and-community/355531CFEE184AFF8B706B24D25EC368). events.title: Marina Dubova in Psychology & Econ Lunch Seminar
events.description: Presenting: "Nothing Deceives Like Success: Social Learning and the Illusion of Understanding in Science"Abstract: Success-driven social learning, in which individuals preferentially adopt the ideas and methods that appear most successful, is a foundational principle of collective behavior across systems ranging from ant colonies to scientific communities. In science, however, the quality of theories and ideas is difficult to assess. Is success bias adaptive in this setting? In agent-based simulations of collective theory building, we find that it might not be. Scientists in our model systematically overestimate the quality of their own theories, creating an illusion of understanding: a persistent gap between perceived and actual performance. Success bias amplifies this illusion: communities that favor seemingly successful theories explore a narrower range of possibilities, efficiently filtering out poor explanations but failing to discover better ones. This effect intensifies with problem complexity, as scientists in more complex environments become increasingly unable to assess how well their theories actually perform. Most strikingly, when agents optimize their social behavior to maximize the perceived success of their theories, they paradoxically undermine their actual performance, and produce levels of inequality that mirror those found in real scientific communities.

events.title: Group Actions and Dynamics Seminar: Large-scale geometry of geodesic currents
events.description: Speaker: Jenya Sapir, BinghamtonFor a closed orientable surface of genus at least 2, we study the large-scale geometry of the (symmetrized) Lipschitz metric on the space of projective filling geodesic currents. We show that the rank and, hence, asymptotic dimension of this space is infinite. This gives the first example of a natural proper space associated to a closed surface, with a metrically proper isometric action of the mapping class group, that has infinite asymptotic dimension. On the other hand, we show that the most natural candidates for flats in the space of projective geodesic currents have rank uniformly bounded by 8g-9. This follows from the simplicial structure on the boundary of our space, which we describe. In contrast, we prove that the Teichmüller space equipped with the Lipschitz metric has rank equal to 3g-3.

events.title: Composition Colloquium: Andrea Agostini
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: Andrea Agostini was born on 21 May 1975 in Bologna, Italy. He studied at the Conservatorio Giovanni Battista Martini, where he received a degree in composition in 2000 (studying under Alessandro Solbiati, Giovanni Verrando, and Paolo Aralla), in electronic music in 2001 (studying with Lelio Camilleri), and piano in 2004. Between 1999 and 2006, he also took masterclasses with Ivan Fedele, Brian Ferneyhough, Michael Jarrell, and François Paris. In 2008-2010, he completed his studies with the Cursus (IRCAM's composition and computer music course). He was an IRCAM scholar-in-residence from 2011 to 2013. Andrea Agostini composes instrumental and electroacoustic music, for which he has won numerous prizes and awards, including the Zucchelli Prize in 1999 and in 2000, and the Magone Award in 2001. In 2002, he was a finalist for the Prix international Noroit-Léonce Petitot. In 2003, he won the Concurso Internacional de Composição Electroacústica Música Viva. In 2005 he received third prize for composition in the Seoul International Music Competition and an honorable mention at the Gaudeamus Festival Composers Awards. In 2007 he was a finalist in the Franco Evangelisti International Composition, sponsored by Nuovo Consonanza, and received a Commande d'état (a commission from the French Ministry of Culture) for Musica per il chiostro di Royaumont. His music is performed in festivals across the world, including Festival Musica in Strasbourg, MiTo and Sincronie in Milan, REC in Emilia-Romagna, the IMEB Festival in Bourges, Festival MIA in Annecy, and Northern Spark in Minneapolis. His curiosity for different musical languages led him to explore rock and improvisation, and to study non-Western musical practices. He plays bass with the rock band Frida X, for which he is also an arranger, progammer, and sound engineer. He also composes music for theater, cinema, and radio, and live electronics and motion capture for Project C, a group specialized in sound design for theater performances. He also designs sound environments for visual art installations. With Daniele Ghisi, he created a digital platform for computer-aided composition titled "bach: automated composer's helper". In 2017, during his research residency at IRCAM, he developed a programming language for the Max environment, creating a set of tools based on the bach library. As a musician, Andrea Agostini has collaborated with ensembles such as Icarus and the Orchestre national de la RAI in Turin, for concerts and recordings of works by Fausto Romitelli, Giovanni Verrando, and Oscar Bianchi. In addition, he has given masterclasses and workshops in the conservatories of Bologna, Genoa, and Strasbourg, and in several universities in the United States (Harvard, San Diego, and Stanford). He is currently professor of computer music (algorithmic and computer-aided composition) at the Conservatory of Turin. NOTE: Andrea is in residence at CNMAT for the Fall semester

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Josh Figueroa, Professor, UC San DiegoTitle: The Carbonyl-Isocyanide Relationship and BeyondRecent results concerning the synthesis and reactivity of low-coordinate transition-metal complexes featuring sterically encumbering m-terphenyl isocyanide ligands are presented. Given the isolobal relationship between organoisocyanides and carbon monoxide, these complexes serve as mimics of the unsaturated binary metal carbonyls. The latter have traditionally been studied in either the gas phase or by matrix-isolation techniques and, consequently, their condensed-phase reactivity patterns are largely unknown. Specifically addressed will be synthetic studies that have delivered homoleptic and heteroleptic isocyanide complexes that mimic several unsaturated binary carbonyls for the middle and late transition metals. An emphasis is placed on the generation of anionic isocyanide complexes and their use as metal-based nucleophiles. The constrained steric environment enabled by m-terphenyl isocyanides has allowed for the isolation of unique organometallic complexes when these anionic isocyanide complexes are treated with main group electrophiles. Such systems support the stabilization of the simple 10e– diatomic molecule boron monofluoride (BF) as a terminal ligand, as well as diphosphorus (P2) as side-on bound ligand to a mononuclear metal center. The reactivity patterns of these complexes are detailed, with purpose of establishing the electronic structure features of the bound diatomic ligands. Also discussed is the synthesis of other, diatomic main-group species within the protective environment of the m-terphenyl isocyanide framework, as well as the use of m-terphenyl isocyanides as agents for the construction of new materials. events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Ioanida Costache (Stanford)
events.description: "Unsilencing the Archive: Enunciation, Song, and Romani History" Dr. Ioanida Costache, Stanford University Abstract: This talk explores the silence of the archive and its attendant epistemic regimes in relation to Romani people, who have served as an "Ontological Other" in the European imaginary (Wynter 1987). I posit that archival silence registers the racialization that undergirds systems of knowledge production and ask: How might sound "augment" a Romani subjectivity conditioned by abjection? At stake is music's capacity to function as an affective archive and alternative site of historical enunciation. Bio: Ioanida Costache is Assistant Professor of Ethnomusicology and, by courtesy, of Anthropology at Stanford University. She is also a faculty affiliate of the Center for Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity. Her work explores the legacies of Romani historical trauma and feminist critiques of the present inscribed in Romani music, sound, and art. Her writing has been published in EuropeNow, Revista ARTA, Critical Romani Studies, and European History Quarterly and is forthcoming in Ethnomusicology. Her research has been supported by two Fulbright grants and the Council for European Studies. She has held visiting and postdoctoral fellowships at the University of Pennsylvania, the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and the USC Shoah Foundation. A reception will follow.

events.title: William Kentridge's The Head & the Load
events.location: Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, Oakland
events.description: Thursday, November 12, 7:30pm Friday, November 13, 7:30pm Saturday, November 14, 7:30pm Sunday, November 15, 3pmTheater William Kentridge'sThe Head & the LoadWith music composed and conceived by Philip Miller with Thuthuka SibisiWilliam Kentridge, concept and director Philip Miller, composerGregory Maqoma, choreography Thuthuka Sibisi, music director and co-composer Visionary South African artist William Kentridge returns to Cal Performances after two previous visits, featuring the US premiere of SIBYL in 2023 and the Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No in 2025. This time, he brings the West Coast premiere of a seminal work that—through dance, projection, speech, song, shadow play, costume, and music—chronicles the untold history of more than two million Africans who labored, fought, and died during the First World War. The Head & the Load takes its name from a Ghanaian proverb, "The head and the load are the troubles of the neck," and continues Kentridge's exploration of history, language, and artistic and political movements through richly layered and inventive performance works. Kentridge's production unfolds on a massive stage, weaving together texts by anticolonial authors and Dada poets in multiple languages, with original music by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi that intermingles traditional African songs with quotes from WWI-era European music by Satie, Hindemith, and Schoenberg. Prior to the Fri, Nov 13 performance William Kentridge will participate in conversation with Debarati Sanyal (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/debarati-sanyal), director of UC Berkeley's Center for Interdisciplinary Critical Inquiry. From 6-7pm the two will explore the creative and historical context of the work, as well as its relationship to Cal Performances' 2026–27 Illuminations theme, "Innocence & Experience." This talk is free to all ticket holders to the performance that evening.

events.title: Across Eurasia with the Sogdians: Trade, Religion, and Cultural Exchange
events.location: Society for Asian Art, Asian Art Museum
events.description: The Sogdians were an Iranian-speaking people from the great Central Asian cities of Samarkand and Bukhara. Between the fourth and eighth centuries CE, they became the most influential merchants of the Silk Roads, establishing trading communities that stretched from Central Asia to China and beyond. More than traders, they served as cultural brokers, carrying not only goods but also artistic traditions, technologies, and religious ideas across Eurasia. Through their far- reaching networks, they helped shape the spread of Buddhism, Manichaeism, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism, leaving a lasting imprint on the art, architecture, and urban life of the Silk Roads. Dr. Sanjyot Mehendale is an archaeologist specializing in the trade, mobility, and cultural exchange networks of Eurasia, with a particular focus on the so-called Silk Roads. She teaches Central Asian and Silk Road art and archaeology at the University of California, Berkeley. Her current research examines medieval highland urbanism in Central Asia through the excavation of the site of Tugunbulak in eastern Uzbekistan, a collaborative project with Michael Frachetti (Washington University in St. Louis) and Farhad Maksudov (Uzbekistan Academy of Sciences). This study group consists of a morning session and an afternoon session. Please note that lunch is not included in theregistration fee. events.title: William Kentridge's The Head & the Load
events.location: Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, Oakland
events.description: Thursday, November 12, 7:30pm Friday, November 13, 7:30pm Saturday, November 14, 7:30pm Sunday, November 15, 3pmTheater William Kentridge'sThe Head & the LoadWith music composed and conceived by Philip Miller with Thuthuka SibisiWilliam Kentridge, concept and director Philip Miller, composerGregory Maqoma, choreography Thuthuka Sibisi, music director and co-composer Visionary South African artist William Kentridge returns to Cal Performances after two previous visits, featuring the US premiere of SIBYL in 2023 and the Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No in 2025. This time, he brings the West Coast premiere of a seminal work that—through dance, projection, speech, song, shadow play, costume, and music—chronicles the untold history of more than two million Africans who labored, fought, and died during the First World War. The Head & the Load takes its name from a Ghanaian proverb, "The head and the load are the troubles of the neck," and continues Kentridge's exploration of history, language, and artistic and political movements through richly layered and inventive performance works. Kentridge's production unfolds on a massive stage, weaving together texts by anticolonial authors and Dada poets in multiple languages, with original music by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi that intermingles traditional African songs with quotes from WWI-era European music by Satie, Hindemith, and Schoenberg.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). Let out only for holidays, the play centers around the inner conflicts of the royal family as they fight over a kingdom during the Christmas of 1183. As Eleanor says, “Every family has its ups and downs,” and this royal family is no exception.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: OpenAI's proof of isomorphism of free group factors, and further developments
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Dima Shlyakhtenko, UCLAWe will present a version of OpenAI's proof of free group factor isomorphism. A strengthening of the proof also shows that the reduced C*-algebras of free groups have strong reduced free products absorption properties. Moreover, C*-algebras generated by n=2, 3,… or countably many semicircular elements are all isomorphic, and the same is true for reduced free products of copies of the Jiang-Su algebra. A common ingredient is a certain automorphism approximation property; a relative version of that property appeared in our recent work on the identification of von Neumann algebras of Fuchsian groups.

events.title: Pavement Management Systems and Preservation Strategies
events.description: Description Pavement networks are often the most valuable asset that an agency owns. This asset is not only expensive to replace, but it is an essential component to the traveling public's safety. Agencies are looking for more cost-effective ways to perform engineering, maintenance, management, and rehabilitation of roadways more than ever before to stretch funding allocations. A pavement management system is an essential tool to assist in cost-effective roadway maintenance planning. This is the primary overview course on pavement management systems and preservation strategies in the training certificate program offered by the City and County Pavement Improvement Center (CCPIC) in partnership with TechTransfer. Topics IncludePavement management principles Street inventory development Pavement condition surveys (pavement distress) Pavement condition indices Quality management Types of PMS software Types of maintenance treatments Performance prediction models Funding scenarios Developing a work plan using appropriate prioritization techniques Data to use in communicating with elected officials What You Will Learn This class will cover the fundamentals of pavement management systems (PMS). The student will learn the types of distresses included in a typical PMS, how pavements are surveyed for condition, and how condition and classification is used within a PMS. In addition, the inner workings of a PMS are described, covering prediction models and the use of varying funding scenarios and prioritization techniques to maximize your pavement network condition. The important topic of communicating with elected officials to sell your program will be covered. And preservation and maintenance techniques, commonly used by local agencies will be presented. Who Should Attend This course is designed for engineers or maintenance superintendents responsible for:Collecting data and updating a pavement management system Determining the types of repairs for streets Preparing cost-effective multi-year work plans e.g. resurfacing, seal programs, etc. Planning how much funding is required for the future Making presentations on funding street repairs to elected officials Managing or maintenance of PMS software Requirements Students should bring a calculator and pencil for in-class problems

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Structured Generative Models for Offline Model-Based Optimization
events.description: How can machine learning move beyond predicting properties and generating familiar objects to designing better ones? This talk studies offline model-based optimization, where a fixed dataset is used to search for high-performing designs without additional objective evaluations. A central challenge is that optimization can exploit errors in learned models rather than discover genuinely better solutions. Drawing inspiration from offline reinforcement learning, I explore how structural decomposition enables the recombination of familiar components into novel designs. I introduce functional graphical models as a theoretical framework for this idea, followed by Cliqueformer, a structured generative model for optimization, and CliqueFlowmer, which extends these principles to crystalline materials discovery. Together, these contributions demonstrate how exploiting the compositional structure of complex objects can enable more effective optimization and scientific discovery.

events.title: Optimal transportation under McKean–Vlasov dynamics (Camilo Hernández, University of Southern California)
events.description:
Title: Optimal transportation under McKean–Vlasov dynamicsAbstract: We study a broad class of stochastic transport problems under controlled McKean–Vlasov dynamics, allowing control of both drift and volatility, with weak terminal constraints. In contrast to the classical Schrödinger problem, the reference dynamics depend on the evolving law of the process, leading to nonlinear optimization problems on path space, while the terminal constraint is formulated through weak optimal transport, permitting a flexible treatment of distributional targets. This framework encompasses several problems of current interest, including the mean field Schrödinger problem, martingale optimal transport, and Schrdinger–Bass bridges. We establish three main results. First, we prove the existence of optimal controls under general coercivity, continuity, and convexity assumptions. Second, we derive a convex dual representation that extends weak Kantorovich duality and stochastic optimal transport duality to controlled McKean–Vlasov dynamics. Finally, for the mean field Schrödinger problem, we prove convergence, at the level of value functions, of the associated finite-particle Schrödinger bridge problems to the mean field limit, thereby identifying the nonlinear problem as the exact infinite-particle limit of finite-particle Schrödinger bridges. As a byproduct, we establish the existence of an optimal mean field Schrödinger potential, providing a variational foundation for duality in nonlinear stochastic transport. This is joint work with Ludovic Tangpi.
Bio: Camilo Hernández is an Assistant Professor in the Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at the University of Southern California. Before joining USC, he was a Presidential Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of Operations Research and Financial Engineering at Princeton University (2022–2024) and a Chapman Fellow in Mathematics at Imperial College London (2021). He received his Ph.D. from the Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research at Columbia University in 2021, where he was a Cheung–Kong Innovation Fellow, and holds an M.S. and B.S. in Mathematics and a B.S. in Economics from Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá, Colombia. His research centers on the theory and applications of continuous-time stochastic control, with interests in Schrödinger problems, Stackelberg games, contract theory, and time inconsistency. He also serves on the Advisory Board of the USC-Capital One Center for Responsible AI and Decision Making in Finance (CREDIF).

events.title: Rahul Parson | Kathā-Kalkattā: Hindi Literature in a Bengali City
events.description:
A talk by Rahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson), Assistant Professor of Hindi Literature and Culture, at UC Berkeley, that recovers Calcutta as a major center of Hindi literary production from the 1950s to the 1990s, showing how its multilingual archives complicate conventional linguistic geographies of Indian literature and illuminate questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition.
Sukanya Banerjee (https://english.berkeley.edu/people/sukanya-banerjee), Associate Professor of English will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Mon, November 16, 2026 (NOTE NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT Calcutta, Kolkata, Kalkattā: three names for one city, and the last one belongs to the Hindi and Urdu speakers who make up more than a third of its population. The conventional geography of Indian literature follows the linguistic boundaries drawn by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 — literary habitations of Bengali for Bengal, Hindi for north India, Tamil for Tamil Nadu — a map that effaces Hindi writing produced outside the Hindi belt. Calcutta has been a Hindi literary city for over two centuries, since Bengal gave Hindi its first printed newspaper. This talk takes up the decades from the 1950s to the 1990s, when writers, editors, and theatre-makers set out to define what a Calcutta Hindi literature might be. They compiled their own archives, collections, and critical practices: R̥shi Jaiminī Kauśika's Kalakattā ke Hindī kathākāra (1952), Sharad Deora's two-volume Mahānagar (1969), the annual Kalkattā (1985–98), the journal Aṇimā, named for the yogic power of becoming infinitesimally small, and Shyamanand Jalan's theatre group Anamika. What emerged was a literature shaped by contact and separation at once — from Bengali locally, and from the movements of the Hindi belt. Reading the city as a literary confluence rather than a single tradition changes our account of both Hindi literature and Calcutta. The map was drawn over the multilingual city; the paper trail shows what it covered. The archive poses questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition in Calcutta and similar global port cities. ABOUT THE SPEAKERRahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson) received an MA and PhD in the Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, with a specialization in Modern Hindi literature. Before returning to the Berkeley in 2021, he served as an Assistant Professor of Hindi and Urdu at the University of Colorado, Boulder (2016-2020) and a Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter (Postdoctoral Researcher) at Max-Weber-Kolleg, Universität Erfurt, Germany (2014-2016). Rahul Parson's area of specialization is Hindi literature and literary history, with a particular emphasis on Hindi movements in Bengal. His book project, Confluences at the End of the Ganges: Modernity, Migration and Hindi Literature in Kolkata, fills in the Bengal portion of the map of Hindi studies. The monograph reveals the dynamism and syncretism of the hitherto overlooked world of Hindi literature in Bengal and the affective archives and narratives of migrants. It inaugurates research on the literatures of displaced and migrant peoples in South Asia by using cultural texts to explore the articulations of life-worlds of women and migrants. Additionally, he researches early-modern Jain poetry and philosophy, particularly the Jain adhyātma (spiritual or mystical) poetry. Dr. Parson participated as a core member of a research group based at the Max-Weber-Kolleg. In this capacity, he worked as a co-editor of a four-volume series entitled: Religious Individualisations: Historical Dimensions and Comparative Perspectives (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2020). events.title: The 2026 Emilio Segrè Lecture Featuring 2026 Nobel Laureate Francis Halzen: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South Pole
events.description: In person at Chevron Auditorium, International House (limited seating)orLivestreamed (https://youtube.com/live/x_feh8RbSjk?feature=share). ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South PoleLivestreamed lecture with 2026 Nobel laureate Francis Halzen (https://youtube.com/live/x_feh8RbSjk?feature=share) — The IceCube project melted 86 holes 2.5 kilometers deep in the Antarctic ice to construct an enormous astronomical observatory, discovering a flux of neutrinos from deep space with energies more than a million times those of neutrinos produced at accelerator laboratories. Francis Halzen, a visiting lecturer and winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, will discuss the telescope, discovery, and launch of multiparticle astronomy. Monday, November 16, 5:30 p.m., in-person at the International House or livestreamed. Learn more, or link to the livestream. (https://youtube.com/live/x_feh8RbSjk?feature=share) Francis Halzen Born in Belgium, Halzen received his Master's and PhD degrees from the KU-Leuven, Belgium, and has been on the physics faculty at UW–Madison since 1972. He is the 2026 Nobel Laureate in Physics. In 2021, Halzen was named a Vilas Research Professor, one of the university's most prestigious honors. He has been a fellow of the American Physical Society since 1994 and a member of the US National Academy since 2024, and is the recipient of numerous awards, including the 2014 Smithsonian American Ingenuity Award, the 2015 Balzan Prize, a 2018 Bruno Pontecorvo Prize, the 2019 IUPAP Yodh Prize, the 2021 Bruno Rossi Prize, the 2021 Homi Bhabha Award, and honorary doctorates at several universities. Halzen is the Principal Investigator of IceCube, a cubic-kilometer neutrino telescope buried in the Antarctic ice at the South Pole. IceCube's first observations of high-energy cosmic neutrinos garnered the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award. In September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from the direction of a blazar called TXS 0506+056. This was the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since they were discovered over one hundred years ago. Also a skilled science communicator, Halzen travels widely, giving about 20 or more invited talks per year at conferences, workshops, and colloquia. He also gives regular public talks to local and national groups and interviews for television and radio. Halzen is the co-author of Quarks and Leptons, a classic textbook on modern particle physics that continues to be used extensively throughout college campuses today. He has a large number of publications to his credit and has written or edited several other books. His essay "Antarctic Dreams," about the early days of AMANDA, IceCube's precursor, was featured in The Best American Science Writing 2000.
