events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Frederik Vestergaard Hyttel | Making sustainable Europe: The growth of sustainability in EU policymaking, 1992-2026
events.description:
Join Ph. D. Candidate Frederik Vestergaard Hyttel in conversation with Professor Stefan-Ludwig Hoffmann for a presentation of new horizons in historical research. Sustainability has become one of the defining political aspirations of our time. Few political actors have embraced it more strongly than the European Union, which has repeatedly cast itself as a global frontrunner of the sustainability transition. Yet today, even as the European Commission insists that Europe must 'stay the course', it is simultaneously weakening parts of the regulatory framework intended to make that transition materialise. How can Europe stay the course while seemingly changing it? This is one of the puzzles that this lecture takes as an entry point into the political economy of sustainability. Rather than treating sustainability as a self-evidently good or politically neutral ideal, it examines how the concept has been constructed, mobilised, and institutionalised in EU policymaking since the early 1990s. Drawing on public and archival documents as well as interviews, it traces how sustainability became a central normative horizon of European integration and how its meaning has changed alongside transformations in European and global political economy.
Frederik Vestergaard Hyttel is a PhD candidate at Aarhus University, and a former visiting researcher at the European University Institute. Holding his MA in International Political economy from King's College London, his research examines the political economy of sustainability in the EU through a focus on discourse, conceptual change, and modes of governance. Before his PhD, he worked on sustainable finance policy and EU-coordination at the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority under the Danish Ministry of Business. Stefan-Ludwig Hoffmann is Chancellor's Professor of History in the Department of History at UC Berkeley. He is an historian of German, European and International History from the late 18thcentury to the present. He is the author, editor or co-editor of 15 books including Geschichte der Menschenrechte (under contract from Princeton University Press).If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Founders and Their Heterogeneous Firms"
events.description: Abstract: Firm creation is at the heart of macroeconomic growth, but entrepreneurial outcomes are highly unequal. In this paper, we study the determinants of which entrants become large firms with macroeconomic importance. Using employer-employee-shareholder linked Canadian administrative data based on tax records, we find that workers with higher employment earnings are more likely both to enter entrepreneurship and to found larger firms with greater growth potential. We incorporate this link between founders' labor-market and entrepreneurial capacities into a quantitative model of endogenous occupational choice. In the presence of ex-ante heterogeneity, small business tax deductions induce negative selection by drawing lower-potential entrepreneurs into entry, largely oﬀsetting their positive eﬀects in alleviating financial frictions and generating a quantity-quality trade-oﬀ in the design of entrepreneurial policies.

events.title: Adam Mahler | 100 Years of Camilo Pessanha: Translating the Other
events.description:
"100 Years of Camilo Pessanha: Translating the Other" — 2026 marked the centenary of the death of Camilo Pessanha (1867-1926), a Portuguese poet who resided in Macau, a colonial enclave of Portugal from 1557 to 1999. A favorite poet of Fernando Pessoa and an influential figure in Luso-Brazilian modernism, Pessanha published only one book in his lifetime, the 1920 Clepsydra. In this lecture, translator and researcher Adam Mahler discusses the significance of the centenary and Pessanha's relationship to Macau. Pessanha's work as a translator, in particular, emerges as a site for reflection on difference across lines of colonial identity and language.
Adam Mahler is a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow in Romance Studies at Cornell University. His scholarship has appeared in PMLA, Hispanic Review, and Speculum, among others. His translation of Shem Tov Ardutiel's Moral Proverbs and Other Old Spanish Poems of Jewish Authorship is forthcoming in the Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library from Harvard University Press.

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
David Limmer, Professor, UC BerkeleyTitle: On the Stability and Function of Chemical Reaction NetworksThe remarkable complexity of living systems emerges from networks of chemical reactions that operate persistently far from equilibrium. These networks sustain stable states despite incessant fluctuations, reorganize in response to changing environments, and process information with extraordinary fidelity. Yet the physical principles that govern their stability and constrain their function remain poorly understood. Unlike equilibrium systems, where free energy provides a unifying organizing principle, nonequilibrium chemical networks lack a comparably general framework. Developing such a framework is a central challenge for modern statistical mechanics. In this talk, I will discuss advances in nonequilibrium theory connecting fluctuations, dissipation, stability, and function. First, I will describe a theory for the stability of reaction–diffusion systems based on the statistical mechanics of rare trajectories. Using instanton approximations and fluctuations around the most probable transition paths, we uncover how nonequilibrium driving and path entropy determine the relative stability of competing states. Second, I will consider biochemical signaling networks and introduce a general dissipation–error bound connecting the energetic cost of driving to the accuracy of responses to time-dependent signals. Together, these results reveal organizing principles that transcend specific molecular mechanisms, with broad implications for chemistry, materials science, and biology.
The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Predicted: How AI is restructuring social life
events.description:
With Mona Sloane, Assistant Professor of Data Science and Media Studies, University of Virginia Drawing on her new book, Predicted (University of California Press, 2026), sociologist Mona Sloane will discuss how AI is best understood as a new type of social infrastructure, one that embeds prediction as a guiding principle of social organization by way of the "prediction paradigm." Rather than treating AI's impacts as downstream effects of engineering design, she traces how AI systems arise from — and in turn reorganize — social practices, institutional logics, and professional authority. At the heart of this project is the development of a sociology of AI: a project of building theory but even more so of active involvement. This sociology of AI demystifies AI and centers qualitative inquiry, institutional analysis, and public engagement to make visible the social arrangements that sustain the prediction paradigm and to reopen space for collective deliberation about alternative futures and forms of innovation.

events.title: Aditya Balasubramanian | Crossings Interrupted or Invisibilized? Rethinking Migration Across the Bay of Bengal
events.description:
A talk by Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a), Senior Lecturer in History at the Australian National University, drawing on a rare archive of family letters and remittances to examine the understudied history of Indian middle-class migration to Southeast Asia and the ways the Depression shaped mobility, economic insecurity, social isolation, and transimperial connections to home. Event moderated by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Nov 17, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–ABSTRACT: Studies of migration across the Bay of Bengal focus largely on the movement of millions of Tamil labourers between the second half of the 19th century and the 1930s to serve the demands of British imperial capital accumulation during the first era of globalization. While connected histories of South and Southeast Asia and memory point to "a large middling group of Indians, clerks in government and private offices, doctors, drivers, lower management in the oilwells and teak sawmills," shopkeepers, and traders (Bayly and Harper, 2005), they fail to say very much about this class of people because of their invisibility to the colonial archive. This paper begins to illuminate what has been hidden thus far. It draws chiefly on the author's collection of 500 pages of remittances and correspondences exchanged between his maternal grandfather P.K. "Java" Raman (1909-97) who migrated to work as a typist in Batavia (today's Jakarta) in the Dutch East Indies and his family members in the Malabar region of British India, between 1930 and 1934. The paper suggests the Depression as a period of migration rather than its eclipse; explores structures of feeling around economic insecurity and isolation of the thin stratum of Indian professionals in Southeast Asia; and sketches an earlier history of remittance between Indians overseas and in the homeland, across empires. Looking beyond the letters, it discusses possible sources and themes for microhistories of crossing the Bay of Bengal.
ABOUT THE SPEAKER:Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a) is a Senior Lecturer at ANU's School of History, in the College of Arts and Social Sciences (CASS). Aditya's first book, Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2023), is a history of economic ideas and politics (UK/US link (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691205243/toward-a-free-economy) South Asia link (https://www.amazon.in/Toward-Free-Economy-Swatantra-Opposition/dp/0691256578)). It was shortlisted for the 2022 Elder Prize in the Social Sciences of the American Institute of Indian Studies and the 2024 W.K. Hancock Prize for best first monograph of the Australian Historical Association, and longlisted for the 2024 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Prize of the New India Foundation. A suite of peer-reviewed articles published over the last several years have interrogated various aspects of Indian political economy between the 1940s and the 1970s. Topics range from India's role in the international economic order, famine in Travancore during World War II, Hindu nationalist economic thought and policy, and anticorruption. He is currently working on two projects. The first is an environmental and economic history of roadbuilding and transport in India. Initial thoughts appeared in this post (https://histecon.fas.harvard.edu/climate-loss/roads/index.html) for the Harvard Center for History and Economics' "Visualizing Climate and Loss" blog in October 2023. During 2025-2028, he is the recipient of an Australian Research Council Discovery Early Career Research Award (DECRA) for this project. The second is a synthetic history of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984, the world's largest industrial disaster. This project is especially concerned with failures of relief and rehabilitation, chronic illnesses, and ongoing environmental pollution. He has just completed an article on forest management in India and is working on an article that sketches a revisionist history of migration between South and Southeast Asia. At ANU, Aditya teaches or has taught historical methods, environmental history, the history of political economy, and South Asian history. His teaching has been recognized with nominations for College and University-wide prizes. He is the Deputy Director of ANU's Center for Environmental History (https://history.cass.anu.edu.au/centres/ceh) and founded the ANU Capitalism Studies Network (http://csn.anu.edu.au/) with Will Bateman (Law) and Melinda Cooper (Sociology). He is completing a second term as Board Member of the South Asia Research Institute (2020-2021, 2024-6). From 2018 to 2024, he created and coordinated the Archives of Economic Life in South and Southeast Asia (https://www.histecon.magd.cam.ac.uk/archives-asia/index.html) website (you can learn more about it in this (https://toynbeeprize.org/posts/doing-online-south-southeast-asian-history/) Toynbee Prize Blog interview). events.title: Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā - Not a moonless night: Śamathadeva's Upāyikā, the oral life of Mūlasarvāstivāda scripture, and early Buddhist philology
events.description:
An exposition of the Abhidharma without the Āgamas, however flawless, "does not capture the heart, just like a moonless night." So runs the colophon of Śamathadeva's Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā (Upāyikā for short), a monumental Sanskrit commentary now extant only in Tibetan translation. The Upāyikā is a commentary of an unusual kind. Rather than explaining Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya through standard exegetical procedures, it traces its scriptural citations back to their authoritative canonical settings in the Āgamas, often reproducing extensive passages, some of which do not otherwise survive in the received corpora. The same colophon states that these canonical materials were recalled from memory. Taking this seriously, the lecture will treat the Upāyikā both as a companion reader to the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya and as a witness to the oral textual life of the contemporaneous Mūlasarvāstivāda lineages of recitation in India. It will examine how the scriptures available to Śamathadeva were organized and transmitted, and will try to locate the otherwise unknown figure of Śamathadeva in time and space. Close philological engagement with this text will show what the practice of early Buddhist philology has to say about what counts as a text and as text-historical evidence.
Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is a Visiting Associate Research Professor in the Department of Buddhist Sudies at Dharma Drum Institute of Liberal Arts (Taiwan), Director of the Āgama Research Group, and currently the Numata Visiting Professor for Buddhist Studies at the University of California at Berkeley. link (https://bhikkhunidhammadinna.com/)

events.title: Dawn Danby & David McConville // Planetary Repair, Shared Futures
events.description:
The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Dawn Danby and David McConville, co-founders of Spherical, an integrative research and design studio working to regenerate the health and integrity of Earth's living systems. Through design, research, and technology, Spherical explores how human systems are embedded within larger ecological, cultural, and planetary webs of relation, and how new forms of infrastructure might support reciprocal relationships with the living Earth. ​In this talk, Dawn and David will examine how climate action is often made politically viable through the language of infrastructure, and why that framing is both necessary and incomplete. Rather than treating infrastructure as a purely technical system, they will argue for a broader understanding that includes the nested scales, living relations, and more-than-human worlds that sustain life. Drawing on their work across ecological design, planetary systems, and media arts, they will explore how climate solutions demand new ways of seeing, mapping, and designing in relation to the Earth. Attendees will be invited to rethink infrastructure not simply as built form, but as a living scaffold for reciprocal care, repair, and transformation. ​This talk is open to the public and is for designers, researchers, students, and anyone interested in climate, systems thinking, and the role of design in shaping more livable futures. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Ignacio Navarrete
events.description: In Sneaking into Print (Toronto, 2026), Ignacio Navarrete (Spanish & Portuguese) explores the impact of early printing on narrative literature in Spain. He reveals how new technology enabled older texts and translations to circulate alongside newly written works, giving rise to a distinct narrative culture. Through an in-depth study of various narrative subgenres including hagiography, the epic, and sentimental fiction, Sneaking into Print integrates historical bibliography, material book features, and literary analysis. By examining texts as physical artifacts and narrative constructs, the book sheds light on their broader implications for narrative theory, offering fresh perspectives on the intersections of literature, materiality, and the early print marketplace. Navarrete is joined by Nicholas Paige (French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Tianyue Zhou (CTML GSR)
events.description:
This week's seminar brings another thought-provoking discussion! Join us on October 28th to hear from CTML GSR Tianyue Zhou (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/tianyue-zhou) presenting his talk on "A CV-TMLE Global Test Approach to Improve Power in Rare Disease Clinical Studies with Multiple-Component Endpoints." The seminar will take place at 12:00 PM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401.
Abstract: Rare disease trials face unique statistical challenges due to limited patient populations and heterogeneous clinical manifestations among patients. Multiple endpoints are often necessary to comprehensively capture treatment benefits. A global test is an approach for evaluating whether a treatment has any beneficial effect across multiple endpoints. We propose a new global test based on a weighted composite endpoint. The proposed global test employs shrinkage-based cross-validated targeted maximum likelihood estimation (CV-TMLE) to learn data-adaptive weights that maximize power while maintaining Type I error control. Shrinkage can be tailored to incorporate existing domain knowledge, such as anticipated relative effect sizes. In simulation studies designed to reflect real rare disease trial settings, the proposed procedure demonstrated improved power over standard multiplicity adjustments and classical global tests (such as the O'Brien test), while maintaining nominal Type I error, when effects are heterogeneous across endpoints. The proposed method simultaneously learns an optimal weighted composite outcome and provides an unbiased and efficient targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE) for the average treatment effect (ATE) on that weighted outcome, with valid inference taking into account that the ATE is data dependent.
Bio: Tianyue Zhou is currently a PhD student in Biostatistics at the University of California, Berkeley, working with Mark van der Laan and Maya Petersen. His research interests primarily lie in the intersection of causal inference and machine learning, with a focus on real-world evidence generation and improving efficiency in randomized trials.

events.title: Colonial Encounters and Resource Exploitation in Ancient West-Central Sardinia: New Work from the Sinis Archaeological Project
events.description:
This talk will take place in person at the ARF and on Zoom.
Register for online attendance here. (https://bit.ly/ARFtalks-2627) About: The Sinis Archaeological Project is a regional survey in west-central Sardinia that explores the landscapes of the Sinis Peninsula and adjacent territories from multi-scalar, diachronic perspectives. The region encompasses a diverse landscape of agricultural plains, coastal areas, and mountainous territory. In antiquity, it was inhabited by both local Nuragic people and foreign colonizers (Phoenicians, Carthaginians, and Romans) who exploited its rich resources, ranging from salt and other marine resources, to metals, to agricultural products. Our aim is to understand the diverse social and environmental factors impacting resource extraction, settlement patterns, and colonial interactions in this varied and dynamic landscape in the 1st millennium BCE through late antiquity, as well as the impacts of modern landscape use on the archaeological record. This talk will present the project methodologies and cumulative results of fieldwork since 2018, with a focus on the Iron Age and Roman periods.

events.title: The Canadian Transition from Whaling to Whale Watching
events.description:
Despite the International Whaling Commission's establishment of a moratorium on commercial whaling in the 1980s, some countries and indigenous communities continue to take part in the practice commercially, for research, or subsistence. Whaling is a centuries-long practice whose data baseline is often set without deep historical consideration, and whale watching has taken the legacy of these human-cetacean relations, rebranded it, and brought it into public view through the lens of conservation and sustainability. One recommendation the IWC makes to shift cultural perceptions and economic viability of what it deems "putting the cetacean population to use" is to transition whaling into a whale watching industry. This highlights the inherent reliance on capitalistic drivers to incentivize international compliance. This study explores the historical trajectory of whaling to whale watching, and investigates arguments regarding their compatibility and continuity within Canadian contexts. It also seeks to elucidate how international nongovernmental organizations have mobilized whale watching as a new purveyor of conservation education, the realistic ability of community-based transitions to an industry highly reliant on tourism, and the ecological implications of whale watching as a capital driven industry. By honing in on Canadian participation in both the whaling and whale watching industries, this study will frame a global issue through commercial and indigenous Canadian and First Nations perspectives. By assessing centuries-long global whaling industries and investigating the fairly new IWC whale watching transition agenda, this historical analysis transcends maritime boundaries to interrogate the realities of imposing strict top-down regulations and expectations on communities whose ability to implement them may be limited or nonexistent.
About the SpeakerSophia Chapple is a PhD candidate at Trinity College Dublin. She is one of four PhD students on the Life in the Currents Project, which seeks to better understand the interplay between marine extraction, ecosystem dynamics, and global climate change by combining methodologies and expertise from computer engineering, zoology, physics, and history. She is particularly interested in the human experience of the Early Modern climatic cooling phenomenon known as the Little Ice Age, and questions whether coastal communities turned to the sea to alleviate terrestrial subsistence pressures, and in what capacity they were able to do so. Her PhD thesis focuses on community resilience and the experiences of marginalized people in Early Modern Scotland, but her background in Political Science and work as a Research Assistant with 4OCEANS has allowed her to expand her scope beyond her typical temporal and spatial boundaries in order to trace specific historical narratives through to present day.

events.title: International Court of Justice: Judicial Fellowship Panel
events.description:
ICJ Judicial Fellowship Panel

Wednesday, November 18 · 1:00 PM · Berkeley Law, Room 141

Each year, the International Court of Justice selects fifteen Judicial Fellows from hundreds of candidates nominated by law schools around the world to clerk at the Peace Palace in The Hague for ten months. Berkeley Law nominates up to four candidates each year and provides a significant fellowship stipend for any Berkeley nominee the Court selects.

Join BJIL and ILS, with support from the Miller Institute, for a conversation with four recent Judicial Fellows: Félix Aguettant (Berkeley Law LL.M. ’23), Allyson Ping, Lara Manbeck, and Marina Wilbraham. They will talk about the application process, their time at the Court, and where the fellowship has taken them since.

PANELISTS

Félix Aguettant is a lawyer in the Legal Service of the European Commission , in the EU External Relations and International Law team, based in Brussels. He is also a PhD candidate in public international law at the Sorbonne. He was a 2024-25 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Abraham and H.E. President Iwasawa . He is an alumnus of Berkeley Law’s executive LLM program and was nominated to the fellowship by Berkeley Law in 2024. He is currently the head coach of Berkeley Law’s 2026-27 Jessup team. Félix is bilingual in English and French and is a member of the California Bar. To date, Felix is the only Berkeley Law alum to have ever been a judicial fellow!

events.title: First Encounters with AI: Writers on Writing
events.description:
Part of a series on the social dimensions of AI organized by CSTMS, this event is a book launch for First Encounters with AI: Writers on Writing, a forthcoming book edited by Nina Beguš (CSTMS). The panel includes your colleague Hannes Bajohr (German), Alex Saum-Pascual (Spanish and Portuguese), and Nicholas Nardini, an LA-based screenwriter who has worked on some major series for Netflix. Nina Beguš will be moderating.
First Encounters with AI gathers some of today's most original literary minds to explore one of the central artistic and cultural questions of our era: What happens to writing when language is no longer used only by humans? As large language models enter the public imagination and everyday creative practice, writers across genres—novelists, poets, screenwriters, essayists, translators, scholars, technologists, language artists—are grappling with profound shifts in how stories are conceived, crafted, and shared. This volume brings together seventeen acclaimed contributors from around the world to reflect on their early, intimate encounters with generative text at a moment when artificial intelligence feels at once thrilling, unsettling, and unavoidable. Their essays portray AI not as a monolith, but as a dynamic field of possibility and tension between creativity and computation, where longstanding human questions about intention, desire, authorship, labor, and value gain new urgency. Ranging from deeply personal meditations to critical provocations, from philosophical investigations to playful experiments, these writers reveal how writing tools shape writing itself—and what is at stake when those tools begin to imitate us. Curated and introduced by editor Nina Beguš, First Encounters with AI offers readers an essential guide to navigating this new literary landscape. Together, these essays map the terrain of our first contact zone with AI, offering clarity, insight, and imaginative depth at a moment of radical change.

events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: Fractional eigenvalue escape rates on quantum graphs, and a Hermitian preparation theorem
events.description:
Speaker: Gregory Berkolaiko, Texas A&M UniversityTake a quantum graph with a core whose edges have length of order s, attach a few infinite leads, and let s go to 0. Some negative eigenvalues will run off to -infinity, and an a priori bound says they cannot go faster than \(s^{-1}\). Simple examples show that this bound is sharp. Surprisingly, an eigenvalue can also escape at the rate \(s^{-2/3}\). Nothing in the problem (the Laplacian, the vertex conditions, the edge lengths) contains a cube root. So which other strange rates are possible?
The answer turns out to be: none. For any graph and any fixed self-adjoint vertex conditions there are exactly two escape rates, \(s^{-1}\) and \(s^{-2/3}\). The number of eigenvalues of each kind, and their leading coefficients, can be read off explicitly from the vertex conditions.
The proof turns the problem into the study of the zero set of an analytic function of two variables, and that brings tools from algebraic geometry into play. The Newton–Puiseux theorem tells us that solution branches follow fractional powers; the difficult part is to show that only two powers are possible. The key tool is a Hermitian matrix version of the Weierstrass preparation theorem, recently proved by Nils Dencker. It leads to an "implicit Rellich theorem": the solutions of a certain class of Hermitian determinantal equations in two variables behave like the eigenvalues of a one-parameter Hermitian family; in particular, they are analytic, as in Rellich's classical theorem. I will explain this result, which may be useful elsewhere, and show how it produces the two rates.
Joint work with Denis Borisov, Marshall King and Julien Royer.

The US nuclear weapons complex is undergoing its biggest transformation since the end of the Cold War. events.organizer: Center for Studies in Higher Education
events.description:
Join us for a talk by Miriam Pawel (Pulitzer Prize winner) on her new book California Dreams: The Making and the Remaking of the University of California (https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/california-dreams-9781639732739/&sa=D&source=calendar&ust=1791997065344272&usg=AOvVaw1px12Uw7pdUP8N5QRGPvQT) Distinguished by its founding mission as an engine of upward mobility, the University of California-a constitutionally independent public trust-is a great American experiment that has persevered through fraught battles over access, funding, and leadership. The University has been at the nexus of nearly every public policy debate and social movement since the Civil War, from women's rights to student protests, from academic freedom to affirmative action, shaping policies that reverberate throughout the United States.
California Dreams narrates UC's rise and resilience through the lens of those whose lives it has transformed-in particular, five pioneering graduates whose diverse paths underscore why the University remains, in the words of Berkeley graduate Joan Didion, "California's best idea of itself." At a time of staggering inequality and uncertainty, as higher education faces unprecedented threats, that role has never been more crucial. Drawing on extensive research in ten archives and dozens of interviews, California Dreams weaves together the linked history of the school and state in all its drama, significance, and humanity; the result is a magisterial narrative of both a remarkable public institution of higher education, and also California itself.

events.title: Descriptive Set Theory Working Seminar: Ergodic theorems for amenable groups
events.description: Speaker: MohammedSaid Alhalimi, UC BerkeleyThe goal of this talk is to introduce amenability of groups and its consequences for the existence of convergent averaging sequences. I will define tempered Følner sequences and Tempelman's condition and explain their relation to averaging problems using the ideas in Ornstein-Weiss (1983). Following Hochman (2006), I will show that finite abelian rank is a sufficient condition for the existence of Tempelman Følner sequence for countable abelian groups. Finally, I will explain the proof of Lindenstrauss (2001) of a pointwise ergodic theorem for amenable groups along tempered Følner sequences.

events.title: EECS Colloquium: Provable Privacy and Security for Autonomous Agents — Are We There Yet?
events.description: In this talk, we take the position that agent security must be approached as a systems problem: the AI model powering the agent must be treated as an untrusted component, and security invariants must be enforced at the system level. Through this lens, efforts to increase model robustness (the dominant viewpoint in the ML community) are insufficient on their own. Instead, we must complement existing efforts with techniques from the systems security domain. We will cover some example solutions that follow this viewpoint, and discuss their pros and cons. We will also identify the challenges that stand in the way of implementing these principles in agents. Somesh Jha received his B.Tech from Indian Institute of Technology, New Delhi in Electrical Engineering. He received his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Carnegie Mellon University under the supervision of Prof. Edmund Clarke (a Turing award winner). Currently, Somesh Jha is the Lubar Professor in the Computer Sciences Department at the University of Wisconsin (Madison). His work focuses on analysis of security protocols, survivability analysis, intrusion detection, formal methods for security, and analyzing malicious code. Recently, he has focused on trustworthy ML. Somesh Jha has published several articles in highly referenced conferences and prominent journals. He has won numerous best-paper and distinguished-paper awards. Prof. Jha received the CAV award for his work on CEGAR and also has received the IIT-Delhi Distinguished Alumni award. Prof. Jha is a fellow of the ACM, IEEE, and AAAS.

events.title: Seminar 291, Department Seminar joint with Labor and Public Finance: Xavier Jaravel (LSE) - Distributional Consumer Price Indices
events.description: Abstract: This paper develops a new public database to estimate inflation heterogeneity across socio-demographic groups in the United States in real time. These distributional CPIs (D-CPIs) are fully consistent with the methodology of the official CPI and are available from 2002 to the present day by household income, age, race and other characteristics. Using this database, I establish three results showing that D-CPIs have important implications for the measurement of long-run trends in inequality and poverty, as well as of real wage dynamics during crises. First, "real" inequality across household income quintiles increased about 45% faster with D- CPIs between 2002 and 2019, compared to the official CPI. While the pre-tax income gap between the top and bottom household income quintiles increased by 15.7 % during this period according to the official CPI, it increased by 22.6 % with D-CPIs. Similarly large adjustments apply to consumption inequality and inequality in pre-tax and post-tax national incomes. Second, today 2.3 million people are below the "real" poverty line using D-CPIs but above the poverty threshold using the official CPI. Third, during the inflation burst following the Covid-19 pandemic, inflation was higher for the middle class, compared to low-income and high-income households. This pattern is driven by gas and vehicles and implies that the compression of "real" wages was about 28% faster with D-CPIs than with the official CPI. Similar patterns of inflation heterogeneity hold in extensions allowing for geographic heterogeneity in inflation, non-homothetic price indices, and expanding the analysis back to 1983. See full paper here (https://www.xavierjaravel.com/_files/ugd/bacd2d_40a5d2231f0847e1a2e20f6ca4031c7d.pdf).

events.title: Closing the AI Divide: A Human-Centered, Equity-Driven Model for College-Level Writing
events.description:
First, an open secret: we use language to communicate with AI. Students must critically evaluate and curate AI-generated text, discerning which of its sometimes dubious suggestions to accept, adapt, or reject — all through the written word. Not surprisingly, "English majors make the best prompt engineers," says Google's senior director of applied AI engineering. The rise of generative AI has made human expertise in critical reading, writing, and editing newly valuable and consequential. College students who flourish understand this and recognize that traditional literacies form the foundation of AI literacy; those who don't risk falling behind. What can be done to close this looming AI divide?
Marit MacArthur discusses PAIRR (Peer and AI Review + Reflection), an award-winning, human-centered curricular model for teaching college-level writing in the age of AI. Developed at the UC Davis Writing Center, where MacArthur teaches and serves as coordinator of AI and emerging technology, PAIRR is designed to build critical AI literacy while simultaneously improving equity in access to writing support for students. PAIRR is being implemented and evaluated at public colleges and universities across California. After her talk, MacArthur engages in conversation with Jenae Cohn, executive director of UC Berkeley's Center for Teaching and Learning, and select undergraduates who reflect on their experiences with AI and writing.

events.title: Earl L. Muetterties Lectures in Chemistry
events.description:
Joesp Cornella, Director, Max-Plank InstituteExploring the Far Reaches of the Periodic Table: Bismuth Redox CatalysisThe success of transition metal catalysis in organic synthesis is rooted in decades of advances in fundamental organometallic reactivity. Bonding theory on d-block elements has allowed synthetic chemists to design novel and powerful catalysts that underpin modern chemical manufacturing. However, the increasing demand, cost, and environmental impact associated with many transition metals highlighted the need for alternatives. To this end, exploration of underutilized regions of the periodic table might reveal unconventional mechanisms inaccessible within established frameworks, making the search for sustainable alternatives a powerful driver of discovery. Beyond the transition metal realm lies a group of elements that have largely been overlooked by the synthetic community: the heavy elements, ignored by many due to the historically bad reputation associated to them. Yet, among them, one can find bismuth (Bi), placed at the fringe of the periodic table, virtually representing the last stable element. Bismuth is the main character of this talk, which will highlight how our laboratory unlocked its potential as redox catalyst for organic synthesis. Importantly, we will discuss how relativistic effects encoded in bismuth's electronic structure are the main driver in certain contexts, thus shaping the kinetic and thermodynamic landscapes of chemical reactions.
Lecture 1 of 2

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: A Fireside Chat with Dr. Lindsay Owens on her new book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet
events.organizer: Berkeley Center for Consumer Law & Economic Justice
events.description:
Everywhere you turn, Americans are getting ripped off: Online ticket sellers hide behind exorbitant extra fees. Landlords use software to band together and organize artificial rent hikes. Surveillance pricing, algorithmic price fixing, and other high-tech forms of price gouging are the latest frontiers in corporate profiteering, and they’re distorting markets and undermining American households’ financial security.

Building on the novel research and analysis in Dr. Lindsay Owens’s new book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet, this conversation explores the modern landscape of predatory pricing and corporate profit-seeking. Dr. Owens will unpack how unprecedented corporate consolidation combined with algorithms that test, personalize, and coordinate prices at a scale unimaginable a decade ago has given companies incredible power and transformed pricing into a highly engineered science. As a result, the old pricing rulebook is gone. In its place, there’s a new credo: The best price is the one you personally are willing to pay.

Join us for a fireside chat and live Q&A with Dr. Lindsay Owens, President and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a leading economic think tank and corporate watchdog.

Date: Thursday, Nov 19, 2026

Time: 1:00-2:00pm

Location: Room 105 (Law Building)

Note that CBS will be filming the event as b-roll for their segment on Gouged ! If you do not wish to be recorded, please contact the Center at consumerlaw@berkeley.edu.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Charles Whittaker, Assistant Professor, Infectious Diseases & Vaccinology, School of Public Health
events.description:
Title: Modelling the next generation of medical countermeasures for pandemic preparedness and controlAbstract: Medical countermeasure (MCM) development has largely been reactive: vaccines and therapeutics are developed against known, circulating pathogens, or only after a novel pathogen has been identified and sequenced. This poses a problem for pandemic preparedness - even on accelerated timelines, reactive development of vaccines or antivirals against a newly emerged novel pathogen may take many months, and leave a substantial gap between detection (of the novel pathogen) and availability (of the MCMs). It is in this window that much of an pandemic's health burden, and the need for costly non-pharmaceutical interventions, accrues. Broad-spectrum MCMs that are active across an entire viral family or genus rather than a single pathogen, offer a way to close that gap. Because they don't depend on knowing the exact threat in advance, they can be manufactured and stockpiled ahead of time, and deployed immediately following novel pathogen detection. In this talk I'll present two case studies exploring what that early availability could achieve. The first examines a broadly protective sarbecovirus vaccine, considering its use for outbreak containment and for protecting high-risk groups during a hypothetical future SARS-X pandemic [1]. The second examines the potential impact of a pan-filoviral oral antiviral used as post-exposure prophylaxis during ebolavirus outbreaks; a use-case motivated by our ongoing work responding to the Bundibugyo epidemic in DRC [2]. In both cases, the work will explore how we can most effectively use these emerging tools to support pandemic preparedness and response efforts; as well as the factors influencing their public health impact and overall value. [1] https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-63399-x (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-63399-x) [2] https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(26)00437-8/fulltext (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/laninf/article/PIIS1473-3099(26)00437-8/fulltext)
Bio: Dr. Charles Whittaker is an Assistant Professor of Infectious Diseases and Vaccinology at Berkeley Public Health, where he directs the Pandemic and Epidemic Threat Analytics Lab (PETAL). His research focuses on the dynamics, detectability and control of pathogens with pandemic potential, and uses state-of-the-art analytical approaches spanning viral phylodynamics, epidemiological modelling and machine learning to uncover new insights into how pathogens spread through populations and to enhance preparedness and response strategies for public health emergencies. Central to this work is a focus on equity, addressing how the inequitable distribution of resources hinders effective outbreak response, and developing solutions to ensure everyone is protected from pandemic threats. Current research topics include projects on novel pathogen surveillance, the drivers of zoonotic spillover, and next-generation medical countermeasures such as broad-spectrum vaccines.

events.title: Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution
events.organizer: Institute for the Study of Societal Issues
events.location: Berkeley Way West (Second Floor Lobby), 2121 Berkeley Way, Berkeley CA
events.description:
The event will feature Nicholas L. Baham III, Jocyl Sacramento, and Carlos Salomon—editors of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution (Routledge, 2026)in conversation with Cati V. de los Rios. The book presents key theories, concepts, practices, and movements in Ethnic Studies, illuminating the complex processes of race-making and power in the U.S.Nicholas L. Baham III is a Professor of Ethnic Studies at California State University East Bay and teaches courses in Black Studies and Genders & Sexualities in Communities of Color. Dr. Baham is a graduate of the College at the University of Chicago, earned his Master's degree in Anthropology at Stanford University, and received his Ph.D. in Anthropology at Indiana University, Bloomington. In addition to serving as co-editor and co-writer of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution, Dr. Baham is also the author of The Coltrane Church: Apostles of Sound, Agents of Social Justice, co-writer for The Podcaster's Dilemma: Decolonizing Podcasters in the Era of Surveillance Capitalism, and co-writer of When is Wakanda: Afrofuturism and Dark Speculative Futurity. He has published articles and book chapters on Jazz, James Baldwin, Afrofuturism, and Critical Media Literacy. In 2015, he published his first mystery novel, The People's Detective: A Sonny Trueheart Mystery, a fictional account of missing and trafficked young women of color in Oakland, California. He is currently serving as Interim Associate Dean for the College of Letters, Arts, and Social Sciences. For more information, go to nicholasbaham.com (http://nicholasbaham.com/)
Jocyl Sacramento (she/her/siya) is an Associate Professor of Ethnic Studies at Cal State East Bay. She specializes in Asian American Studies, K-12 Ethnic Studies, critical pedagogies, comparative racialization, and Pinayism. Dr. Sacramento completed her MA and Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley School of Education, where she was a Graduate Fellow at the Institute for the Study of Societal Issues. She received her BA in Ethnic Studies and Sociology from the University of California, Riverside and earned her MA in Asian American Studies from San Francisco State University, where she taught Filipinx American Studies with Pin@y Educational Partnerships. Her praxis-oriented work emerged from her participation in youth-led action research and her service with various youth programs and schools. Dr. Sacramento currently serves as Co-Principal Investigator for Cal State East Bay's AANHPI Student Achievement Program. You can find Dr. Sacramento's published work in Amerasia Journal, AAPI Nexus, Journal of Asian American Studies, The Urban Review, Equity & Excellence in Education, Peabody Journal of Education, Review of Educational Research, and Journal of Educational Psychology. She is co-editor of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution (Routledge). Carlos Manuel Salomon is a Chicano author, educator and activist with indigenous roots in the Arizona and California borderlands region and Professor of Ethnic Studies, California State University, East Bay. His research interests include borderlands ancestry, collective and cultural memory, Chicano/a folklore, migration, and oral history. He received his Ph.D. from the University of New Mexico in Borderlands and Latin American History. He is the author of "Pio Pico: The Last Governor of Mexican California (https://www.oupress.com/books/9782065/pio-pico)" (Oklahoma 2010), which covers the astonishing life of the nineteenth-century Afro-Mexican politician Pío de Jesús Pico. Dr. Salomon is the Editor of the "Routledge History of Latin American Culture (https://www.routledge.com/The-Routledge-History-of-Latin-American-Culture/Salomon/p/book/9780367217839)" (Routledge, 2018). The volume gathers authors from Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Uruguay, Mexico, the United States and other nations to reveal the enduring impact of resistance on Latin American and US Chicano/Latina cultural production. He is co-editor of Introduction to Comparative Ethnic Studies: Decolonial Love, Knowledge, and Revolution (Routledge, 2026), which brings together over 50 of the top Ethnic Studies researchers in the country to guide students and instructors toward new avenues of praxis-centered, community-driven learning. Moderator:Cati V. de los Ríos is an Associate Professor of Language, Literacy, and Culture at UC Berkeley's School of Education and a former Spanish, ELD, and Ethnic Studies high school teacher. Her ethnographic, community-based, and participatory research is situated at the axes of literacy studies, educational anthropology, civic and political learning, and ethnic studies, with an emphasis on studying the linguistic-semiotic repertoires that Latina/o/x youth and families deploy and develop across educational settings. Her writing has been published in Aztlán: A Journal of Chicano Studies;Applied Linguistics; TESOL Quarterly; Language Learning; Harvard Educational Review; Reading Research Quarterly; Journal of Literacy Research; Research in the Teaching of English; Anthropology & Education Quarterly; Written Communication; and Learning, Media and Technology.

events.title: Life and Death in the New El Salvador
events.location: CLACS Conference Room (2334 Bowditch St, Berkeley, CA 94720)
events.description:
El Salvador's twenty-first century is defined by a social dialectic where life and death remain in entangled relation and in which popular lifeways exist in a fragile state between function and disrepair. Seemingly, society vacillates between authoritarian safety and gang insecurity. Today, the Central American nation finds itself also in a critical moment of political and organizational enclosure due to the violence wrought by Nayib Bukele alongside the exhaustion of the traditional Salvadoran left. Situated within the longer histories of civil war, postwar violence, neoliberal restructuring, migration, political disillusionment, and the erosion of democratic institutions, the talk argues that Bukelismo cannot be understood solely as a product of propaganda or charismatic populism. Rather, it has drawn force from widespread exhaustion with insecurity, corruption, exclusion, unending hurt, and the unfulfilled promises of the postwar order. Against this backdrop, I identify a source of nonviolent counterpower emerging to confront rising authoritarianism that, often virally, appears to us as carcerality, punitivism, and militarized order. Theorizing from within Bukele's regime, I locate practical activities that are taking place inside El Salvador's contemporary death-world that are, curiously, focusing on an important cultural figure, Monsignor Óscar Romero, whose "living corpus" is being reworked to imagine new horizons, overturn progressive slowdown and reconnect political efforts with the cultural and spiritual lives of ordinary Salvadorans.
Speaker bio:Jorge Cuéllar is an interdisciplinary scholar who focuses on the politics and daily life of modern Central America. Cuéllar's first book, a grounded study of El Salvador's turbulent postwar to "post-postwar" transition is entitled, Everyday Life and Everyday Death in El Salvador, forthcoming with Duke University Press. In addition to publications in scholarly journals and volumes, his writing appears in El Faro, NACLA, The Los Angeles Review of Books, New Left Review, and The Abusable Past. Cuéllar is appointed Assistant Professor of Central American Studies in the Department of Latin American, Latino & Caribbean Studies at Dartmouth College and is a Co-Executive Editor of the North American Congress on Latin America (NACLA)
Co-sponsors: Associate Professor of Comparative Literature, Spanish & Portuguese, and New Media and Craigslist chair Tom McEnaney; Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies; Department of History; Central American Studies Working Group, Townsend Center for the Humanities

events.title: Esha Niyogi De | Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia
events.description:
A talk by Esha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/), Senior Lecturer in UCLA's Writing Programs, on her new book, Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p088285) (University of Illinois Press, December 2024). The book uncovers the overlooked histories of women who worked as producers, directors, performers, and "star-authors" across the film industries of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. De examines how these women used stardom, collaboration, and creative labor to cross geographic, institutional, and gendered boundaries, claim greater authority over filmmaking, and challenge the structures that often obscured their contributions to South Asian cinema.
Maya Sidhu (https://french.berkeley.edu/people/maya-sidhu), Lecturer in the Department of French and a scholar of film and media studies, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Thu, November 19, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOK This book talk delves into previously submerged histories and hidden voices of women directors and film entrepreneurs from Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India. Drawing on neglected archives and rare field interviews with filmmakers and fans, Esha tells a comparative story of women's creative authority and entrepreneurial labor in selected film industries of South Asia—industries and markets that share languages, arts, and geopolitical rifts. Using "transborder" to refer not only to territorial borders but also to institutional and conceptual ones, her story dwells on two eras of women's cinema in this postcolonial region. In the era of the "star-authors" (50s-90s), female stars in Dhaka, Lahore, and Kolkata perform personas ambiguously to access infrastructures and direct fiction films that breach sexual and national borders. In the era of the "woman director" (2000s), even though opportunities appear to burgeon across the region, women negotiate transnational borders that take less obvious forms of brand-making and censorship. The talk will include rare footage from fiction films made by Kohinoor Akhtar Suchanda, Babita, Nargis Akhter (Bangladesh), Shamim Ara (Pakistan), and Kanan Devi (India). SPEAKER BIOEsha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/)'s research interests lie in South Asian gender politics, film and performance history, and literary history. She is the author of two monographs, a recent study of women's cinemas in selected film industries of Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India titled Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (University of Illinois Press, 2024), and an earlier book on sexual politics and postcoloniality in literature, cinema, and choreography in the Bengal region titled Empire, Media, and the Autonomous Woman: A Feminist Critique of Postcolonial Thought (Oxford University Press, 2011). Other publications include two co-edited books, from University of Washington Press and Duke University Press, and many articles. She is working on two new book projects. The first, a study of the renowned Pakistani actress-singer and film director Noor Jehan in relation to Muslim nationalist arts in the mid-twentieth century, is titled Recasting Noor Jehan:Melody Queen, Film Pioneer, and the Making of National Cultures in South Asia (co-authored with Gwendolyn Sarah Kirk). The second, a comparative study of gendered choreographies of protest in twentieth century avant-garde and industrial films, made by Zahir Raihan, Satyajit Ray, Rangeela, among others, is tentatively titled Moving Bodies Out of Line: Filmic Choreographies, Protest Movements, and Queerness in South Asian Cinemas. Esha is a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Writing Programs at UCLA and a Faculty Affiliate of the UCLA Center for India and South Asia.

events.title: Lecture | Camera Palestina: War, Spectacle and the Flaneur
events.description:
The Center for Middle Eastern Studies, the UC Berkeley Department of History, the Palestinian and Arab Studies Program, and the History of Art Department welcome Professor Salim Tamari for a lecture titled:Camera Palestina: War, Spectacle and the Flaneur This talk will examine how the notion of spectacle and the spectacular in photography was influenced by the situationist text of Guy Labord's Society of Spectacles—which describes how capitalist modernity has degraded social life by replacing all experienced phenomena into its representation. WWI images from Palestine deal with the spectacle of war and its degradation against theatrical images from shadow theatre (Karagoz) in Palestine collected by the musician Wasif Jawhariyyeh.
Wasif's diary has been described by the Guardian newspaper as one of the top ten witness accounts of the twentieth century. The British Historian Montefiore selected it as one of the best five historical narratives of all time.
Bio Salim Tamari is a Senior Research Associate at the Institute for Palestine Studies and Professor Emeritus of Sociology at Birzeit University. He is the outgoing editor of The Jerusalem Quarterly and holds a Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of Manchester. His research focuses on Palestinian social history, urban transformation, and the Ottoman era in Palestine. His books include The Great War and the Remaking of Palestine (2017), The Storyteller of Jerusalem: The Life and Times of Wasif Jawhariyyeh (2015), and Camera Palestina: Patronage and Photography (2022). He received the Palestine Prize for Achievements in the Social Sciences and Humanities in 2018 and the Middle East Monitor Prize for Lifetime Achievement in Social History that same year.

events.title: Screening: "Malês"
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description:
Directed by Antônio Pitanga (Brazil, 2024)
Sinopse (portugus) (English below)
Malês é uma jornada de resistência e coragem, ambientada na Salvador de 1835. Durante seu casamento, dois jovens muçulmanos são arrancados de sua terra natal na África e escravizados no Brasil. Separados pelo destino cruel, ambos lutam para sobreviver e reencontrar-se, enquanto se veem envolvidos na maior insurreição de escravizados da história do Brasil: a Revolta dos Malês.
Malês se consolidou como um marco no audiovisual brasileiro, ultrapassando os 100 mil espectadores em salas de cinema, um grande feito para filmes históricos da época. Sua pré-estreia foi em Salvador, a cidade com maior população negra fora do Continente Africano, onde mais de mil pessoas assistiram ao filme no evento a céu aberto de frente para a praia, o OpenAir. Esta exibição é gratuita e aberta ao público. Não é necessário ingresso, os assentos são por ordem de chegada.114 minutos. Em português e iorubá com legendas em inglês. Trailer: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4EGvbqw_X7A (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tkJA-pN5eno)
Synopsis (English)
Malês is a journey of resistance and courage, set in the city of Salvador in 1835. During their wedding, a young Muslim couple is torn from their homeland and enslaved in Brazil. Separated by a cruel fate, they each struggle to survive and reunite, finding themselves caught up in the largest uprising of enslaved people in Brazilian history: the Malê Revolt.
Malês has established itself as a landmark in Brazilian cinema, drawing more than 100,000 moviegoers to theaters — a remarkable achievement for a historical film of its time. The film's premiere screening took place in Salvador, the city with the largest Black population outside the African continent, where more than 1,000 people watched the film at OpenAir, an outdoor event held by the beach. This film screening is free and open to the public. No tickets required, seating on a first-come, first-served basis.114 minutes. Portuguese and Yoruba with English subtitles. Trailer: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4EGvbqw_X7A (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tkJA-pN5eno)
Co-sponsorsOrganized by CLACS with support from the Consulate General of Brazil in San Francisco and theGuimarães Rosa Institute.
Co-sponsored by the Department of African American Studies.

events.title: Film Screening: La Chinoise
events.description: In an apartment defaced with political graffiti, Jean-Luc Godard's "petit Maoists" debate the principles of the Cultural Revolution, their shortwave tuned to Radio Peking. This Parisian cell, consisting of five young people—Veronique, a student; Guillaume, an actor; Henri, a chemical engineer; Kirilov, an artist; and Yvonne, a country girl—deliberates on the need for action while gorged on the predigested language of revolution. In an almost slapstick assemblage of skits that joins Pop and agitprop, La Chinoise charts the progress of these radicals as they veer from playing at revolution to making it. Godard advances his self-possessed film forward with a lucidity of means that refuses distraction.

events.title: Qalandariyya as Method: Tracing Baba Rahim Mashrab in Contemporary Central Asian Culture
events.description: The figure of Baba Rahim Mashrab, the 17th century poet and itinerant dervish is an important icon amongst Uzbeks and Uyghurs. Born in Namangan, Mashrab travelled across the region of Central Asia, to Kashgar, Khotan, Bukhara, and Balkh, leaving behind a rich repertoire of ecstatic ghazal poetry, and a collection of extraordinary tales of his exploits and encounters, in the Divan-i Mashrab. This paper traces Mashrab's journeys and his legacy in contemporary musical performance. It reflects on the diverse ways in which his poetry is realised musically in different contexts and locales, and the diverse ways in which his poetic texts and his life stories are listened to and interpreted. Taking the qalandar as our starting point allows a richer kind of mobile and connected cultural history to emerge. The footsteps of Baba Rahim Mashrab traverse multiple boundaries and binaries : secular-religious, national-local, classical-folk, traditional-popular. The multiple interpretations of his repertoire in different locales cast light on patterns of oral tradition, twentieth century processes of national culture making, and the legacy and practice of Sufism in Central Asia. Professor Rachel Harris's research is centered on China and Central Asia, with a particular focus on the Uyghurs. She has conducted ethnographic fieldwork in Xinjiang, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan over a period of twenty years. Her work focuses on maqam traditions, intangible cultural heritage, music and Islam, soundscapes, and state projects of territorialization. She applies her research through performance and transmission projects, including concerts, workshops, and recording projects. With twenty years of experience in teaching and doctoral supervision in the field of ethnomusicology, she welcomes inquiries from prospective PhD students. Her most recent book is Soundscapes of Uyghur Islam (IUP 2020), and her most recent edited volume is Ethnographies of Islam in China (U Hawaii 2020). She has previously co-edited the journal Ethnomusicology Forum and served as series editor for the Routledge SOAS Studies in Music series.

events.title: Anatomy of Disintegration: What Brazil Reveals About the Global Far Right
events.description: For four years, Jair Bolsonaro led Brazil and the popular, far-right movement that bore his name. His rise, defeat, and the chaos he left in his wake reflect patterns that are playing out in several countries, from the US to Argentina to India. In Anatomy of Disintegration(Haymarket Books, 2026), Rodrigo Nunes uses Brazil as a point of departure to make sense of why the far right is on the rise all over the world, where its appeal comes from, and explain the dystopian horizon it is moving toward. Through sharp, original analyses of the social composition of its supporters, the material and affective conditions that underpin it, and the mainstream's inability to respond to it, Rodrigo Nunes argues that the contemporary far right is better understood not as an effort to block but as an attempt to harness and accelerate forces of social disintegration set in motion by capital and intensified by the crisis of neoliberalism. Rodrigo Nunes is an associate professor in philosophy at PUC-Rio, Brazil, and a visiting fellow at the University of Essex, UK. He is the author of Neither Vertical nor Horizontal: A Theory of Political Organisation and Organisation of the Organisationless: Collective Action After Networks. His articles have appeared in Boston Review, Les Temps Modernes, Radical Philosophy, Jacobin, and The Guardian. He lives between London and Rio de Janeiro.

events.title: Earl L. Muetterties Lectures in Chemistry
events.description:
Joesp Cornella, Director, Max-Plank InstituteExploring the Far Reaches of the Periodic Table: Bismuth Redox CatalysisThe success of transition metal catalysis in organic synthesis is rooted in decades of advances in fundamental organometallic reactivity. Bonding theory on d-block elements has allowed synthetic chemists to design novel and powerful catalysts that underpin modern chemical manufacturing. However, the increasing demand, cost, and environmental impact associated with many transition metals highlighted the need for alternatives. To this end, exploration of underutilized regions of the periodic table might reveal unconventional mechanisms inaccessible within established frameworks, making the search for sustainable alternatives a powerful driver of discovery. Beyond the transition metal realm lies a group of elements that have largely been overlooked by the synthetic community: the heavy elements, ignored by many due to the historically bad reputation associated to them. Yet, among them, one can find bismuth (Bi), placed at the fringe of the periodic table, virtually representing the last stable element. Bismuth is the main character of this talk, which will highlight how our laboratory unlocked its potential as redox catalyst for organic synthesis. Importantly, we will discuss how relativistic effects encoded in bismuth's electronic structure are the main driver in certain contexts, thus shaping the kinetic and thermodynamic landscapes of chemical reactions.

events.title: Film Screening: Harakiri
events.description: Masaki Kobayashi harnesses the breathtaking beauty of black-and-white, widescreen cinematography to create an abstract epic. Starring Tatsuya Nakadai, the film depicts one man's desperate attempt to crack the blind, absolute authority that characterizes the feudal age and, Kobayashi suggests, our own. In an Edo-period mansion, the camera inches down hallways and finds rooms within rooms to explicate a complex flashback narration. In the bloody climax, the black-robed figures who were caught and dissected by a stationary camera throughout the film come into their own as an inexorable prophecy, like Toru Takemitsu's haunting music and the words that emerge almost rhythmically from the dialogue: harakiri . . . (seppuku).

events.title: Film Screening: Samurai Rebellion
events.description: Rebellion is the fitting original title of this relentless social portrait of those who demand subservience and those who have had enough. A magisterial Toshiro Mifune slow burns his way through the role of dutiful samurai Sasahara, whose attempts to be a "good servant" are about to end. "You retreat, and retreat," says his friend Asano (Tatsuya Nakadai), "until finally you attack." Rare for the genre, the film's plot is set in motion by a woman, one whose willful stand against injustice inspires the men to act. Effective or not, it is the act of rebellion, Masaki Kobayashi implies, that matters.

events.title: Film Screening: Raging Bull
events.description: Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro make the biography of boxer Jake LaMotta into a visceral meditation on existential suffering. Eschewing the romance associated with the sport, Raging Bull shows the struggle of an athlete whose willful determination to succeed on his own terms takes its toll on all those around him—friends and adversaries in equal measure—before he is undermined by self-loathing. Every punch is framed, lit, and cut for maximum impact, with black-and-white cinematography inspired by James Wong Howe. "A fusion of Hollywood genre with personal vision . . . closer to poetry than pulp. Its sculptural weight can only be appreciated on the big screen" (Amy Taubin, Village Voice).

events.title: Jason Moran and the Harlem Hell Fighters: James Reese Europe and the Absence of Ruin
events.description: Saturday, November 21, 7:30pmJazzJason Moran and the Harlem HellfightersJames Reese Europe and the Absence of RuinProgram:The Absence of Ruin is jazz pianist and composer Jason Moran's multidisciplinary meditation on the life and legacy of James Reese Europe, the underrecognized Black American composer and bandleader who landed in France with the Harlem Hellfighters on New Year's Day 1918. The celebrated all-Black unit helped break the stalemate on the Western Front during the First World War, while composer Europe's finely honed military music ensemble popularized the new spirit of jazz in a war-torn France fascinated with Black culture. Moran's layered work explores the idea of memory in Black culture, augmenting his long-standing Bandwagon bandmates––bassist Tarus Mateen and drummer Nasheet Waits––with a seven-piece horn section and visuals by Oscar-nominated cinematographer Bradford Young. An Illuminations: "Innocence & Experience" event. Visit calperformances.org/illuminations for details. Through Cal Performances' Golden Bear Circle program, UC Berkeley students are eligible to purchase a limited number of $10 tickets for this evening's performances.
