events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Film Screening: Rouge
events.description: Rouge is a sensuous and melancholy film about a beautiful ghost searching for her lost lover in modern Hong Kong. Fleur (Anita Mui) and "Twelfth Master" (Leslie Cheung) committed suicide fifty years ago, intending to spend eternity together in Hell rather than be separated by his disapproving parents. But when "Twelfth Master" fails to join her in the afterlife, Fleur returns to Earth to find him. She befriends a journalist couple. Fascinated by her archaic clothes, language, and otherworldly manner, they agree to help. Slipping back and forth in time, "Rouge is something like the Platonic ideal of a cinematic ghost story" (Dennis Lim, Criterion Collection).

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Real Infinitesimal Freeness of Wigner Matrices
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Samuel Gurrola Viramontes, CIMAT GuanajatoIn this talk, within the framework of real infinitesimal free probability introduced by Cebron and Mingo, we will discuss the calculation of the real infinitesimal free cumulants of independent complex Wigner matrices. Our approach relies on establishing a combinatorial relation between annular non-crossing partitions and families of directed graphs. As a consequence, we show that independent complex Wigner matrices are asymptotically real infinitesimally free. In particular, under mild conditions, a complex Wigner matrix is asymptotically infinitesimally free from its transpose. This is based on joint work with James A. Mingo (arXiv:2609.24023).

events.title: Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Bias and Steady-State Convergence (Qiaomin Xie, University of Wisconsin–Madison)
events.description:
Title: Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Bias and Steady-State ConvergenceAbstract: Stochastic approximation (SA) underpins many algorithms in machine learning and reinforcement learning, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD), TD learning, and Q-learning. Constant-stepsize SA is widely used in practice for its simplicity and fast initial progress. Viewing the joint data–iterate sequence as a Markov chain, we establish its geometric convergence to a stepsize-dependent stationary distribution; the iterates thus keep fluctuating around the target, with a bias that averaging cannot remove. We first quantify this bias. In the smooth regime with Markovian data, exemplified by SGD and TD learning, we give an exact leading-order expansion: the bias scales linearly with the stepsize, with a term that couples Markovian dependence and nonlinearity. We then study steady-state convergence (SSC), the behavior of the diffusion-scaled stationary distribution as the stepsize vanishes, through coupling techniques that reduce the recursion to simpler ones sharing the same steady state. For smooth problems, SSC provides a Gaussian approximation of the scaled steady state at the optimal rate in Wasserstein-2 distance, along with finite-time Gaussian approximations for the raw iterates. For nonsmooth problems, exemplified by Q-learning, the picture changes qualitatively: the scaled steady state converges to a non-Gaussian limit, and the bias scales with the square root of the stepsize. This characterization enables a Richardson–Romberg-type extrapolation that removes the leading-order bias without prior knowledge of the smoothness regime, as illustrated on asynchronous Q-learning.
Bio: Qiaomin Xie is an assistant professor in the Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Her research lies in the fields of reinforcement learning, applied probability, game theory and stochastic networks. She was previously a visiting assistant professor at School of Operations Research and Information Engineering at Cornell University. Prior to that, she was a postdoctoral researcher with LIDS at MIT. Qiaomin received her Ph.D. in Electrical and Computing Engineering from University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, and her B.S. in Electronic Engineering from Tsinghua University. Her research has been recognized by the Best Student Paper Award from ACM SIGMETRICS (2026), NSF CAREER Award (2024), JPMorgan Faculty Research Award (2021), Google Systems Research Award (2020) and UIUC CSL PhD Thesis Award (2017).

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis"
events.description:
Please join us on Tuesday, November 24th from 4:00–5:30pm for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis by Matthew Shutzer, Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. Professor Shutzer will be joined in conversation by Youjin Chung, Associate Professor in the Department of Environmental Science, Policy & Management and the Energy & Resources Group at UC Berkeley, and Daniel Aldana Cohen, Assistant Professor of Sociology at UC Berkeley. The talk will be moderated by Michael Watts, Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Departments of South & Southeast Asia Studies and Geography, and the Energy and Resources Group.
About the Book India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. In the book, Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.
PanelistsMatthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching are concerned with the place of the environment in global history, with a particular focus on fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. He has also worked on topics that connect global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. He is currently at work on a second book project on climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945.
Youjin B. Chung (https://youjinbchung.net/about) studies the relationship between gender and inequality, rural development, and socio-environmental change in East Africa, with a focus on Tanzania. The overarching question that drives her research program is: how and why do development policies and processes that aim to improve sustainability and equity outcomes often reinforce existing power structures and marginalize the groups they intend to serve? Over the years, she has channeled this central animating concern into three specific research projects. Using Tanzania as an analytic case, these projects investigate some of the most contentious issues in global development and environmental politics: large-scale farmland investments, sustainable livestock intensification, and the critical minerals rush. She is the author of Sweet Deal, Bitter Landscape: Gender Politics and Liminality in Tanzania's New Enclosures (Cornell University Press, 2024). At Berkeley, she convenes the Critical Ruralities Lab, a research workshop and collaborative mentoring space that promotes empirically grounded and justice-oriented scholarship on development and socio-environmental change in the global countryside.
Daniel Aldana Cohen (https://aldanacohen.com/) is Assistant Professor of Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley, where he is Director of the Socio-Spatial Climate Collaborative, or (SC)2 (https://sc2.berkeley.edu/), and serves as a faculty affiliate in the graduate program on Political Economy. He is also Founding Co-Director of the Climate and Community Institute, a progressive climate and economy think tank. He has been a CIFAR Azrieli Global Scholar (2021-24) and Member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey (2018-19). He is the co-author of A Planet to Win: Why We Need a Green New Deal (Verso 2019). Cohen works on the intersections of the climate emergency, housing, political economy, social movements, and inequalities of race and class in the United States and Brazil. As Director of (SC)2, he is leading qualitative and quantitative research projects on Whole Community Climate Mapping, green political economy, and eco-apartheid. He was also co-founder and co-PI of the Superstorm Research Lab (https://superstormresearchlab.org/), in New York City.
Michael Watts (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-emeritus-michael-watts) is Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. He served as the Director of the Institute of International Studies at Berkeley from 1994 to 2004 and was Director of Social Science Matrix at Berkeley in 2019–20. He was most recently a Non-resident Long-term Fellow at the Swedish Collegium for Advanced Study (SCAS). Watts is a member of the British Academy, was a Guggenheim Fellow in 2003, and was awarded the Victoria Medal by the Royal Geographical Society in 2004, and the Berlin Prize by the American Academy in Berlin in 2016. He was awarded the Ester Boserup Prize in 2024. Watts' writing has addressed a number of development issues especially famine and food security, political violence and the agrarian question in Africa, South Asia and Vietnam, natural resources and especially the energy and mineral sectors, and the political economy of development and governance, more generally. Watts has worked for UNDP, OECD and other development organizations, including the Ford, Rockefeller and MacArthur Foundations. He has published over fifteen books and three hundred articles and has worked extensively with the renowned photographer Ed Kashi. Watts has written extensively on the oil industry, extractive economies and international commodity trading firms.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.
Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Laura M.K. Dassama, Assistant Professor of Chemistry and of Microbiology and Immunology, StanfordTitle: Fat foraging: how pathogenic bacteria construct unusual cell envelopesAs critical components of cell membranes, lipids establish the barrier between cells and their environments and can serve as signaling molecules; they are essential in all domains of life. Despite their importance, some pathogenic bacteria lack the biosynthetic pathways to fatty acids and are reliant on hosts for the provision of lipids. This talk will describe our efforts to unravel the lipid uptake and storage strategies these organisms employ, as well as describe their (limited) synthesis of unusual lipids using environmental precursors. These efforts have provided new insights into mediators of host-pathogen interactions and highlighted metabolic vulnerabilities that can be exploited for the design of anti-infective agents.
The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.description: The Haas Scholars program offers $14,800 scholarships to qualified Berkeley undergraduates to complete research-intensive capstone projects. Every year the program sponsors an interdisciplinary cohort of twenty academically talented undergraduates with demonstrated financial need. To be eligible, students must intend to graduate in Fall 2024 or Spring/Summer 2025, have a 3.45 GPA, and have need-based financial aid (with an Estimated Family Contribution of less than $26,000).This information session will cover all aspects of the Haas Scholars Program, including program commitments, eligibility requirements, program milestones, faculty mentorship requirements and the cohort experience. Students will also learn about the application process and receive tips about how to prepare a successful application.

events.title: Film Screening: Modern Times
events.description: It starts with an overhead shot of sheep and cuts to the throngs coming out of a subway station. Was Charlie Chaplin a Surrealist, or just a realist? His version of modern times looks forward in equal measure to Jacques Tati and 1984. This "silent" is full of modern sounds, heard over loudspeakers and big corporate television screens (not to mention the Tramp's outburst of French-inspired gibberish). Charlie, the ever-elegant Tramp, is an industrial swashbuckler with an oilcan for a sword, but he's begun taking on the characteristics of factory machines, obsessively twisting buttons no matter where they are.

events.title: Film Screening: The Last Waltz
events.description: Martin Scorsese grew up listening to seminal rock DJ Alan Freed, and from Mean Streets onward, his movies have been driven by the power of rock and roll. His love of music is innate and instinctual, so when The Band decided to hang it up after seventeen years on the road, they chose Scorsese to film their farewell concert at Winterland Ballroom on Thanksgiving 1976. The film intercuts the glorious music from one of the all-time great concert lineups with interviews with members of The Band as they talk about their lives and music. The Last Waltz is an elegiac masterpiece that captures a special moment in music history.

events.title: Film Screening: Center Stage
events.description: After a string of memorable performances as strong-willed, beautiful, and virtuous women, the actress Ruan Lingyu committed suicide in 1935, at the age of twenty-four. Stanley Kwan's innovative film goes far beyond the traditional biopic to offer up several strata of "reality," "reenactment," and "cinema." Detailed re-creations of scenes from the actress's too-short life combine with documentary interviews of her contemporaries, actual footage from her existing silent films, and even discussions between star Maggie Cheung, Kwan, and other cast members. Like a Russian doll, Center Stage reveals a Modernist take on the ways in which cinema and culture create an actress, a legend, and a woman.

events.title: Bellissima
events.location: BAMPFA — Berkeley Art Museum & Pacific Film Archive
events.description: Luchino Visconti is in an unusually comic mode for this satire on urban life and movieland ambition. The incomparable Anna Magnani plays a mother trying to launch her young daughter in show business.

events.title: Film Screening: Bellissima
events.description: "What is acting after all?" Maddalena (Anna Magnani) rhetorically asks before the mirror in Luchino Visconti's melodrama of mother love and misplaced ambition. Magnani's extraordinary performance is its own answer. As a working-class mother desperate to get her young daughter a shot at stardom through a Cinecittà casting call, Magnani turns what might have been a simplistic caricature of a domineering stage mother into a fully rendered character, both hilarious and tragically human. Visconti's direction similarly refuses to distinguish between satire and sincerity; even while it mocks the business of moviemaking, Bellissima is an exquisite example of the filmmaker's craft.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Film Screening: White Nights
events.description: This adaptation of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's tale about displaced, disconnected people drifting along crossing, doubling paths was shot in moody black-and-white on a soundstage simulacrum of Livorno, Italy. With it Luchino Visconti veered away from verisimilitude and toward an emphatically subjective style—from neorealism to neoromanticism. As a quiet man who accidentally befriends a troubled, lonely young woman (Maria Schell) and finds himself playing understudy for the absent object of her affections (Jean Marais), Marcello Mastroianni mingles subtly passionate yearnings with a characteristic note of annoyance. His character is both distrustful of and seduced by the romantic dreams that preoccupy the woman he loves.

events.title: Film Screening: GoodFellas
events.description: Working with trusted accomplices, including editor Thelma Schoonmaker, cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, actors Robert De Niro and Joe Pesci, and brilliant first-time collaborators Ray Liotta and Lorraine Bracco, Martin Scorsese combines varied cinematic styles, camera techniques, and a precisely executed collage of popular music, adapting Nicholas Pileggi's chronicle of real-life Mafia associate Henry Hill. Hurtling through some twenty-five years of "family" life, the riveting Liotta gives voice to Hill's chilling and funny first-person account. As focused on quotidian details as on dramatic moments, Scorsese wanted the movie to have a documentary feel, "as if you had 16mm cameras with these guys for 20, 25 years."

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: The hyperinvariant subspace problem
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Hari Bercovici, Indiana University at BloomingtonAmong the results announced by Open AI, there is a solution of the hyperinvariant subspace problem: there is an operator T on a Hilbert space that is not a scalar multiple of the identity, does have nontrivial invariant subspaces, but none of these subspaces is invariant under every operator in the commutant of T. In particular, the commutant (T)' is a nonselfadjoint transitive algebra. The construction uses weighted shifts with few invariant subspaces, and a modicum of ergodic theory: a transformation known as an odometer. The resulting operator T is quasinilpotent. I will argue that the example is correct. Moreover, the example can be modified so that it yields a contraction with essential spectrum equal to the closed unit disk. Such contractions are known to have a large variety of invariant subspaces, and one could ask whether the techniques used to produce these subspaces can be improved to yield a hyperinvariant subspace.

events.title: Adaptive Traffic Control Systems
events.description: Description This newly updated online course offers a summary of fundamental principles, operational requirements and expected benefits of some of the frequently deployed Adaptive Traffic Control Systems. The first session presents various traffic control systems and general characteristics, market state, and evaluations of the ATCS along with other solutions like traffic responsive and Artificial Intelligent (AI) based signal timing. The second session focuses on SCATS (one of the oldest and widely deployed systems in the entire world) and other ATCSs from the US market. The third session presents SynchroGreen and InSync, recent ATCSs which recently gained a lot of popularity among the US customers. Finally, the fourth session addresses SCOOT and ACS Lite, two systems with similarities in algorithms but various detection and communication requirements. Each session is divided into three major parts: the first offers a summary of fundamental principles of a selected adaptive technology, the second covers summary of operational and institutional requirements to run adaptive control, and the third presents operational benefits from available case studies. Topics IncludeFundamental principles of ATCS operations Adjustment of signal timings and operational flexibility Traffic responsive and AI based signal timing Detection requirements Communication requirements Software and hardware requirements Reported operational modes Institutional preparation for deployment of an ATCS Reported operational benefits What You Will Learn Students will obtain a significant amount of technical information to understand fundamental principles of operations, deployment requirements, and reported operational benefits (highlighted through exemplary case studies) of some of the frequently deployed Adaptive Traffic Control Systems. This information will help students to become familiar with these relatively new signal control technologies and develop a realistic set of expectations regarding their deployments and operational benefits. Who Should Attend This course is intended for traffic engineers, planners, technicians, and decision makers in municipal, county, and state agencies interested in the operations, requirements and benefits of Adaptive Traffic Control System technologies, particularly those with the responsibility for the planning, design, implementation, operation, and maintenance of traffic signal control systems for urban areas.

events.title: Aashish Manglik: "Improvising on a Fold: From Odorants to Opioids"
events.description: The seven-transmembrane fold is among evolution's most heavily reused solutions to molecular detection, elaborated in humans into roughly 800 receptors that transduce stimuli from single photons and protons to peptide hormones and much of the sensible volatile chemical space. Yet we still cannot specify from sequence alone what a receptor detects, or how strongly a ligand will activate it. I will describe how deep mutational scanning, paired with structural interrogation, resolves this mapping in two systems at opposite extremes of ligand promiscuity: odorant receptors, where broad chemical tuning appears purchased at the expense of folding stability, and the opioid receptors, where saturating mutagenesis exposes the determinants of agonist efficacy. Together they begin to define how evolution repurposes a single fold to meet new demands.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Amy Weeks, Assistant Professor, University of Wisconsin, MadisonNew enzyme chemistry to decipher post-translational modification function Spatial organization and temporal dynamics are essential properties of cellular signaling. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) to proteins relay biological signals by exerting precise spatiotemporal control over protein function, localization, and lifetime. A systems-level experimental map of post-translationally modified proteins across subcellular space and time would transform our understanding of how PTMs orchestrate complex cellular functions in response to biological stimuli. However, such a map is inaccessible with current technologies. To meet this challenge, the Weeks lab is focused on developing new chemical and enzymatic tools for PTM proteomics with subcellular spatial and temporal resolution. We develop chemical probes and genetically targetable, PTM-selective proximity labeling enzymes to covalently tag post-translationally modified proteins in specific subcellular locations, enabling their enrichment and analysis with mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments. We focus on two pervasive PTMs, proteolysis and phosphorylation, both of which play critical roles in myriad biological signaling pathways relevant to human health and disease. Our technologies are broadly applicable to a wide variety of protease and kinase signaling pathways and provide an integrated view of cellular signaling with implications for both fundamental biological discovery and therapeutic innovation.
The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Julia Bowes | Book Talk: Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (CRG Forum Series)
events.description:
CRG Forum Series + Book Talk*Every Man’s Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism withJulia Bowes, Lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, and author of Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026) and discussantLydia Mathews, PhD Candidate, Department of History, UC Berkeley Dr. JuliaBowes is a lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, where her research focuses on the relationship between gender, the family, and conservatism in the United States. Her first book, Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026), examines how a sovereign conception of the white patriarchal family was at the crux of an emerging conservative ideology opposed to the modern liberal state. The book is an extended version of her dissertation, which was awarded the 2019 Lerner-Scott Prize for the best dissertation in US women's history by the Organization of American Historians. events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Importing Aggregate Demand"
events.description: Abstract: How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

events.title: OpenADMET (Bay Area Open Science Group)
events.description:
OpenADMET - Raising the bar on ADMET prediction with open sciencevZoom information registrationDrug discovery programs frequently stall due to the Avoid-ome, which comprises the complex off-target interactions and ADMET liabilities that traditional heuristic methods struggle to address. To solve this, OpenADMET combines high-resolution structural biology, directed data generation, and machine learning into a systematic framework for predicting and mitigating these liabilities. Central to this mission is generating targeted datasets to host large-scale blind benchmarks that test community predictive models on real-world drug design problems. By uniting hundreds of academic and industry teams through these challenges, webinars, and conferences, the initiative fosters widespread collaboration to establish transparent, data-driven standards across the field.
Pat Walters is Chief Scientist at OpenADMET, an open-science initiative that integrates high-throughput experimentation, structural biology, and machine learning to advance ADMET prediction. Alongside his work at OpenADMET, he serves as an Adjunct Professor in the Department of Bioengineering & Therapeutic Sciences at UCSF. Pat brings over thirty years of industry leadership to his roles, having previously held senior positions at Relay Therapeutics and Vertex Pharmaceuticals. A dedicated educator and communicator, he is the author of the widely read blog "Practical Cheminformatics," where he shares technical insights on computational drug discovery.
Bay Area Open Science GroupThe Bay Area Open Science Group is a growing community for Bay Area academics and researchers interested in incorporating open science into their research, teaching, and learning. Targeting students, faculty, and staff at UCSF, Berkeley, and Stanford, the goal of the community is to increase awareness of and engagement with all things open science, including open access articles, open research data, open source software, and open educational resources. Through this work the group hopes to connect researchers with tools they can use to make the products and process of science more equitable and reproducible.

events.title: Aaron Nyerges, "Counter-Mapping Modernism: Literature, Oil, and the Cartographic Imagination"
events.description:
Aaron Nyerges' recent book American Modernism and the Cartographic Imagination (Cambridge UP, 2025) is a new reading of American modernism that examines the cartographic literature of the United States and places it in context of the state's overseas expansion. Dr Nyerges stretches the map of US literature across an imperial archipelago of territories and outlines a method of comparative reading that brings canonical American authors into dialogue with under-represented writers from across the contested dominions of US empire. He argues that literary artists from across US dominion responded to space-dominating technologies of empire and retooled them to imagine counter-cartographies, designs that challenged the official geographies of the United States. This talk explores the cartographic imagination of modernist literature as it relates to the territorial expansions of the United States in the early decades of the twentieth century. We begin with Langston Hughes's construction and destruction of cartographic material, his tearing apart of his world atlas, and his vision of a nation made errant by oceanic flux. From there we will assemble – and collaboratively analyse – a group of poems that make visible the divergent investments modernists made in the production of "counter-maps," forms of geographic knowledge that challenge the maps made by governments and corporations. In particular, we will attend to the oil maps deposited in Ezra Pound's Cantos, by which he critiques the resource expropriation of former Ottoman territories by Anglo-American cartels. At that very locus, the Iraqi modernist poet Nazik al-Malā'ikah envisions a different kind of energy poetics, where the dividing line between oil's extractive and consumptive spheres is decidedly smudged. Her mapping of an abysmal geography provides anti-colonial counterpoint to the expanding highway infrastructure of the United States, as well as the thermodynamic aesthetics that exhilarate the lyrics of Pound and William Carlos Williams.
Aaron Nyerges (https://www.ussc.edu.au/aaron-nyerges) is a Senior Lecturer in American Studies at the United States Studies Centre, University of Sydney. His book, American Modernism and the Cartographic Imagination, was published by Cambridge University Press in 2025.

events.title: Book Talk: An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa
events.description: Book Talk:An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa (Cambridge University Press, 2026) In what measure could education be an agent of African freedom? Combining histories of race, economics, and education, Elisa Prosperetti examines this question in two West African contexts, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, from the 1890s to the 1980s. She argues that a Black Atlantic perspective changes how we see decolonization and development in West Africa, by revealing schooling's essential role in aspirations of African emancipation. Rejecting colonial exploitation of the African body, proponents of anticolonial development instead claimed the mind as the site of economic productivity for African people. An Anticolonial Development shows how, in the middle of the twentieth century, Africans proposed an original understanding of development that fused antiracism to economic theory, and human dignity to material productivity. Elisa Prosperetti is an Assistant Professor of History at the National Institute of Education/Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. She is a historian of modern African and global history, specializing in histories of race, development, education, and decolonization, with a geographic focus on West Africa and the Black Atlantic world. She received her PhD in History from Princeton University in 2020, and currently serves on the Editorial Review Board of the African Studies Review and as a podcast host for the African Studies channel of the New Books Network.

events.title: Film Screening | My Father and Qaddafi
events.description:
My Father and Qaddafi Film Screening and Director Q&ADate and time of event: Tuesday, December 1, 5:00 PMEvent location: Richard & Rhoda Goldman Theater • David Brower Center • 2150 Allston Way, Suite 100 • BerkeleyThe Center for Middle Eastern Studies presents a film screening of My Father and Qaddafi, followed by a Q&A with director JihanKikhia. Film Summary: When Jihan was six years old, her father flew to Cairo and never returned. Mansur Rashid Kikhia was the Foreign Minister of Libya, ambassador to the United Nations, and a human rights lawyer. After serving in Qaddafi's increasingly brutal regime, he defected from the government and became the leader of the peaceful opposition. For many, Kikhia was a rising star who could have been the next leader of Libya, however, in 1993 he disappeared from his hotel in Egypt. Jihan's mother Baha Al Omary, a strong-willed Syrian-American artist, began searching for him, launching the family into an international political maze. Her mission to find justice brought her to the Libyan desert in the middle of the night, face to face with Qaddafi to negotiate her husband's release. Yet it wasn't until after the regime's fall, 19 years later, that his body was found in a freezer near Qaddafi's palace.
My Father and Qaddafi takes the audience on a raw and reflective journey as Jihan pieces together a father she barely remembers, while discovering the troubled history and politics of Libya. Her journey starts from fading personal memories, leading to encounters with family members, her father's peers, and historical archive footage. Hoping at first to uncover the truth, Jihan instead transforms the mystery into a curiosity that brings her closer to her father and her Libyan identity. She approaches politics not as a distant subject, but as a lived experience that penetrates into every human relationship - even between a little girl and her father. events.description:
Join us for a book launch and signing by Harjant S. Gil (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html)l, Professor of Anthropology at Towson University and an award-winning documentary filmmaker, based on his new book, Coming of Age in Macholand: Masculinity, Patriarchy, and the Search for Freedom in Indian Punjab (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand) (University of Chicago Press, forthcoming in Nov 2026), an eye-opening examination of masculinity, violence, and transnational migration focused on present-day Indian Punjab. Pre-order the book now. Only limited copies will be available to purchase at the event" - https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand). Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ———–DATE: Tue, Dec 1, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKIn Coming of Age in Macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand), anthropologist and filmmaker Harjant Gill examines how Punjabi men in India, disillusioned by promises of power and control, contend with patriarchy: by submitting to it, attempting to transgress it, migrating to escape it, or coming undone by it. Gill takes readers deep inside men's worlds to show how boys come of age and how masculinity is produced through pervasive violence, while also being underwritten by intimacy, fraternal love, and homosocial bonds. Based on four years of fieldwork conducted over a decade and hundreds of interviews, Gill explores how boys learn to become men against the backdrop of patriarchal constraints, political violence, shifting agrarian economies, and steady outward migration. He shows the extent to which violence is a function and a reflection of powerlessness. By tracing the making of masculinity in a society where sexuality is sanctioned almost exclusively through heteronormative frameworks of marriage and family, this book documents how patriarchy forecloses agency and autonomy. Ultimately, Coming of Age in Macholand offers a powerful indictment of patriarchy as a system that not only oppresses women and queer people, but also constricts men's intimate, sexual, and emotional lives. ABOUT THE AUTHORHarjant Gill (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html) is a professor of anthropology and an award-winning documentary filmmaker whose work bridges ethnography, visual storytelling, and public scholarship. His research and creative practice explore masculinity, migration, media, religion, and popular culture in South Asia and its diasporas, with a particular focus on Punjab and Sikh communities. Through film and writing, he examines how intimate lives are shaped by patriarchy, nationalism, violence, and transnational mobility. Gill is the director of the internationally recognized documentary films Roots of Love, Mardistan/Macholand, and Sent Away Boys. His work has been broadcast on the BBC, PBS, and Doordarshan and screened widely at universities, film festivals, and public forums around the world. His scholarship appears in leading journals including American Anthropologist, Ethnography, and Visual Anthropology Review. His forthcoming book, Coming of Age in Macholand (University of Chicago Press), offers a deeply personal ethnographic exploration of patriarchy, masculinity, violence, and migration in Indian Punjab. Gill has received fellowships and awards from the American Institute of Indian Studies, Fulbright-Nehru, Point Foundation, Wenner-Gren, Whiting, and Woodrow Wilson foundations. Born in Chandigarh (India), Gill grew up in SF Bay Area and now lives in Washington, DC. EVENT POSTER _________________ Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Claudine Chalmers | French Eyes on the Gold Rush – Artists and Chroniclers witness early California's astonishing transformation
events.description:
Long before the frenzy of the 1849 Gold Rush, French explorers such as the Comte de La Pérouse visited and charted the coast of California. They were followed by French diplomats in Monterey, notably Jacques-Antoine Moerenhout, whose official reports documented the early discovery of gold and the extraordinary changes it set in motion. Beginning in 1849, the Gold Rush brought a new wave of French emigrants to California, drawn by the dream of El Dorado. These fortune seekers—who came to be known as "Argonauts," after the adventurers of Greek mythology—did more than search for gold. A remarkable number of them observed, wrote, sketched, and recorded what they saw, aware that they were witnessing an extraordinary moment in history. Through travel accounts, letters, journals, and drawings, these French-speaking witnesses captured the unruly excitement of San Francisco, the hardships and disappointments of life in the mining camps, and the cultural encounters—and collisions—of a new cosmopolitan society taking shape almost overnight. Their distinctive perspective, shaped by European traditions, a critical eye, and a certain Romantic sensibility, complements the accounts of French diplomats and earlier explorers. Together, these voices offer a vivid and surprisingly rich record of what California felt and looked like as it transformed almost overnight into one of the most dynamic places in the West. Born in Cannes, Claudine Chalmers, Ph.D., is a historian, author, and independent researcher. Her passion for art, history, and the American West led her to dedicate several decades to tracing the lives of the French men and women who left for California in the 19th century. Her work include Chronicling the West for Harper's, and Splendide Californie!
Drawing on archives in France and the United States, she seeks to breathe new life into figures whom history has gradually forgotten—artists, explorers, pioneers, and adventurers whose stories reveal a French presence in the American West far richer than is commonly imagined. events.title: Dissertation Talk: Enforcing Least Privilege in the Cloud
events.description: Cloud developers increasingly hand their infrastructure and data to third-party services, such as orchestrators that launch and manage jobs, chains of services that process data on their behalf, and data lakes that store it. To do their work, these services typically receive broad access to everything a developer owns. Attackers have exploited that over-privilege in incidents ranging from the ShadowRay cluster takeovers to the Capital One breach, hijacking compute, stealing credentials, and exfiltrating data at massive scale. The principle of least privilege offers a clear fix, but today's cloud permission models cannot express it for these settings. My dissertation shows how combining proxy-based system design with cryptographic protocols makes least privilege practical without changing cloud providers or the services themselves. In this talk, I will focus on Skydentity, which enforces least privilege on third-party workload orchestrators by separating a service's ability to manage resources from its ability to access them. I will show that Skydentity reduces exposure to real-world attacks, including ShadowRay, SCARLETEEL, and cryptomining campaigns on EC2, at modest cost. I will also briefly discuss how these ideas extend to chains of services.

events.title: PMB Seminar with Vivian Irish | Thorny questions: citrus development and disease
events.description: Thorns are plant defensive structures that arise from axillary shoot apical meristems that proliferate for a time and then terminally differentiate into a sharp hard tip. Like other meristems, thorn meristems contain stem cells but, in the case of thorns, these stem cells undergo a programmed cessation of proliferative activity. Using citrus as a model system to examine this unusual form of stem cell regulation, we have characterized a transcriptional gene network necessary for thorn development. Not only has this work illuminated some of the molecular mechanisms controlling plant stem cell activity, but the methods we have developed have allowed us to tackle some of the challenges facing citrus agriculture today.

events.title: Restless Ground: Lilah Nethanel on Writing Israel
events.description:
Helen Diller Institute Literary Series, Session II*Co-sponsored by the Center for Jewish Studies and the Department of Comparative Literature, UC Berkeley What can a sleepless man reveal about the history of a country, and what forgotten paths might Hebrew literature have taken? Israeli novelist and literary scholar Lilah Nethanel approaches some of Hebrew literature's most familiar and contested subjects—home, land, desire, language, and belonging—from startlingly unexpected angles. In The Tired Ones, one man's longing for sleep opens onto Israel's fraught histories of land and ownership, while Works and Days compresses fifteen years of marriage, desire, and betrayal into two hours of an ordinary summer evening. Her newly published study, The Last European-Hebrew Writer, returns to David Frishman to recover two possibilities for modern Hebrew culture that once coexisted: a European-Hebrew literature centered in Warsaw and a Hebrew-Arabic literature emerging in Ottoman Jerusalem. In conversation with Yael Segalovitz, Nethanel will explore how intimate lives and forgotten literary alternatives can unsettle the familiar stories Israel tells about itself.
Lilah Nethanel, Literary scholar and Israeli novelist; Senior Lecturer, Department of Literature, Bar-Ilan UniversityYael Segalovitz, Joan Bieder Visiting Professor of Jewish and Hebrew Literature, Helen Diller Institute, UC Berkeley; Comparative Literature Department, UC Berkeley; Assistant Professor, Ben-Gurion University of the NegevRegister: https://HDILitSeries2.rsvpify.com (https://hdilitseries2.rsvpify.com)

events.title: 2026 Berkeley Bioengineering Distinguished Lecture with Clifford Brangwynne, PhD
events.description: Fluid Machinery: The Nucleolus, Ribosomes, and Aging Abstract: Research combining insights from materials physics and cell biology has ushered in a new paradigm for understanding how the chaotic intracellular environment is brought to order, through the collective condensation of biomolecules into droplets of living information. In this talk, I will present an overview of these principles and ongoing work in this field, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between liquid-like condensates and traditional biomolecular machines, such as the ribosome, which forms through a complex assembly process in the multiphase nucleolus. Our lab has recently developed a set of tools to probe and engineer the nucleolus and the production of ribosomes, as well as their cytoplasmic function in protein translation. These studies are yielding new insights into how assembled ribosomes function in space and time, and how ribosomes can become dysregulated by molecular and organismal aging.

events.title: Dave Pagliarini: Mining mitochondria—proteins, pathways, and pathogenesis
events.description:
Despite their iconic status in cell biology, mitochondria remain surprisingly mysterious. These organelles harbor hundreds of uncharacterized "orphan" proteins and are linked to a vast array of physiological processes, often through unclear means. Many well-known mitochondrial activities rely on enzymes, chaperones, and transporters yet to be identified. Mitochondrial dysfunction underlies hundreds of rare diseases, yet nearly half lack molecular diagnoses and there remains but two FDA-approved drugs to treat them. My talk will cover how we aim to clarify this remarkable opacity by blending new systematic methods with rigorous mechanistic biochemistry and chemical biology to discover new protein activities, link them to new biology and unresolved diseases, and manipulate them through customized small molecule interventions.
Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: From dispersal to divergence: exploring the many faces of allopatric speciation
events.description: Freshwater fishes of eastern North America, particularly darters, are an exceptional system for studying the mechanisms and outcomes of allopatric speciation, given their high regional diversity and strong habitat specificity. Allopatric speciation is predicted to leave sister species in separate but adjacent river systems; yet a time-calibrated phylogeny of nearly all 290 darter species, combined with genomic species delimitation, reveals far more varied outcomes. Some sister lineages achieve secondary sympatry rapidly, while others persist in deep allopatry, never overlapping even with distant relatives, raising questions about why lineages differ in their transition rates from isolation to co-occurrence. At finer scales, case studies of recently delimited species complexes identify multiple drivers of allopatric speciation, including dispersal into newly available habitat and ecological divergence along resource axes like diet and substrate, extending well beyond classic vicariance models. This work establishes a research program linking speciation mechanisms to their long-term geographic and ecological consequences, contrasted with dynamics of island and lake adaptive radiations.

events.title: CCB Seminar: Pilar Cossio, Senior Research Scientist, Flatiron Institute
events.description:
Title: Inferring Biomolecular Ensembles from Cryo-EM Images with Physical and Generative PriorsAbstract: Biomolecules are dynamic, and understanding their function requires characterizing not just individual structures but entire conformational ensembles and their populations. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) captures noisy snapshots of individual molecules, providing direct experimental access to these ensembles, yet extracting them remains challenging. In this talk, I will present a unified framework for ensemble inference in which prior knowledge, either from molecular dynamics (MD) force fields or pretrained diffusion models, is integrated by cryo-EM data. With MD, we bias simulations using a likelihood computed directly from particle images, jointly inferring structures and population weights without a pre-sampled ensemble. With diffusion models, we guide generation toward experimental data, including by optimizing the model's conditioning to shift the prior itself. Applied to proteins and RNAs, these approaches recover multiple conformational states and their populations from synthetic and experimental data, opening the way to ensemble-level quantitative structural biology of flexible biomolecules.
Bio:Pilar Cossio has worked at the Flatiron Institute, Center for Computational Mathematics, since 2021 as the Research Scientist and Project Leader for Biomolecular and Biophysical Inference (BBI). Previously, Cossio was Max Planck Tandem Group Leader associated with the University of Antioquia (Colombia) and the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics (Germany). She also has held postdoctoral positions at the National Institute of Health (NIH, USA) and the Max Planck Institute of Biophysics. Cossio focuses on the development of mathematical and computational methods to characterize proteins' structures and dynamics from cryo-electron microscopy, single-molecule spectroscopy and biomolecular simulations. Cossio holds a Ph.D. in Physics and Chemistry of Biological Systems from the International School for Advanced Studies (SISSA) in Italy and a B.S. in Physics from the University of Antioquia.

events.title: Creativity and Playwriting: A Conversation with Stan Lai
events.description:
What does it take to create a theatrical masterpiece? Where do great ideas come from, and how do playwrights transform them into unforgettable experiences onstage? Join us for a special conversation with internationally acclaimed playwright, director, and UC Berkeley alumnus Stan Lai (Ph.D. Dramatic Art '83), one of the most influential voices in contemporary theater. Hosted by TDPS Department Chair Abigail De Kosnik and TDPS Professor Lisa Wymore, this conversation will explore Lai's creative process, the evolution of his groundbreaking body of work, and his journey from graduate student at UC Berkeley to internationally celebrated theatermaker. Lai's Secret Love in Peach Blossom Land was recently named by The New York Times as one of the essential works of theater of the past 100 years. Drawing on decades of artistic innovation, Lai will share insights into the art and craft of playwriting, reflect on his past and current projects, and offer inspiration and advice to the next generation of theatermakers, artists, and storytellers.
About Stan Lai: Stan Lai (Lai Shengchuan) has been called "The best Chinese language playwright and director in the world" (BBC) and "Asia's top theatre director." (Asiaweek) Robert Brustein considered him "unchallenged as the major contemporary Asian playwright of his time, perhaps of all time." Lai was born in Washington, DC in 1954, and grew up in the US and Taiwan. After receiving his PhD in Dramatic Art at Berkeley in 1983, Lai began his creative journey in Taipei, Taiwan, creating bold new plays that brought audiences into the theatre, at a time when there was no organized theatre industry. Over the decades, many a Chinese-speaking theatregoer's first experience of theatre has been a play of Stan Lai's. To date he has written and directed over 40 original full length plays, including those regarded as masterpieces of the modern Chinese-language theatre such as Secret Love in Peach Blossom Land (1986, chosen by the New York Times in 2026 as one of the "Essential Plays of the Past 100 Years"), The Village (2008, called "The pinnacle of theatre in our time" by the Beijing News), and A Dream Like A Dream (2000, called by China Daily "possibly the greatest Chinese-language play since time immemorial.") Lai's awards include Taiwan's National Arts Award an unprecedented twice. He was also awarded a star on the Walk of Fame at the Sibiu International Theatre Festival. Lai is also an award-winning feature filmmaker and acclaimed opera and events director, as well as a noted theatre educator, having taught over two decades at Taipei National university of the Arts, and also at Stanford, Berkeley, CalArts and the Shanghai Theatre Academy. Two of Lai's most acclaimed works, A Dream Like A Dream and AGO were created in workshop form while teaching at Berkeley. Lai's publications in English include Selected Plays of Stan Lai (3 vols, 12 plays in his own English translations, U. of Michigan Press, 2022) and Creativitry: Asia's Iconic Playwright Reveals the Art of Creativity (Anthem, 2025), the English version of his groundbreaking Chinese work on creativity, which has sold over one million copies. Lai is currently Artistic Director of Performance Workshop, Taiwan, and Theatre Above, Shanghai, a venue dedicated to the performance of his works, as well as Artistic Founder of the Huichang Theatre Village. He is Co-founder, Festival Director and Jury Head of the Wuzhen Theatre Festival.
