events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description:
A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.
Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, December 3, 2026 (NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: On FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.

Talk Summary: The rise of the illiberal, far-right politics threatens democratic system throughout the world. The South Korean president Yoon Seok-yeol's martial law declaration in December 2024 stunned the world. More puzzling is that Yoon's insurrection unexpectedly gained substantial support from the ruling right-wing party and ordinary citizens. Why do ordinary citizens support authoritarian leaders and martial law in a democratic country? What draws these citizens to extreme actions and ideas? Through eighteen months of field research and drawing from rich qualitative data, this talk will provide an in-depth account of the ideas and practices of the far-right groups and organizations, and help to understand the roots of current democratic regression. Speaker Bio: Myungji Yang is Professor of Sociology at the University of Hawai'i-Mānoa. A political sociologist and social movement scholar, she is interested in the issues of power, inequality, civil society and democracy. Her research has appeared in Nations and Nationalism, Politics and Society, Mobilization: An International Inquiry, Urban Studies, and Sociological Inquiry, among other venues. She is the author of two books, From Miracle to Mirage (2018, Cornell University Press) and Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization (2026, Cambridge University Press). She is currently developing a research project on young men's radicalization and anti-feminist politics.

events.title: California Live! Our Strange Land: On Stolen Pride and the Road Ahead
events.location: Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive
events.description:
Arlie Hochschild has spent a decade thinking and writing about communities on the political right. For her bestselling Strangers in Their Own Land (2016), she embedded in Lousiana's Calcasieu Parish to help explain the Tea Party to Americans who were bewildered by it. Eight years later, she returned with Stolen Pride, about Pikeville, Kentucky—a MAGA stronghold in one of the country's whitest and poorest congressional districts. A New York Times Best Book of the Year, it makes the case that the region's politics are driven less by policies or economics than by shame and a narrative of "stolen" pride. Join California magazine's Pat Joseph in conversation with Hochschild as they discuss what she's learned from her time amongst Donald Trump's supporters and how that knowledge might help us mend our fractured democracy. ARLIE HOCHSCHILD Arlie Russell Hochschild is a professor emerita of sociology at the University of California, Berkeley. A bestselling author and National Book Award finalist, she has made a career of turning academic fieldwork into compelling literature. Her other books include The Managed Heart, The Second Shift, The Time Bind, and The Outsourced Self. ABOUT CALIFORNIA LIVE! The California Live! series presents some of Berkeley's most distinguished faculty and alumni discussing today's most pressing issues. In partnership with BAMPFA, the Cal Alumni Association and its award-winning California magazine invite you to join us for our next episode. Tickets to this event include free access to the galleries at BAMPFA and a wine reception. COME EARLY Enjoy free access to the galleries at BAMPFA. Established in 1991 by June Jordan and rooted in her work in the departments of African American Studies and Gender and Women's Studies at UC Berkeley, Poetry for the People (P4P) taught students to speak their truth through poetry. Drawing students from a range of backgrounds and areas of study, June Jordan's P4P engaged in rigorous study of a diversity of poetic traditions, organized public poetry readings and open mics, published anthologies of student work, and brought P4P to community partners around the Bay Area. Today, with the clarity and political commitment of June's vision more necessary than ever, "Poetry for the People: A Blueprint for the Future" asks, how do we teach P4P now? "Poetry for the People: A Blueprint for the Future" is a convening intended for UC Berkeley faculty, students, and staff; P4P program alumni; P4P instructors; community partners; and anyone committed to the future of P4P at UC Berkeley and beyond. The day-long program will include workshops about the history and legacy of P4P, how P4P is being taught today, and new models of P4P for the modern university. Together, we will envision how to bring P4P to the next generation of student poets. All members of the public are invited to an evening conversation at 6:00 pm to celebrate the forthcoming publication of June Jordan's Poetry for the People (Expanded Edition): A Revolutionary Blueprint from Haymarket Books. Learn more and register to attend (https://events.berkeley.edu/africam/event/p4p-blueprint). This event is organized by the Departments of African American & African Diaspora Studies and Gender and Women's Studies at UC Berkeley with Adrienne Torf. The program is sponsored by the American Cultures Center, Professor Solmaz Sharif, the Social Sciences Dean's Office, the Center for Race and Gender, the Center for the Study of Sexual Cultures, the Department of Comparative Literature, the College Writing Programs, the Townsend Center for the Humanities, the Office of the Vice Chancellor of Equity and Inclusion, the Othering & Belonging Institute's LGBT Citizenship Cluster, and the Ethnic Studies Library at UC Berkeley.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Prof. Valla Fatemi, Cornell University | Toward Robust Superconducting Quantum Computation: From Nanofabrication to Logical Control
events.description: Abstract: Superconducting circuits are a leading hardware platform for quantum computation. The way to fabricate the devices, arrange them, and then control them in operando remains a major open question. In any implementation, we desire physical devices that preserve coherence as long as possible alongside robust logical operations. In this talk, I will present two complementary advances toward these goals. First, I will describe a new tantalum thin-film synthesis procedure, alongside the rest of our fabrication method, that enables high-performance superconducting qubit circuits. Our qubits are at the leading edge, with quality factors exceeding 16 million. I will then turn to protecting quantum information during computation in the context of bosonic codes. Bosonic codes encode a logical qubit in the states of a harmonic oscillator, which can offer advantages in hardware-efficiency. However, preserving protection against physical errors during logical gate operations remains a major challenge. I will introduce a framework that enables standard microwave controls to implement a universal set of single-logical-qubit gates that are approximately 'transparent' to photon loss, allowing for correction of errors after gate operations. Experiments demonstrate a five-fold reduction in gate infidelity conditioned on photon loss, and improved preservation of information during active control with error correction. Together, these efforts represent a dual-pronged effort to advance the frontier of protecting quantum information. Bio: Dr. Valla Fatemi received his PhD in Physics in the group of Pablo Jarillo-Herrero at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2018. There he worked on electronic and quantum transport in topological insulator materials, including discovery of superconductor and topological insulator states in monolayer tungsten ditelluride. He then joined the group of Michel Devoret at Yale University as the post-doctoral associate on the teams researching the physics of Andreev bound states in superconductor-semiconductor quantum devices, helping to demonstrate the first Andreev spin qubit. In 2022 he joined the faculty of the School of Applied and Engineering Physics at Cornell University, where he is building a lab researching the basic and applied physics of quantum materials, quantum control, superconducting quantum circuits, and their intersections, including a focus on materials and nanofabrication for improving superconducting qubits.

events.title: BLC Talk | Creating the Conditions for Languages to Thrive: Advocacy, Leadership, and Institutional Change | Deb Reisinger
events.description: Creating the Conditions for Languages to Thrive: Advocacy, Leadership, and Institutional Change Deb Reisinger Dean of Undergraduate Education; Trinity College, Duke University In "Creating the Conditions", Reisinger examines how content-based language programs can expand the role and reach of language study within a contemporary liberal arts education. Drawing on established approaches in Cultures and Languages Across the Curriculum (CLAC), community-based language learning (CBLL), and Languages for Specific Purposes (LSP), she considers how language courses and programs can connect linguistic development with disciplinary knowledge, critical inquiry, experiential learning, and transferable skills. Examples from undergraduate curricula illustrate the distinct possibilities of these models. CLAC integrates languages and intercultural perspectives across disciplines; CBLL creates reciprocal relationships between classroom learning and community engagement, and LSP connects language learning to professional fields and practices. Together, these approaches make visible the intellectual and practical value of language study across academic, professional, and civic contexts. This presentation also considers what allows such programs to take root and thrive. Curricular innovation depends on more than compelling individual courses. It requires faculty leadership, meaningful institutional partnerships, coherent pathways for students, and structures that support collaboration across departments, programs, and schools. It also requires clear narratives that help students, faculty colleagues, and university leaders understand how language learning advances broader institutional commitments. By bringing curricular models into conversation with questions of advocacy, leadership, and institutional design, Reisinger invites participants to consider the conditions that support language study at their own institution. Ultimately, she asks how content-based programs can help build connections, create new points of entry, and position linguistic and intercultural learning as essential dimensions of a liberal arts education. Bio: Deb Reisinger is Dean of Undergraduate Education at Duke University. A professor of French Studies and affiliate faculty in Global Health and Markets & Management, Deb directs Duke's Language Outreach Initiatives(link is external), including Cultures and Languages Across the Curriculum and the Shared Online Consortium for LCTLs. Deb's work explores the connections between language learning and the disciplines. She is lead author of Affaires globales: S'engager dans le monde professionnel en francais, niveau avancé and co-author of Community-based Language Learning, a methodology of critical service-learning in world languages. In 2022, she was named Chevalier dans l'Ordre des Palmes Académiques by the French Republic.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Stefan Minasian, Staff Chemist, LBNLThe Counterintuitive Relationship between Orbital Energy, Orbital Overlap,and Covalency in f-Element Molecules Why are some metal–ligand bonds more covalent than others? Typically, chemists invoke two factors: how well the metal and ligand orbitals overlap in space, and how closely their energies match. Yet these contributions have been surprisingly difficult to separate, by either experiment or theory. This lecture will describe how ligand K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), combined with high-level spectral simulations, can measure both. Comparisons of isostructural fluoride and chloride complexes of transition metals (Ti, Zr, Hf), lanthanides (Ce), and actinides (U, Np, Pu) show that the two factors often work against each other. Greater orbital overlap does not necessarily produce a more covalent bond, and the balance between overlap and energy matching depends on the metal and on the symmetry of the interaction. These results also provide experimental benchmarks against which computational descriptions of bonding can be tested. The second part of the lecture will extend this approach to organometallic lanthanide complexes, probed using carbon K-edge XAS. In molecules such as cerocene, Ce(C8H8)2, and Cp′3Eu, the ground state cannot be described by a single electronic configuration. In these systems, the 4f orbital mixing observed by X-ray spectroscopy also appears as partial charge transfer from the ligands to the metal. Relating these two descriptions shows how 4f electrons can participate in bonding while remaining largely localized, and how 4f covalency can shape physical properties such as magnetic susceptibility. This leads to broader questions about how covalency and multiconfigurational ground states are connected across the f-block.
The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: On counterexamples to the unification of $\chi$ and $\chi^*$
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: David Jekel, University of OttawaOpen AI recently generated the first examples with $-\infty \chi \chi ^*$. I will contextualize and give a detailed proof of similar example, and more explicitly show the separation between free Fisher information and the large-n limit of classical Fisher information. The upper bound on free Fisher information comes from a cumulant-bound for Fisher information that draws on higher-order conjugate variable/Stein kernel techniques from classical and free settings. The lower bound on classical Fisher information comes from volume bounds on the space of matrices admitting a noticeable block structure with respect to some projections reminiscent of the volume arguments in Voiculescu's paper on absence of Cartan algebras and many subsequent works. I will derive the upper bound using a sup-formula and showing the relationship with my study of model theory and Wasserstein distance in the context of random matrices.

events.title: Soft Separation for Adaptive Robust Optimization (Ruiwei Jiang, University of Michigan)
events.description:
Talk title: Soft Separation for Adaptive Robust OptimizationAbstract: Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) finds a wide range of applications including, for example, electric power systems, supply chains, and transportation. Unfortunately, ARO models are NP-hard in general, and practical applications of ARO often resort to decision rules for tractability but sacrifice accuracy. In this talk, we propose a novel algorithmic framework for solving ARO with performance guarantees in both tractability and accuracy. The framework introduces soft separation, a probabilistic mechanism for identifying worst-case uncertainty realizations. As opposed to solving an exact separation problem iteratively, which is intractable in general, soft separation carries adversarial information forward, co-evolves with the optimization iterates, and recovers exact separation at terminal iterates with high probability. When the first-stage (here-and-now) decisions are continuous, we design a first-order method that uses soft separation to produce adaptive gradient estimates. Accordingly, we prove polynomial convergence to a surrogate that approximates the true optimum to any prescribed accuracy. When the first-stage decisions are mixed-integer, we embed soft separation in a branch-and-cut framework to generate valid cuts for the robust objective and obtain a high-probability final optimality certificate. Numerical experiments show strong performance against state-of-the-art methods, especially under scenario-based uncertainty.
Bio: Ruiwei Jiang is an Associate Professor of Industrial and Operations Engineering at the University of Michigan. His research and teaching interests lie in stochastic and integer optimization, with applications in power systems and healthcare operations. Recognitions of his work include an NSF CAREER Award, two INFORMS Junior Faculty Interest Group paper awards (1st place and honorable mention), an INFORMS Computing Society prize (honorable mention), and an IISE Operations Research Division Teaching Award.

events.title: An attempt towards the Autistic Image feat. Perwana Nazif
events.description: A History & Theory of New Media lecture with Perwana Nazif Visiting Faculty, California Institute of the Arts, and Artistic Director, Los Angeles Review of Books - Monday, December 7, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfCVu9yc8DDE25JwxXsk8JBXMFwmawFEoFCQw71XrKximqkdQ/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MGxuYnJuZWpqNGd2ZGo1MGppNXRzMmVyM2UgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - It's here that the two attempts—allowing autistic children to exist and camering— have a trait in common: to evade intention, which requires a strange rigour that can't be intentional. "Miscreating" (1979) Just as tracing is not drawing, camering is not filming. "Miscreating" (1979) An attempt lays itself bare—and you can certainly hear all the connotations of that word. It does not present itself as a request. Le Croire et le Craindre (1978) In 1968, French educator and writer Fernand Deligny began the "Cévennes network," also known as the attempt. The Cévennes attempt was an informal, non-clinical collective of autistic children and (non-autistic) "close presences," who together enabled autistic existence. The Cévennes experiment attempted to work within a non-verbal and non-institutional framework, to respond to what Deligny marked as the autistic children's needs to experience life in the absence of language and neurotypical relation. The network both followed and radically departed from Deligny's prior para-clinical and social work with neurodivergent, psychotic, "troubled" or "delinquent," children, many of whom would have otherwise been incarcerated or permanently institutionalized. Here, in the attempt, they experimented with collective aesthetic and/or media practices outside of language: purposeless objects and common actions, non-representational cartography, tracing (unlike drawing), and camering (unlike filming). So, what or how is the collective attempt—when its conditions of emergence are indeterminacy, precarity, non-relation, and detours from if not a total outside to language and the subject? To hazard a presentation of the (Cévennes) attempt is to present it through what Deligny calls the autistic image—that which means nothing, says nothing, or does anything. This talk, then, will explore the apparatus of the autistic image, its point of seeing, and what it enables to come into the world. About Perwana Nazif Perwana Nazif teaches at the California Institute of the Arts and serves as the artistic director of the Los Angeles Review of Books. She recently edited Everybody Wants to Be a Fascist: Institutional Psychotherapy as a Resistance Movement (semiotext(e), 2025) and is a contributing editor at Parapraxis Magazine. She recently curated François Pain, Psychiatry is what Psychiatrists do at JOAN, Los Angeles and is currently working on an exhibition at CAC Brétigny in France. About History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series The History & Theory of New Media Lecture Series brings to campus leading humanities scholars working on issues of media transition and technological emergence. The series promotes new, interdisciplinary approaches to questions about the uses, meanings, causes, and effects of rapid or dramatic shifts in techno-infrastructure, information management, and forms of mediated expression. Presented by BCNM, these events are free and open to the public.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Research & Writing in the Age of AI: Legal and Practical Considerations
events.description:
RSVP to get the Zoom linkThis workshop will help you navigate the legal and practical questions that AI tools raise for academic authors.
The first part of the session will explore how using AI tools in research implicates a range of legal issues that researchers—and the libraries that support them—need to navigate. We'll examine whether feeding content into AI tools qualifies as fair use under copyright law, and how overarching contracts such as library e-resource agreements or a website's terms of use may restrict, shape, or even override your fair use rights. We'll explore whether those clickthrough or browsewrap terms of use are enforceable, and why you may need to pay closer attention to them than you think.
The second part of the session will cover how using AI in your writing can affect your copyright and authorship, what current publisher and journal policies require you to disclose, and how AI training on scholarly work intersects with your rights as an author.
You'll leave with a working understanding of where the law currently stands, what remains unsettled, and how to make informed choices about using these tools in your own work.
If you require an accommodation to fully participate in this event, please contact schol-comm@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7 days before the event.

events.title: Multimodal Transportation Impact Analysis: California Best Practices
events.description: Description The multi-modal Transportation Impact Study (TIS) is one of the most effective tools for assessing the impacts of new land development (or redevelopment) and establishing a nexus with project mitigations, including impact fees. Recent legislation as well as public sentiment have made it imperative that transportation professionals better understand how to prepare and review these studies. Although current California environmental regulations (CEQA) require specific methods for use in analyzing transportation impacts, focusing on vehicle-miles traveled, this class will consider a broader variety of transportation impacts. A good TIS can consider a much wider range of impacts than CEQA and therefore can better reflect local community values. The class will consider such topics as site access and off-site improvements to satisfactorily accommodate project traffic, including traffic signals. It also considers how impact fees can be applied consistent with California law to recover costs associated with the new development. It also considers non-VMT impacts, such as multi-modal impacts, delay to buses, providing the right amount of parking, internal circulation, and improving the pedestrian/ bicycle environment. This 8-hour course (in 4 two-hour modules) provides the basics and practical applications of analysis procedures for determining impacts using various performance metrics on all modes (pedestrian, bicycle, transit, and auto). It emphasizes the best practices that are being employed in California and other areas. This course focuses on urban/suburban streets (non-freeways), internal circulation planning, and providing just the right amount of parking. Applications of analyses include improving transportation impact studies, environmental impact reports (EIRs) and project mitigation, new development design standards, and the CEQA review process. Attendees will also become familiar with:Labor-saving shortcuts for data collection (because some multimodal level of service methodologies can be very "data hungry") How 'induced travel demand' is defined, and when it does (or does not) create a significant environmental impact under the law Cross-modal impacts (when capacity or physical characteristics of one mode are changed and thereby affect another mode using the street) How to assess "fair share" impact fees to pay for project mitigations How parking can be used as an effective demand-management measure Available resources (web and paper) that provide further guidance This class has been updated to reflect many changes in California law between 2020 and 2024. Updates to important references-such as the 2023 Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, and ITE Recommended Practice on TIA-will also be considered. This course is a combination of instructor presentations with interactive engagements to apply the techniques in the real-world, with case studies and applications of the material. The material complements TE-43 (Multimodal Transportation Operations: Evaluation Methods & Performance Measures) (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/CourseStatus.awp?&course=0500TE430000), and TE-60 (VMT Metrics Policy Applications and Technical Analysis for SB 743 Compliance) (https://registration.techtransfer.berkeley.edu/CourseStatus.awp?&course=0500TE600000), although each can be taken as a stand-alone class. Topics IncludeLevel-of-Service (LOS) concept– what it means and why do it, pros and cons of different methods cross-modal impacts how to calculate VMT from a proposed project gathering field information & data collection shortcuts software available to assist in analysis California statutory requirements (especially CEQA and SB 743) relationship to the latest Caltrans' guidance applications to Context Sensitive Design assessing safety impacts of projects relationship to Sustainable Transportation Indicators incorporation as part of project mitigation typical schedule and budgetary requirements increasing transit as a share of regional VMT applying analytical and simulation tools to multi-modal impact analysis What You Will Learn Students will learn how to prepare– and review– a comprehensive multi-modal transportation impact study. This includes studies prepared both to support CEQA documentation as well as stand-alone studies. Topics include basic level-of-service (LOS) concepts for all modes, and how to apply them to conduct performance and level-of-service analysis for various types of urban streets with various levels of accommodation for different modes; determine the impacts of system improvements using vehicle miles traveled (VMT); and analyze operational impacts of possible changes in the allocation of street cross-section to various modes. Who Should Attend Planners, engineers, technicians, and others at all levels of experience, who prepare or review transportation impacts from land developments will benefit from this class. A minimal level of mathematics is required (basic algebra). Requirements Participants will need a basic calculator for several in-class problem sets. A complete PDF set of Course Notes will be provided by the instructors.

events.title: Danette Daniels: Towards new cancer medicines with degraders of chromatin regulatory proteins
events.description:
Targeted protein degradation as a therapeutic modality has experienced an explosion in research the past several years resulting in advancements of numerous degraders to the clinic addressing a wide variety of disease indications. The strengths of this induced proximity modality include its catalytic mechanism, the ability to drug non-enzymatic targets which serve as scaffolds, and introduction of selectivity amongst paralog family members. In this talk, we will highlight our work developing highly selective and potent degraders to CREB binding protein (CBP), E1A binding protein (EP300), and a historically intractable target, ARID1B. Each of these targets regulate a myriad of cellular processes and have been implicated in numerous oncology diseases. CBP and EP300 are two paralog histone acetyltransferases and while several classes of inhibitors have been developed to CBP/EP300, they have dual activity leading to tolerability challenges. Meanwhile, ARID1B, a core component of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, has long been considered undruggable due to the absence of known binders and lack of ligandable pockets. Striking dependency on ARID1B is observed across multiple cancer indications harboring ARID1A mutations, highlighting a synthetic lethal relationship between these paralogs. In this talk I will highlight the mechanisms for which enabled development of binders and subsequently selective degraders to each other these targets. With these selective compounds in hand, we then demonstrate strong anti-proliferative effects and for CBP and EP300, in vivo tumor growth inhibition across numerous oncology indications with an improved therapeutic window as compared to dual inhibition.
Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.
If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection (copy)
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.
Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. The Magnes generates new knowledge and understanding of Jewish cultures with and for its academic and public audiences through its collections-based exhibitions and programs. events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description:
On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.
Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Tuning In Together: Using Music to Navigate Caregiving
events.description: This workshop explores the healing potential of music for both caregivers and their loved ones. Drawing from neuroscience, psychology, and lived clinical experience, psychologist and musician Barbara Minton will discuss how music affects the brain, supports emotional regulation, reduces stress, enhances connection, and can create moments of presence and meaning even in the midst of caregiving demands. She will be joined by her colleague, Peppino D'Agostino, a virtuosic guitarist, who will perform live music from their collaborative work in which they create compositions designed to support nervous system regulation and emotional well-being. Participants will leave with practical insights and simple music-based tools to support resilience, connection, and well-being in everyday life. Presenter: Dr. Barbara Minton, Phd Dr. Minton earned her BA in Psychology, summa cum laude, from the University of Denver, followed by PhDs in Psychology with an emphasis in developmental and child clinical practice. Demonstrating her deep commitment to brain science, she is Board Certified in Neurofeedback and holds the distinction of Diplomate in Quantitative Electroencephalogram (QEEG). Her diverse career includes private clinical practice in Boise, Idaho, serving as Mental Health Education Coordinator for the State of Alaska's Department of Health and Social Services, and as Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Alaska Southeast. These roles have allowed her to cultivate expertise not just in psychological assessment and neurofeedback, but also in the deeply human areas of giftedness and hypnotherapy. Peppino D'Agostino A native of Italy, D'Agostino has made his considerable international mark as a musical artist on the guitar since he arrived in America 40 years ago. In 2017 Guitar Player listed him as one of the 50 transcendent guitar superheroes of all times. The CD "Every Step of The Way" was awarded by Acoustic Guitar's People's Choice Awards with a Bronze medal for Best Acoustic Album of All Time. His signature Seagull acoustic guitar has been voted among the ten best signature guitars by Guitar Player magazine. Peppino gives guitar workshops, master classes and seminars worldwide. To date Peppino has recorded 19 CD's, performed in over thirty five countries at international festivals and concert halls. Please Note: The Zoom link will be sent to the participants by email, and add it to this workshop description a day before the workshop. All participants and hosts must sign into a Zoom account before joining meetings hosted by UC Berkeley. Participants who are not eligible for a UC Berkeley-provided Zoom account can use a Zoom account provided by their institution, can create a free consumer Zoom account (at https://zoom.us/freesignup/), or can dial in via the phone.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description:
An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. events.title: MAS-E Program Info Session
events.description: The Master of Advanced Study in Engineering (MAS-E) program at UC Berkeley's College of Engineering will be conducting a virtual info session on Thursday, December 17 from 4pm-5pm PT. UC Berkeley MAS-E program staff will be present to answer your questions and discuss our innovative leadership curriculum, capstone projects, technical concentrations, and admissions criteria. * About UC Berkeley Master of Advanced Study in Engineering (MAS-E) Program The Master of Advanced Study in Engineering (MAS-E) is a flexible online Berkeley Engineering master's degree designed for working technical professionals seeking to build expertise in the technologies reshaping industry. The MAS-E offers three concentrations, designed around emerging engineering domains shaping the future of industry — from AI and robotics to advanced manufacturing, energy systems, and resilient infrastructure. Beyond the concentration, students personalize their degree through a broad elective curriculum that supports interdisciplinary learning across engineering, computation, systems design, optimization, and leadership. This flexible structure allows working professionals to build both specialized expertise and broader technical fluency aligned with evolving career goals and industry demands.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Tim Su, Assistant Professor, UC RiversideTitle: Main Group Molecular ElectronicsThis talk will describe our program to explore the synthesis and quantum transport properties of main group molecular electronics. The field of single-molecule electronics is primarily built upon charge transport studies of organic molecules. The boundaries for what we think is possible in molecular electronics are thus defined by the electronic idiosyncrasies of a single element—carbon. What new quantum transport phenomena may emerge if we expand our view beyond carbon? Molecular silicon wires represent an attractive gateway to expand this understanding, as silicon is structurally similar to its group 14 congener, carbon, yet possesses distinct electronics due to the increased electropositivity, orbital energy, diffuseness, and size of its atomic orbitals. Over the last several years, we have developed synthetic approaches to exquisitely tune the peripheral and core structure of Si diamondoids, molecular cutouts of crystalline silicon. This precise synthetic control has allowed us to build higher-order materials as well as wire individual clusters between electrodes to interrogate their quantum transport via the scanning tunneling microscope break-junction (STM-BJ) technique. In this endeavor, we have discovered for the first time how to dynamically control destructive σ-quantum interference (σ-DQI) in molecular junctions and how to dictate the quantity and energetic ordering of midgap transmission anti-resonances, the hallmark signatures of DQI. We are now broadening our view beyond saturated silicon toward the broader p-block to reach new frontiers in quantum electronic transport.
The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Lecture | The Invention of the Fertile Crescent: Historical Lessons from American Orientalism
events.description:
Abstract: During five decades that spanned the turn of the twentieth century (about 1870 to 1920), a tradition of oriental scholarship took firm root in the United States. American orientalists conducted rigorous research into the history and languages of the ancient Near East. These scholars were early defenders of a modern liberal education in the United States. They invented the idea of "Western civilization" and argued that the origins of the West lay in the ancient Orient. They coined the concept of the "fertile crescent" to suggest that the lands of the Near East gently nurtured humanity in its early days, "cradling" civilization in the nascent stage. This lecture will examine American orientalism's quest to find historical, rather than biblical, origin stories for humanity. In the orientalist scheme, the civilizations of the East were the first to develop monotheistic religion and thus to foster humankind's capacity for empathy. Empathy, in turn, played an essential role in the functioning of democratic society in the modern West.
Bio: Serena Shah is a PhD candidate in U.S. History at Stanford University. She works on the history of ideas and the production of knowledge in major American cultural institutions, especially universities and museums. Her dissertation examines the uses of American oriental scholarship for liberal education in the fin-de-siècle United States. Serena also broadly studies Americans' ideas about antiquity in the nineteenth century; she is in the process of publishing a research article on Greek and Roman slave-naming practices in the antebellum era. She received her A.B. (summa cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa) from Harvard University in 2021 and her M.A. in History from Stanford in 2023.

events.title: Danielle Roper | Hemispheric Blackface: A Reflection on Racial Impersonation
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description:
Event description In Hemispheric Blackface, Danielle Roper examines blackface performance and its relationship to 20th- and 21st-century nationalist fictions of mestizaje, creole nationalism, and other versions of postracialism in the Americas. Challenging both the dominance of the US minstrel tradition and the focus on the nation in blackface studies, Roper maps a hemispheric network of racial impersonation in Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, Jamaica, Cuba, and Miami. She analyzes blackface performance in the aftermath of the turn to multiculturalism in Latin America, the emergence of modern blackness in Jamaica, and the rise of Barack Obama in the United States, showing how blackface remains embedded in cultural entertainment. Contending that the Americas are linked by repeating nationalist fictions of postracialism, colorblindness, and myths of racial democracy, Roper assesses how acts of impersonation mediate the ongoing power of these narratives and enable people to comprehend advancements and reversals in racial equality. Rather than simply framing blackface as liberatory or oppressive, Roper traces its emergence from a shared history of slavery and the varied politics of racial enjoyment throughout the hemisphere. Roper will also lead a two-hour mini-seminar titled "Abject Pleasures in the Postcolonial Below: Theatre in Jamaica." The mini seminar will take place on Friday, January 29, at 9:30 am and is for Berkeley graduate students. Interested students should email clacs@berkeley.edu for consideration.
Organized by CLACS and Nadia Ellis (English). Co-sponsored by the Department of African American Studies.
SpeakerDanielle Roper is Associate Professor of Romance Languages and Literatures at the University of Chicago. She is the author of Hemispheric Blackface: Impersonation and Nationalist Fiction in the Americas (Duke University Press 2025) which was written with the support of Neubauer Family Assistant Professorship. Her work on racial impersonation, radical feminist activism, queer visual art across the Hemispheric Americas has been published in GLQ, Latin American Research Review, SmallAxe, TDR, and elsewhere. She is the curator of the digital exhibit Visualizing/Performing Blackness in the Afterlives of Slavery: A Caribbean Archive.

events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Christian Limberg, Professor, Humboldt University of BerlinBiomimetic Thiolate Dioxygenation at Iron Centres and Bioinspired Carbonite Binding at Nickel/Iron SitesLecture 1 of 2 In the first part the generation of Ni–CO22-…M complexes (M = alkali,1-3 earth alkaline4 or transition metal ion6) via hitherto rarely observed formate β‑deprotonation is reported.1-3 The CO22- (carbonite) ligand is bound like a carbene to the nickel centre and was found to interact with the counterions M+, introduced via the used bases or salt metathesis reactions. Through their properties they thus significantly influence the stability and reactivity of the complexes, which resemble the CO2 bound state in Ni,Fe carbon monoxide dehydrogenases (CODH),5 in particular the Ni–CO22-…Fe representative.6 For the series of systems presented an inverse relation between redox behaviour and activation emerged: transition metal ions reduce the reduction potential of the carbonite unit but increase its tendency to undergo C-O bond cleavage.6 Mononuclear non-heme iron enzymes, which activate dioxygen for the subsequent oxygenation of substrates, form the background of the second part. The cysteine dioxygenase (CDO) is a representative of the (His)3Fe-enzyme family and catalyzes the reaction between cysteine and dioxygen to yield cysteine sulfinic acid, which lies at the branching point of cysteine catabolism. Understanding of the CDO may guide the way to suitable catalysts for synthetically highly interesting thiol dioxygenations and hence the development of model complexes that mimic the active sites of these enzymes is a valuable but also challenging target: iron oxidation instead of S‐oxygenation as well as overoxidation at the S atom has to be avoided.8 The lecture reflects our progress in the development of low-molecular weight analogues, were the (His)3Fe moiety is simulated by a tris(pyrazolyl)borate-iron complex metal fragment.7-12 Recent findings concerning the replacement of thiolates by selenium-based substrates are also presented.7

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description:
Sandeep Sharma, Professor, CaltechNew Avenues in Cyclase Phase SynthesisInspired by the biosynthetic logic of terpene cyclase phase, we report a general strategy for the rapid and stereocontrolled construction of terpenoid architectures by overriding the inherent stereochemical outcome of polyolefin cyclizations. A central feature of this approach is a quaternary carbon center epimerization that precisely remodels the stereochemistry at one stereocenter, overcoming the conformational bias of the cyclization reaction. The key to our ketone epimerization is the design of a photoactive imine that circumvents the pitfalls of traditional carbonyl photochemistry. Visible-light excitation with a photosensitizer enables reversible C–C bond cleavage and reformation through a tertiary radical intermediate, thereby allowing epimerization of the adjacent quaternary center. We have recently applied this tactic toward the synthesis of several terpenoid natural products, including dasyscyphin A. This line of research is yielding protocols that reconfigure functionally inert stereocenters with unprecedented precision, unlocking new molecular skeletons and transformations long unattainable through existing methods.
The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: TDPS presents "Berkeley Dance Project: What Moves Between Us"
events.description: Choreography by SanSan Kwan (Two Doors) and Lisa Wymore (Cycle) Zellerbach Playhouse Showtimes: Thursday, February 18th at 8pm Friday, February 19th at 8pm Saturday, February 20th at 2pm Saturday, February 20th at 8pm Sunday, February 21st at 2pm Presented by the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies (TDPS) This collaboration offers two dance works that sit inside the friction of seeing and not seeing, doing and not doing. Together they unsettle passivity. They treat perception not as something fixed or solitary, but as something shared and in motion. The audience is invited not only to watch, but to notice and to sense where attention settles, and where it drifts. In this space, seeing, listening, and feeling become forms of participation. Two Doors is inspired by an incident in New York City in 2021 in which doormen closed their doors just afer seeing an attack on an Asian woman outside their lobby. Through a choreographic study of the aftermath of violence, Two Doors explores the viscerality of anti-Asian racism and the sovereignty that we wrest for ourselves in response. Dancers experiment with closings and openings, weight sharing and weight bearing, playing with the kinetics of in/visibility, and Asian American model minoritization. Two Doors depicts a journey toward self-possession via relational vulnerability. Cycle, inspired by Professor Georgina Kleege's book More Than Meets the Eye, is built with language and sound as equal partners with the dance. Audio description does not trail behind the movement - it generates it. The result is a reorientation of how we watch dance, and an insistence that dance can be heard, felt, and imagined beyond the primacy of sight. Ticket Sales: Online ticket sales can be found at tickets.berkeley.edu (https://secure-tickets.berkeley.edu/29353) and end 2 hours before each performance. In-person ticket sales begin 1 hour before each performance at Zellerbach Playhouse. events.title: Lecture: Manuel Trummer, "Raving Heritage: Berlin Techno between Underground and UNESCO"
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description: The Folklore Program presents a lecture by Professor Manuel Trummer (Munich), "Raving Heritage: Berlin Techno between Underground and UNESCO."

events.title: Manuel Trummer, "Raving Heritage: Berlin Techno between Underground and UNESCO"
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description: In March 2024, the German Commission for UNESCO added Berlin's techno culture to the national inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage. For a music scene that emerged from the vacant spaces, squats, and legal grey zones of post-wall Berlin, official recognition is a complicated milestone. Professor Trummer will analyze why club collectives and activist networks deliberately pursued the UNESCO title and what happened once they got it. Rather than seeking state prestige, organizers mobilized the heritage campaign as an urban planning defense against commercial real estate pressures, soaring rents, and venue closures (Clubsterben). Yet reframing underground dance music as protected public heritage creates its own problems and new lines of conflict. Drawing on interviews with key scene actors, UNESCO policy debates, and a discourse analysis of the public media response to this unusual „cultural heritage", the talk examines the realities of this compromise. It asks whether intangible heritage status provides any real legal protection against eviction and noise complaints, or merely functions as cultural marketing for the city. It also looks at the internal tensions within the scene itself: how promoters, DJs, and ravers handle the contradiction between preserving an unruly, night-time counterculture and managing a state-sanctioned tradition. Finally, the case offers a broader perspective on the UNESCO framework today, pointing to how the heritage paradigm is shifting from regional crafts and rural folklore toward electronic, urban subcultures. Manuel Trummer is Professor and Chair of Empirical Cultural Studies and European Ethnology at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munich. Before that, he served as Managing Director of the Institute for Folklore Studies at the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, taught at the University of Regensburg as an Associate Professor (Privatdozent), held a visiting fellowship at Leeds Beckett University, and was an extraordinary member of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences. Trained in European ethnology, folklore, and art history in Regensburg, where he earned both his doctorate and habilitation, Manuel Trummer explores how communities make sense of transformation across past and post-digital worlds. His work bridges vernacular narrative traditions—reflected in his role as co-editor of Fabula – Journal of Folktale Studies—with the politics of everyday culture, particularly in rural contexts. He currently directs two major, government-funded research projects investigating infrastructures and heritage practices across peripheral rural landscapes, and serves on the German Commission for UNESCO's Expert Committee on Intangible Cultural Heritage. His recent publications on these topics include "Listed! And Now What? Negotiating Uncertainty and Intangible Cultural Heritage in Rural Areas" (2025) and "The Rural as a Cultural Category" (Das Ländliche als kulturelle Kategorie, 2020). Alongside his work on folklore and space, he has written extensively on popular culture, rock music, and religion in mass media, including the co-edited volumes "Pop the Nation!" (2023) and "Sympathy for the Devil?" (2014). Outside this work, he spends his time with heavy guitar music and vintage folk horror.

events.title: 2027 Sheng Yen Conference
events.description:
The scholastic traditions associated with Sarvāstivāda and the Abhidharma corpus more broadly were transmitted to China beginning in the fourth and fifth centuries and became a significant focus of translation activity under the direction of Xuanzang in the seventh century. Yet modern scholarship often assumes that Chinese Buddhist scholiasts had little sustained interest in, or use for, Abhidharma. According to this view, Abhidharma was dismissed as "Hīnayāna" and overshadowed by the rise of indigenous Chinese Buddhist traditions such as Chan, Tiantai, and Huayan. There is, however, ample evidence that Abhidharma continued to be studied and valued by Chinese exegetes irrespective of their doctrinal or school affiliation, and that it retained an important place in monastic curricula from the medieval period down to the present day. This conference seeks to reconsider the reception and enduring influence of Abhidharma in Chinese Buddhism.
Titles, Abstracts, and Bios (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/66-titles-abstracts-and-biospdf).Friday 2:30-5:30 pmAbhidharma Learning in China Chair: Alexander von Rospatt Eric Greene (Yale University): "Abhidharma Methodology in the First Era of Chinese Buddhist Scholasticism." Hou Xiaoming (Ghent University): "A Curriculum in Diagram: Dunhuang Path Charts and the Teaching of Abhidharma." Patrick Magoffin (Postdoctoral Fellow, UC Berkeley): "Interpreting and Teaching the Lengyan jing: A Conduit for Abhidharmic Learning and Textual Practices in the Song (960–1279)."Saturday 9:30 to 12:30 pmChinese Exegesis I Chair: Jacob Dalton Lu Huang (UC Berkeley): "Views of Pre-Xuanzang Abhidharma Masters as Preserved in the Jushe lun ji." Howard Mu (UC Berkeley): "Shentai's Interpretative Approach: Some General Features of the Jushe lunshu 俱舍論疏." Lin Xueni (University of Heidelberg): "A New Understanding of Dharmas: The Concept of shifa (實法) in the *Chengshilun yi shu 成實論義疏 (Dunhuang Pelliot 2335)."Saturday 2:00 to 5:00 pmChinese Exegesis II Chair: Lu Huang Wang Xingyi (Chinese University of Hong Kong): "Avijñaptirūpa in Abhidharma, Tattvasiddhi, and Its Rebirth in Yogācāra." Jackson Cole Macor (UC Berkeley): "Jizang's Critique of Abhidharma in the Sanlun xuanyi." Lin Qian (Qing Dao University): "Analysis of Mind in Zongjinglu: The Adoption of Abhidharma Methods in Chan Buddhism."Sunday 9:30 to 12:30 pmChinese Abhidharma Philosophy Chair: Robert Sharf Ernest Brewster (Austrian Academy of Sciences): "On the Nature and Existence of Cessation: Sinitic Analysis of Indic Intra-Abhidharma Debates." events.title: J. S. Bach's St. Matthew Passion
events.description: Sunday, February 21, 5pm Early Music: Opera & OratorioS. Bach'sSt. Matthew PassionMonteverdi ChoirEnglish Baroque SoloistsMasaaki Suzuki,conductor Cast to include:Nick Pritchard, tenor (Evangelist) Florian Störtz, bass (Jesus) Program: Bach/St. Matthew Passion Period-music ensembles the English Baroque Soloists and the Monteverdi Choir—the gold standard in Baroque performance for decades—join forces with conductor Masaaki Suzuki for Bach's crowning masterpiece during its 300th anniversary year. The powerfully dramatic St. Matthew Passion sets the 26th and 27th chapters of the Bible's Gospel of Matthew to music with interspersed chorales and arias, and is scored for massive forces: a double choir, double orchestra, and vocal soloists. Bach's transcendent oratorio conveys the story's intense human drama and moral dilemma, as recounted here by featured soloists Nick Pritchard as the Evangelist and Florian Störtz as Jesus. events.title: Talk and Film Screening: Disavowal as Belonging
events.description:
This talk expands on Gelare Khoshgozaran's ongoing explorations of exile as a generative space to form a resonant collectivity—one that embodies alienation, embraces the impossibility of return, and makes a home through the continuous negotiation of borders. Three short films by the artist invite viewers to rethink cinema as a space to find our kin and comrades in exile spatially defined through the politics of belonging and disavowal.
Gelare Khoshgozaran is an undisciplinary artist and filmmaker whose work engages with legacies of imperial violence manifested in war, militarization, and borders. They use film and video to form narratives that seek to redefine existing constructions of 'home' as a means of conceptualizing other forms of belonging. Born and raised in a city of four seasons, they are an assistant professor of art at UCLA School of Art and Architecture.

events.title: Genentech Lecture
events.description: Huw Davies, Asa Griggs Candler Professor, Harvard UniversitySite-selective and enantioselective C–H functionalization controlled by induced fitting and secondary noncovalent interactions A major challenge in organic synthesis is the selective functionalization of C–H bonds. As most organic compounds contain multiple C–H bonds with similar properties, distinguishing between them requires precise control. For some time, we have been using high symmetry chiral dirhodium catalysts to control C-H functionalization with donor acceptor carbenes. In this presentation we will highlight the design of our most recent high symmetry dirhodium catalysts (C4 symmetric and D4 symmetric) and illustrate the subtle site-selectivity exhibited by these catalysts. We will show how they can adopt many of the characteristics atypically associated with enzymes, leading to unprecedented site-selectivity of nonactivated C–H bonds. The catalysts adopt a bowl-shape on formation and the flexible microenvironment within the bowl causes an induced fitting to occur as the reagent and the substrate approach the catalyst. Recent synthetic application of this methodology to the synthesis of various chiral scaffolds will be described.

The revered 185-year-old orchestra and star conductor have enjoyed a close partnership over many years, a relationship finely honed through numerous tours and recordings. For these performances the focus is Mahler, a particularly important figure in the Philharmonic's history whose Ninth Symphony received its posthumous premiere by the orchestra in 1912. The composer's music is a perfect match for the towering institution, which will be joined by a selection of internationally acclaimed guest artists throughout the Berkeley residency. The first performance features Mahler's poignant final completed symphony, one of the most profound and emotionally complex works in the orchestral repertoire. The second night features both Mahler's Fourth Symphony, with Christiane Karg as soprano soloist, and Prokofiev's Concerto in C major, with superstar pianist Yuja Wang joining at the keyboard. In the final program, Mahler's Resurrection symphony takes the listener on a journey through earthly trials to ultimate transcendence, and features vocalists Christiane Karg and Elīna Garanča, and the San Francisco Symphony Chorus.
